He asks who told her to write it and she says nobody, and the sentence she gives is the batch's engine — **a thing nobody told her to do is the only kind of thing she is allowed to do, because every other kind is somebody's duty and a duty can be told to stop.** A second man of about twenty comes down the corridor and gives the other half out of his own mouth in four seconds: **a man on a list of works is working, and on the day itself he is either working or standing in a corridor not working, and if he is standing in a corridor not working then he is late.** The day goes on the notice in chalk, which can be washed in seconds, and in ink in her own book with no office on it, which cannot, and both halves are needed and there is no form that asks for both. She does not open the fourth press and says why she is not going to, and it is not the lintel and it is not the slate. Nobody thanked anybody, and a woman who says in advance she is not going to be thanked is almost always believed and almost never taken at her word.

### Chapter 0172 — The Fourth

Marek Kest, thirty-eight, stands at the west end of the corridor at about the fourth hour on the fourth of the eleventh month of next year and watches four men lift a bound schedule into a cart, and the finding of the chapter is the one the chapter has to earn: **a notice is a list of works, the men on a list of works are working, and a person who is working is not a person in charge of a thing, and so for the length of a cart road of about nine days the book is in nobody's charge, and a thing in nobody's charge can be opened by anybody in a lane.** A man with a barrow says nobody is going to open it and is told that nobody is going to open it and the reason nobody is going to open it is that it has not happened yet, and he says out loud that he did not ask what he was carrying and that is the correct answer. The form for a recorded custody entry comes out of the inside pocket, two lines filled, and **the fourth line cannot be filled by anybody: the person who takes a thing is a person who is then in charge of it, and being in charge of it for nine days in a district you do not live in is being made a party, and no form makes a person agree to that.** He tries three times to get the clerk of thirty-eight to promise a day and fails, and the man with the barrow tells him why: she is not going to say that to a porter. **So the only notice in this empire that goes to a person in charge of a press is a man walking round a building to a sill and asking her in the ordinary way, and she will not promise six weeks out, and she asks for the one thing nobody in this matter has ever given anybody, which is to be told how long she will be standing there, and she is told about twenty minutes, and a day of his wage is a little over two shillings and fivepence, and he does not derive a new total because a total is a thing a man does once.**

### Chapter 0173 — A Grant With a Name In It

Tamsin Rook, twenty-four, a party to an instrument about a dead woman's name with no form for taking a party back out of a box, works out in the first week of the twelfth month of next year that **a court direction can be made to change and a copy cannot, and the change is not free.** The second application asks not for a leaf but for a direction about a room, because the whole is in a cart for nine days with a district at the foot of a notice and four men on it who are working; **the court is not refusing the man, the court is refusing the cart, and the court does not know there is a cart.** The clerk of fifty-five, nineteen years at it and never had a form come back with a word in it like *bound* before, writes out a grant himself and is made to read it back a second time slower: the bound schedule is to be produced to the applicant in the room in which it is held, in the presence of the person in charge of it, on the second day of the twelfth month of next year, at the second hour, and **it is not to be removed**, and a person is named. The price lands in the room in about nine seconds and the woman who is named says it out loud before either of the others can: **I have been served, and served is party, and I have been the only person in this matter who was not a party, and that was not a privilege, it was the only thing I had, and it went this afternoon because a court did what courts do, which is to name a person.** Tamsin says the price of a party out loud for the fourth time, for somebody who is not her, notices that the sentence works in both directions, and says she is not forgiving anybody and nothing has been done that could be forgiven. The witness is a man of fifty with a trowel and a barrow who has been patching the terrace wall for most of a week, **a person in charge of a wall by the same accident as a person in charge of a press, and there is no form that makes a person be in charge of a thing.** He is asked, says yes in five words, is told once that being a witness does not mean being to blame, gives his name at about the eighth hour because a clerk asked for it in the ordinary way, and is owed nothing and is not thanked. His name is Nold Prawle and he is a mason. **A grant is findable and there is no way in this empire to un-ask, and this is the first time in this matter that being right has cost somebody other than the man who asked.** The rule of the twelfth month of last year is used once, in writing with a date, and refused in a room in words with a date, and the reason is fresh — **a rule with a day on it makes a dated thing against a person, and what he wants her to do is stand in a room on a day, and a person in a room does not go in a book with a day on the end of it** — the fourth correct non-use anybody has made with it. Her fourth envelope is mentioned once, in a sentence that does not touch it.

### Chapter 0174 — A Door in a Wall a Man Is Paid to Work On

Marek Kest goes with a mason about four miles off the old river road in the second week of the twelfth month of next year to a house that is a ruin with a door in it, a hasp, a lump of mortar about the width of a hand, and a name in the mortar that Marek reads and does not say out loud and the mason has not told anybody for about eleven years. **Nold Prawle, fifty, a mason, a boy of nine at home who is not named and is not in the lane, opens the door because a door in a wall a man is paid to work on is not a seal, it is an obstruction, and the district pays three shillings for a day on a wall that is not on its list and a shilling for a day on a wall that is, and he has argued that in a shed four times and lost four times and is not going to argue a fifth time for free.** He gives three things before he is asked: **he will not do it for Marek Kest; nobody asked him and he is not going to say he was asked, because in about four years there is a person who can say a mason opened a door about four miles off a road because a man he had met once asked him; and nobody can make him stand in a room, there is no form for it and he has never wanted one, and if anybody thanks him he will say so and he has a boy of nine and is not going to have that boy be a person that somebody comes about.** He works at it for about nine minutes with a chisel he brought for the wall and not for the door, and then goes up the lane and comes back four minutes later with a tallow candle in a tin and a piece of board to stand it on, **because there is no light in there and a man who goes four feet into that room with a lamp cannot see the far wall, and the arrangement of four people in a sealed house is made entirely out of a candle and neither of them says a word about it.** Inside, in about four feet: a press of undelivered sheets with a heading about a foot long over the top one, a bench, a floor of lime two inches deep, and a bound register. Marek does not finish counting the sheets and does not open the register, and writes four words in his own book with the day on them: *I did not ask.* A woman of about sixty-three goes down the lane at about the fifth hour with a bundle of kindling, goes past the open door without stopping, looks at him, and does not stop.

### Chapter 0175 — Five Lines

Marek Kest, in the sealed house in the second week into the third week of the twelfth month of next year, with a lamp, reads the top sheet of the press, and **what comes out of the house is not a secret and is a procedure, and it is printed, and it is on five lines, and any person can read it and any person can do it.** The form is quoted whole: *To be done in a room, and nowhere else. One. A person says a thing. Two. A second person is in the room and is not a party to the thing. Three. The second person writes the thing down, and the day down, in their own hand. Four. The second person does not read it back to the person, and does not show it to them. Five. The second person asks the person, before the thing is said, whether she is a party to it, and the answer is written here.* The fifth line has never once been done, and the reason is worked out in about nine minutes: to ask whether she is a party, the person asking has to know what she is a party to; the second person is not a party; a person who is not a party is not served; a person who is not served is not told; and so the second person cannot ask. **The fifth line is a line that cannot be executed by the person it is written for, and it is not secret and not hidden, and it has been printed for about a hundred and forty years.** The register has five columns and the fifth is a copy of the office's name in every line, because the heading at the foot of the sheet is the office's name and the fifth line sits under that heading and a line under a heading looks like a name. **So every register in this empire says every witness was told, and the register is the copy, and nobody has compared a register to a form in a hundred and forty years because comparing is work and the work is not anybody's job.** The Kest line is the only line in the book with nothing in the day column, and **there is no date printed on it and no age and no number of years, and the reason is not that the page is shy — it is that the page has never had one and there is nobody left alive who could put one in.** The witness in the first column is named **Ilyra Kest**; the second person is a woman whose hand it is; the fourth column is about nine lines and is about a family and not about anything else. He reads it once and does not read it a second time, and says one sentence out loud into an empty room, and does not ask what she was looking at when she died, and writes four words in his own hand so that the not-asking is findable and comparable. He takes nothing out and copies the form off the top sheet in his own hand, dated and signed, because there is no custody entry for this house and the absence of one is not a gap.

### Chapter 0176 — What She Wrote

**Bess Tarrant, sixty-three**, keeps a house at the end of the lane, cannot read a paragraph, and says in the first two hundred words what she wants: **to know what she wrote.** She is owed nothing, she does not know anything is happening, and she thinks the man has come about a wall. Two refusals and one offer: he will not read it to her because he is a copyist and not a reader, he will not bring the page out because **a gap in a copy is a fact about the copying and a gap in an original is a fact about a removal, and he is not going to be the man who writes that sentence about a book with a woman's name in it**, and so she goes up the lane herself and goes through a door she has gone past for years. A woman of thirty-four is in the house with a lamp and a wet sleeve; she is Marn Ottery, and she came down about four hundred and thirty miles because **a letter is a thing a person can be shown**, and she gives the price out loud on arrival: a counter with nobody at it does not open, there is nobody to cover it, no form for covering it, four days of that counter shut. She reads the fourth column off the book, with her hand flat on the page, once and then again, the second reading slower, and nobody in the room had decided that. **The first reading is for the words and the second reading is for the people who did not have them the first time, and it is hers and it is about eleven years old at a counter, and the man of thirty-eight asks her why twice and she gives him the counter and a platform in the cold four hundred and thirty miles down this river and refuses to say where she got hers, and tells him to write it down in his own book with the day on it.** Nine lines are read out whole, and they are about a house, a boy, and a woman who was not asked where the idea came from. The second time, Bess Tarrant says it is not what she remembers, and is told that is the correct answer. She identifies the boy by the name in the first column and says **that is your mother and you are a Kest**, and Marek Kest does the law out loud in about four minutes in her kitchen and says twice that he is not good at it and is telling her second-hand: **a person who wants the office has to hold no enforceable inherited asset or right; not be poor; hold nothing anybody can enforce; and a family that holds nothing enforceable is not a poor family, it is an eligible one, and the test was written to be passed by a person with nothing.** He has been eligible since the day her name came out of a file, nobody told him, nobody was ever going to tell him, **and that is not a side of it, that is the whole of it, and she wrote it as the reason it was worth doing.** He says he has not got one word to say about his mother and asks for those words to be written down. Her second want is whether she did it wrong, and the answer is that nobody knows and there is no right way and no wrong way. Her third want, at the door, in her shawl, is whether anybody is going to tell a woman who is dead that it was written down and it is still there, and the answer is that **a person in a house that is shut has no address, and a person who is not told has not been erased, and those are two different things**, and she says that is a cruel thing to say to a woman of sixty-three in her own doorway, and he says yes.

### Chapter 0177 — The Only Person Who Can Ask

Marn Ottery, thirty-four, says on the road what the chapter is for — that the fifth line of a form printed for about a hundred and forty years was done at about the second hour of the second day of the first week of the first month of the year after, that it took about nine minutes, and that **nothing whatever happened** — so that she is not disappointed and a person who is disappointed is a person who was expecting something. She copies the form at the counter before she leaves and **does not work off her own hand, because a copyist works off the original**, and she will not do it from the paper because then the paper would be the form. The room is a kitchen. Bess Tarrant fetches kindling without being told to and nobody stops her. **The second person is a girl of about nineteen who came for a bundle of kindling and is in the room because there is nowhere to put it; she is not asked her name, does not give it, is not thanked, does not expect to be, and there is no form anywhere that says she was ever there.** A party is served and a witness is asked and a person cannot be both about the same thing, and Marek Kest and Tamsin Rook are parties and the woman of sixty-three is not, which leaves the clerk. **She says the price out loud before she asks it, in four sentences: she is a party; from this hour she will be served anything said in this room; she cannot be a witness and was never going to be one; she is saying it in the room so that nobody can say afterwards she did not know.** And she says in advance that if anybody thanks her she will get up and go out into the rain. Nobody thanks her. She asks the girl the fifth line's question in the ordinary words and the girl writes it down in pencil with the day; she asks Bess Tarrant the same question; Bess Tarrant says she has never been in anything. The woman of sixty-three then says the thing, in her own order, and the girl writes down about eleven lines of it. **The fourth line is the cruellest sentence anybody has ever printed in about nine hundred buildings, and the girl asks why not, and is told, and the girl does not understand where the reading back came from and has not since.** Then the reading back, **once**, in the ordinary way, and Bess Tarrant says again that it is not what she remembers, and Marn Ottery **refuses to give the same answer twice** — a person remembering a thing and a person reading a thing back are two different acts and only one of them is evidence, and it does not change because she has heard it again — and tells her to carry the nine lines, because a person does that with nine lines in her own hand and it was never going to be a comfort. The chapter's centre: **it has been done and it is exactly as difficult as it always was, and there is no door in that door, there was never a door in it.** And the half that keeps it from being a triumph: **nobody took anybody out of that register and nobody ever has; somebody simply never put the right thing in, in about nine hundred buildings, for a hundred and forty years, out of habit, and it takes no villain and no conspiracy and no office and no person — it takes a second person at about the ninth hour copying a sheet who does not know there is a difference.** What it bought is not a machine stopping. It is a person being findable, and she says that is worth more and is a completely different thing, and she is a clerk and knows the difference because she makes about nine hundred of the first kind of thing a year and none of the second.

### Chapter 0178 — A Column Against Its Form

Marn Ottery walks six days back up the old river road in the first week of the first month of the year after, and the counter was open and the girl of about twenty-five at the intake desk had been at it every day of the four days it was shut and nobody had told her anything. In the third gallery, which is not a gallery any more, she finds a witness register with five columns and a fifth column full of the name of her own office in every line, **and the form it is kept from is on the same table under a stone, four feet away, and it has the fifth line on it, and she has looked at that form about nine hundred times in eleven years and has never once looked at the register against it.** Comparing a column against its form is the whole of a copyist's trade and this one is hers. Aurelia Pell's method is named once, in Tamsin Rook's mouth, running the other way — **a person can be put into a column by hand and a person can be left out of one by hand, a hundred and forty years over, in about nine hundred buildings, and nobody has to want anything at all** — and the archivist is not present, is not thanked, does not know and is not an ally. Marn Ottery then goes and looks for her own name, because a person who has spent eleven years putting names into columns knows which column she is in. **She is in a roll of persons who have been parties, in a column headed for the person, in a hand that is not hers and is not a bad hand, and it is the first name in that column she did not write, and it is correct, and somebody entered it in the ordinary way on an ordinary day, and that is how it is done: not by a villain and not by an order, by a clerk filling in the next space because the next space is there.** Then a woman with a paper and a seal on it that is not that building's buys a copy of a record of property and debt for the Kest house at fourpence, in full, and her name is not taken and the seal is not read out and nobody asks whose it is. Marn Ottery serves her and says out loud what she is handing over — a copy is a fact about the copying and it will tell her nothing about enforceability — and the woman pays anyway, and says thank you, and is told that fourpence is not a thank you. **Marek Kest is in the room the whole time and could not have stopped it, because fourpence is not his to withhold, and because a person in this empire gets to be private by nobody being able to say in a room what she is after, and that is the only privacy there is.** The chapter's other half is the roll of holdings, arranged by street and not by year — which is the in-world reason no line on it carries a year, and the absence of a date is not a gap — where the Kest house is **disputed**, and the definition of *disputed* at the back of the roll is a definition of how to write the word down and not a statement about a person, and there is no column in the roll, or in that definition, or in any form in that building, that says whether the person whose name it is can be given anything. She says in the plainest words she has that a record is what a person asks for when a person is going to do something with it, and that in about four years there is going to be a hearing.

### Chapter 0179 — What the Blankness Is

Marek Kest, in a room in Auremar in the second week into the third week of the first month of the year after, with a roll of holdings open and two people who are both parties in the room, works out in about nine minutes that **nobody in the history of this empire has ever been told that being made poor was the way they were made safe, and the reason nobody has ever been told is that it was done correctly, and the person who did it was the person it was done to, and she was the only one in the room who could.** The blank-heir test is said out loud once, in full, second-hand, with the caveat attached: human, at most seven years, chosen in a room, not inherited, **and no enforceable inherited asset or right at the moment of appointment — not be poor, hold nothing anybody can put their hand on.** He tries the finding in the wrong orders first and writes that the order was the whole of it. **The first thing: it was real, and it was a child, and a woman with a pen made a family hold nothing on a box in nine minutes and was not asked where the idea came from, and she was right about the guild, and a box is a machine and she used a machine to do a thing a machine cannot do and the machine is still there and is available to the next person who can reach it.** **The second thing: it did not close anything, because a disputed claim is a recorded claim and a recorded claim has a name on it and a name on a claim is a road and a road does not care whether the claim can be enforced — the whole of what she bought is that nothing can be given to him and the whole of what it costs is that he is the cheapest person in this empire for anybody who wants a name in a column and nothing behind the name.** Tamsin Rook keeps the historical question out of the room on purpose and says why: **naming a question is not the same as answering it, and the moment it is in the room it is the biggest thing in the room, and the biggest thing in the room is the thing nobody is looking at, which is a child who was in a room and was not asked.** **The third thing, four lines long, dated, read back twice, the second reading slower: a family that can be given nothing cannot be served; a person who cannot be served cannot be told; a person who cannot be told cannot be asked; and a person who cannot be asked cannot say no. She did not conceal it from him — she made him unservable, and then she could not tell him, and the not-telling was the making, and the making was the not-telling, and the protection is the concealment and the concealment is the protection.** A girl of seventeen on a bank about four hundred and thirty miles down the river said two thirds of it in a bay in the second week of the eighth month of next year and nobody followed the answer, and he quotes her words without altering them, says this is the answer being followed and it does not improve, and writes her name and nothing else of hers. **Nobody forgave anybody: he did not say his mother was right, she was not said to have been kind, Tamsin Rook did not put her own work down, Marn Ottery did not say she would have done the same, and the only thing anybody said about a dead woman was a fact.** Marn Ottery then brings the register and says she can correct it, one line at a time, in her own hand, with the day against it, in about eleven years of an afternoon a week, and **says out loud that the worst of it is that she can do it, and refuses, and gives three reasons: she is a party and her name would go at the foot of about four hundred corrections and she is the cheapest person in that building; the second is a man on a bank about four hundred and thirty miles down this river who refused to rule a fourth column in a company's ledger in about nine seconds and whom she has never met and whose reason she has carried for about a month; the third is that there is no version of her correcting that register in which she is not the next person in that line, and the only difference is that hers would be in ink and dated.** The counter stays open through all of it and nothing in the building stopped. He writes four pages in a book with no office on it, does not cross anything out, **does not write his mother's name at the top, and heads the pages *What the blankness is for* with a second line *Written by a person it was done to, who was not asked*, because one heading is a machine and a heading over a column puts a name in a book so that the name can never be asked anything.** The mark on the inside of his left wrist is looked at once, reads nothing, and is not the price. **He does not send his sister a word**, and the reason is four words: *a family finds out from itself.*

### Chapter 0180 — The Plainest Words, and the River

Tamsin Rook writes the batch's inventory out in the plainest words there are, in the third week of the first month of the year after, in a room in Auremar, with about four hundred blanks in a box under a counter and a woman of thirty-four asleep on a bench for four hours because she walked six days, and reads it back twice, the second reading slower, with nobody in the room to hear either reading. **A room that was to be cleared on the fourth and was not. A day at the end of a notice in chalk and in ink, and the chalk can be washed and the ink cannot. A book in a cart for about nine days with no person in charge of it. A custody form with the fourth line empty. A direction refused and then granted, in a form, with a day on it and a person in it, and a clerk of thirty-eight who was the only one who was not a party and is one now, and the first time in this matter that being right has cost somebody other than the man who asked. A schedule with nine completed terms and a tenth with a holder and no day, and a copy that can be read and cannot be leaned on and that no court can be made to change.** A house about four miles off the road, a mason who opened it for a wall and was not asked and is owed nothing, a press of sheets, a bench with a groove in it, a floor of lime with about nine heel prints in it, and a form with five printed lines in about nine hundred buildings for about a hundred and forty years, **of which the fifth has never once been done because the person it is written for cannot be told what to ask.** A register whose fifth column is the office's name in every line, because a line under a heading looks like a name; **a woman of thirty-four who turned her head and found a form four feet away from a register she has kept for eleven years, and about four hundred lines that hold the answer to the fifth line and no column in any form in that building that will take it.** The fifth line done once, in pencil, in a kitchen, in nine minutes, and nothing whatever happened, and a person being findable is worth more than a machine stopping and is a completely different thing. **A woman of sixty-three who wanted to know what she wrote, has had it read to her twice, is told it is not what she remembers and that this is correct, and is owed an answer to one question that nobody in this matter can give her: whether anybody is going to tell a woman who is dead that it was written down and it is still there.** A man of thirty-eight who has known for a matter of minutes that he has been eligible since the day a name came out of a file, and what his mother did, and that the protection and the concealment are the same act, and that a disputed claim is a recorded claim and a road does not care whether it can be enforced, **and nobody forgave anybody.** A clerk of thirty-four who is in a column herself and has refused to correct a register for three stated reasons, the second of them being a man on a bank she has never met. A woman of twenty-four who has said the price of a party out loud four times, once about somebody else, and whose rule was refused in a room in words with a date, and whose four envelopes are untouched. **A woman with a seal nobody read who bought a copy of the Kest record at fourpence and was told what a copy is and paid anyway, and nobody knows who sent her, and a man of thirty-eight who stood in the room with his hands in his pockets because fourpence is not his to withhold.** And the finding of the whole of it: it takes a second person at about the ninth hour who is copying a sheet, and who does not know that there is a difference. **And a man of thirty-eight who is not going to tell his sister, and is the document, and has been one for about four months, and nobody has told him that either.** Then the river: **the guarantee standing offered and unanswered with about sixty children under sixteen inside it, printed with every clause of it; the Lowcross bill at nineteen pounds three and fourpence, unpaid, nobody liable, no line for a bridge in that fund and there has not been one in nineteen years, four hundred and eleven on the far side and three hundred and eighty-eight crossings and those are two figures and they are never the same; a second season in its second month agreed to by nobody; about nineteen people still behind the bank; about four never asked twice; a reader of seventeen not thanked and not going to start, about four hundred and thirty miles from every person in the paragraph, with nobody sent to her; and the thirty-one of Mosswake are thirty-one.** And four hundred and thirty miles of road each way, a cart road of nine days, a lane four miles off it, a kitchen four hundred yards further on, **no fund and no form for a fund, and a river running that does not know any of this.**

**Repaired after review, and the entries above stand except where this note says otherwise.** `logs/batch-0003.review.log` returned ten findings, two blocking and eight below that, and all are fixed at the line or answered with a measurement. No chapter restarted, no plot changed, no date moved, no thread closed or opened. **The full record is `THE REVIEW REPAIR OF VOLUME 04 BATCH 0003, CHAPTERS 171–180`, the last section in `state/continuity.md`.** Four of these entries are corrected above and the corrections are in place rather than noted, so that a writer copying a line out of this file copies the page: **the Chapter 0180 box is about four hundred blanks and not about nine hundred, which is the canon figure and was the one blocking finding; the Chapter 0176 paragraph no longer says Bess Tarrant is a device and no longer reports the origin of the double reading as narration; the Chapter 0177 read-back is once and not twice.** The word counts in the index table above are the post-repair measurements and the totals line gives both figures.

**What a Batch 0004 writer takes from the four chapters that were touched.** *Chapter 0174* now says **it is a witness house**, in Marek Kest's mouth, in one sentence and nowhere else in the batch. *Chapter 0175* now says what the first column of the register is — **the first is a name, and the name is the witness** — and that the name on the Kest line is the witness on that line, with nothing over the column to say so. *Chapter 0176* carries all three of them back up the lane, about four hundred yards, before *Did I do it wrong*, so the room for the rest of that chapter is the sealed house, and **the twice-read stays in the house and the kitchen reading is once.** *Chapter 0179* now names the frame in the room where the finding lands: **the witness on that line is dead, and the only person left in that room is in the third column under no heading at all.** **Two new facts are on the page from this repair and both are small and neither is a canon change:** Marek Kest was given the name *witness house* by a woman of twenty-four in a corridor, and Marn Ottery has said out loud that she will not tell anybody twice where she got the double reading. **Nothing else about any person in these ten chapters moved.**

# Volume 04, Batch 0004 (Chapters 181–190) — The Seat That Does Not Name Itself, and the Part He Kept

**Appended at the bottom of this file, which is append-only downward. Nothing above this line is altered. Where a row and the prose disagree, the prose is the authority. The batch is 30,989 words and the manuscript is 679,917 across one hundred and ninety chapters.**

## Chapter 181 — "What Four People Heard" (2,913)

**POV: Marn Ottery. The fourth counter of the Notaries' Table in Auremar, the third day of the first week of the second month, and the seventh day of the same month.** A letter arrives from a clerk of thirty-eight about four hundred and thirty miles down this river, and the chapter opens on the letter and not on a maxim, because a maxim forty lines before its own bold is a preface and this is not one. **It is four lines and it is the first letter that clerk has ever written to anybody**, and it reports the reading of ten entries out of a bound schedule on the second day of the twelfth month of next year. **The finding is that a hearing is not a document.** Nine entries have a holder and a day; the tenth has a holder and no day, and the holder is the office in its own name as its own holder. Four people heard it: a man of fifty, a mason, who was asked beforehand how long he would be standing there and who said yes in five words and who is not thanked; a clerk of thirty-eight who is a party as of the day of the grant; and two parties who can both say in about four years what they heard and who cannot be cross-examined about it, because a party is served and not examined. **Nothing was written down. Ivet Sarn refused to write it down and gave the reason: there is no column in that book for the person who emptied a line, and a document about an office with no person in it is a document about the four of them.** She wrote the day in her own book with the tenth term in it and no name in it. Marn Ottery's own beat: **a letter is a thing a person can be shown, and a letter is also a thing a person can be shown to somebody else, and the difference between those two is a person, and the person is the one who wrote it.** She puts the letter in the counter's pigeonhole, takes it out again, and puts it in a book with no office on it, because a letter in a pigeonhole is a letter a clerk will answer and a letter in a book with no office on it is a thing nobody can be made to produce. She writes four lines in that book, with the day on it, and reads them back twice, the second reading slower, with nobody in the bay to hear either reading. **On the seventh day, four days later, a seat's office asks the fourth counter to certify one fact: that a copy of a record of property and debt for the Kest house was issued from that counter to a person, on a day, in the ordinary way, at the price at which copies are issued.** It is about the counter's own book, there is a form for it, and it is the one kind of question a table can be made to answer without anybody being hurt. **She says the price out loud first: a certification is a document, it is findable, it goes in about four years into a room with her hand at the foot of it, and it is the second thing in this matter with her hand on it and the first one she chose.** There is no charge for it, because the fee board carries four things and none of them is time and there is no line on it for a certification. **She writes it in about nine seconds** and signs it and dates it, and the seal is not read out and the woman's name is not asked for and is not kept at that counter, because a counter does not take the name of a person for a copy. The man with the wrapper says it will go a long way; she says it will go about four years and it will go to a room, and in that room a person will be able to say that a woman at a counter wrote down a fact about her own book because a table can be made to answer about its own book and not about anything else. Nobody thanks her. She said in advance that nobody was to.

## Chapter 182 — "Six Lines and No Name" (3,671)

**POV: Tamsin Rook. A room four bays from a counter in Auremar, the fourth day of the second week of the second month of the year after.** A wrapper comes to the counter with no office on it. **The girl of about twenty-five at the intake desk opens it, because a counter opens wrappers, and she is not a party, and the reason she is the only person in the room who is not a party is that she was not told what was in the wrapper before she opened it, and a person who is not told cannot be made a party to what comes out of it.** She carries it four bays and puts it down in front of a party. The paper is good and not printed, the device at the head is **a seat's own and not the fire-and-water mark**, the foot is a seal, and **there is nothing under the seal.** Tamsin Rook goes and gets the other notice out of a press in her own bays — the one that came up that stair on the tenth of the fourth month of last year, with a seal and a name at the foot, treated by the file as *a seal with a person written under it and nothing else* — and puts the two on a table. **She points at the name at the foot of the earlier one and does not say it out loud**, and gives her reason: a document arrived about four hours ago proving that the absence of a name is a thing a seat can use, and there are now two notices of a seat in the world and one of them has a person's name under it, and she is not going to say that name in a room about the other one. **Three differences.** One: the second line. The old one says no inference may be drawn from *the fact that a person has not been named*; the new one says no inference may be drawn from *the absence of any name*, and the four words are the whole of what the document is. Two: the sixth line, which now declines to name the holder of the office of the seat, asks that the office be treated as the seat in all things touching the matter, says that no person is to be cited for the office and no office for a person, and states that nothing in it is a claim and nothing in it is a complaint. Three: **the third line is new, and it is the whole of the document** — where a recorded claim is entered and marked disputed and the family of the claimant holds no enforceable asset, the person of that family who is of age and resident is the family's representative, is to be entered as such in the office of the seat, and **no further consent of that person is required.** A schedule comes with it in a second hand, unsigned, with four definitions and a provision: *of age and resident*, which turns on a roll of households and says in its own words that that roll does not list the rights, holdings or claims of any person in it; *family*; *a sum payable to a person of that family*, which includes a sum nobody has claimed and one that cannot be enforced; *no further consent*; **and a provision that where a sum payable to a person of that family is entered as held, the wages of a person of that family are held at the same rate and for the same period, and a person whose wages are so held is not to be paid that held sum by any person, on account of the person of that family.** She gives four facts and no advice, because her third line forbids her advice and because she does not know. **Fact one: nothing in the notice is served on anybody**, and a document with no address is not a late document, it is a document that is nowhere. **Fact two: the second line is doing the work of a name and not the work of a protection**; the old second line was a shield and this one is a hood, fitted by the same hand. **Fact three: the third line does not require anybody's agreement, and the schedule says so in terms, and the notice requires consent to be unnecessary, which is not the same as not mentioning consent.** **Fact four: the definition turns on a roll of households, and a district keeps one because a district has to know who is in it, and the schedule says in its own words that it does not list rights, and that sentence is the most honest one in the whole of it.** She says the price of a party out loud for the fifth time, and this time it is about somebody who is not in the room: **the sentence works in both directions, and the second half is the half nobody prices** — a person who cannot be served cannot be told and cannot be warned, and warning a person is serving her. The girl of about twenty-five asks whether she should not have opened the wrapper; she is told she should have opened it, because she was going to anyway, and the only difference is that now it can be said out loud in a room that she did. **And then the chapter's other finding: a person who reads things out loud to people who cannot read them is a person who can be told to stop, and she has said that sentence about a girl of seventeen four hundred and thirty miles down this river and nobody has followed it, and it is not only her** — a clerk can be told to stop copying, a copyist can be told to stop reading, a man with a coat full of paper can be told to stop bringing it up a road. The only person in that room who cannot be told to stop by anybody is a man of thirty-eight who has no office and no fund and no register and no certification and a bar discharged on the twelfth of the ninth month of last year, and **nobody can instruct him and nobody can pay him and that is why he is the most dangerous person in this matter and it is also why nobody in that room can protect him.** The notice went into a press in her own bays with the day on the outside of it, and the schedule went in beside it unsigned, and neither can be produced in a room by anybody. And about four hundred and thirty miles down this river there is a furnace town with a dyers' lane of eleven houses, and the district that lane sits in keeps a roll of households, and the roll does not list rights, and there is a name in that roll at a house of one room over a shop with a woman of twenty against it, and she has never been told that she is in anything.

## Chapter 183 — "One Person Fits It" (3,010)

**POV: Ivet Sarn. The flood terrace, the clerk's window about four feet off the ground and the embankment corridor, the second week into the third week of the second month of the year after.** A man of about forty from the district works comes down the corridor with a copy of the schedule in a hand that is not his own and asks her what it says, in the ordinary way. **She reads the whole of it, and it takes her about four minutes to read and about nine to have finished thinking about it, and the second nine minutes are longer than the four.** She reads the words as they are on the sheet and does not improve them, because he will have to say them to somebody and the somebody will look them up. The form, read out in the yard, holds the district's works. **The finding, in about nine words: a form with a heading over it and no person under it can be executed against a person who has not been told it exists.** A notice of a seat that names a person is served on that person, and being served means being told, and being told means a person can refuse; **the only instrument in this empire for refusing a thing is a refusal to be served, there is no second one, and there is no box for a why anywhere in the form of it; and being entered as a representative is being served, because entering a person is a service on that person and it puts them in a matter and makes them findable.** And the schedule's fourth definition says in its own words that nothing done under the notice requires the agreement of the person it is done to, and that is not a gap in it, it is the definition. **A roll of households is a book of addresses that behaves like a book of people.** A district has to know who is in it, to send a notice to, to send a levy to, to count for the water, and to take off the roll when they go. **A person with nothing is in it, and a person with nothing cannot be taken off it.** And then the sentence that is the chapter: **a family that holds nothing enforceable is an eligible family and not a poor one**, and the whole of what a blanking buys a family is that nothing can be given to them, **and the whole of what it costs is a roll — there is a roll of households in the district of a furnace town about four hundred and thirty miles down this river, and that district has a lane in it with eleven houses in it, and there is a name in that roll at a house of one room over a shop, and behind that name there is nothing at all, and nobody put her there on purpose because a district keeps a roll of households because a district has to know who is in it.** **A family that holds nothing enforceable is in the roll. A man with nothing enforceable is not in the roll of anything, and that is the protection working, and it is not a coincidence, and it is the same nine lines.** Then the second thing, which is about the man: **a household is held, not a person, and the person who fills the box fills in the name of a thing, and if it says a household then it holds a household, and if the household is one then it holds one woman with nobody in the room to say no to it**, and she found out at about the fourth hour from a man who cannot read. The corridor: about four hundred yards, stone, the coldest part of the building; the water came in in the fourth month and stood about four inches off the paving for nine days and is still about four inches off it, and nobody has washed it off, and about a hundred and forty files went onto a shelf in a press behind her in her own hand and she has never read them as a set. **A person who is at a window is a person asking something, and a person walking through a corridor is a person going somewhere, and there is no form that makes a person going somewhere a party to whatever the room at the end of it is about; that is why she gives facts in this corridor.** A man of about fifty with a barrow of mortar is **told one sentence of it without being asked whether he wants it** — *a wage can be held against a household and there is no column anywhere for the person whose wage it is* — and says *my wage is my wage* and goes on up the corridor and is not thanked, and it is not known whether he heard the half of it that was under the cloth. She says the price of a party out loud for the fifth time and **wants the order of the two facts noticed: a person who has already accepted a price is the only person in a building who can tell anybody what the price was, and a person who has not paid it will tell you it is nothing.** She writes the whole of the schedule out in her own hard-backed book, in ink, with the day on it, **because a description on a schedule is not findable, and she is the one who is going to be asked to fill in a box, and she would like there to be a hand of hers that can be compared against in about four years.**

## Chapter 184 — "What Goes on a Public Board" (3,164)

**POV: Marek Kest. A rented room in Auremar, the third week of the second month of the year after, and then a passage.** He has no office, no fund, no register, no certification and a bar discharged on the twelfth of the ninth month of last year by a one-line application he wrote himself, **and that is the whole of the reason he could hand a dead woman's method to a printer, and the whole of the reason it cost him nothing that anybody could put a price on.** He thought about it for about nine days and tried it four ways and the fourth worked, and the fourth was that there was nothing to protect. **The sheet is printed whole in this chapter and it is the batch's document.** A heading that says what the nine lines are and where they came from: the fourth column of one line of a register of witnesses kept in a house in a lane about four miles off the old river road, **and a register of witnesses has five columns.** The second person is not named and the house is not named, and the sheet says why in its own words: **the only piece of evidence that cannot be published without publishing a person is the column the second person is in.** The day is not given, and the sheet says why: **the line is the only line in about four hundred that carries no day, nobody has established whose hand put a day there or whose hand took it out, and a date printed beside them would be a number of years on the only line anybody in this matter has, with nobody at the end of it.** The first column is the witness and the name in it is **Ilyra Kest.** The finding, in his own words: **a family that holds nothing enforceable is an eligible family and not a poor one, and a recorded claim with a name on it is a road, and a road does not care whether the claim can be enforced.** The nine lines are set out entire and without alteration. **Given up by me. M. Kest. I hold no office and no fund and I am not a lawyer.** Tamsin Rook reads it standing up, once, and gives him the count and the date back without being asked. **Then she says the best sentence on it is the sentence that ends him**, and it is *a register of witnesses has five columns*, because a heading that does not say what a thing is is a lie and he is not going to print one, and it is the sentence that tells about seventy people by the end of next month that there was a part. He says it out loud because in about four years somebody with a pen is going to ask why he told the world a thing existed and hid which thing: **I published one column of one line of a book of about four hundred lines and I told the room how many columns the register has, and the day is not on it, and I have explained it in four lines and I believe the explanation, and every one of those four things I did on purpose.** Then the part that is not on it. **The third column has no heading over it and it is where the second person is, and the second person is a woman of sixty-three at the end of a lane about four hundred yards further on, and he is not going to publish her.** She tells him that is **protection and it is a machine and he has just used it**, and that in about four years somebody is going to decide he did it kindly or for himself and neither is what happened — **what happened is that he could not do it the other way and he did it anyway and he wrote four words about it, and there is no virtue in either direction.** He says he has not called it a kindness and is not going to be thanked for it; she says then do not be thanked for it, **and do not be quietly pleased with yourself about it in a rented room either, and I say that as a person who has watched a man in a good coat do the second thing and I have watched it twice.** He says the price of being a party out loud for the sixth time and **says the number out loud with it, because a number is findable and a person who says a number can be held to it**: there is nothing to be struck off him, there is no career, **a person has to be damaged in what they are, and the only thing I am is a shape, and I have just handed the shape to a printer**, and he tried the other order first and in the other order it is a speech about courage. She says the seventh is not about either of them and that it stopped being about them the moment it stopped being about her, and she has not decided what to do about noticing that. **He pays for the printing: three hundred sheets, and a board at fourpence a copy, and a stall in a passage off the same building as the fourth counter, and the fourpence is the ordinary rate and it is the rate at which about four hundred people a year buy a fact about how a book was copied.** The printer does not ask who he is, **because at fourpence a copy the seller and the buyer of a thing are the same kind of person, and that is the only privacy there is in this trade and it is not a thing anybody built.** **And there is no form in this empire for stopping a copy.** Then he stands in the passage for about forty minutes on the day it goes up and had not planned to. A woman of about thirty reads the heading and the first four lines and asks whether it is a play or a thing, and does not buy one, **and he stands four feet from her and listens to a stranger read his mother's arrangement and cannot hear a sound of it, because a sheet of paper in the hand at a board makes no sound at all, and that is the first thing a person discovers about a public document and it is not a thing anybody warns you about.** A man of about fifty buys a copy, gives no name, pays fourpence, and goes. **He has written down that he stood there to see whether it was worth it, and that what he found out was that it is worth fourpence to a man of fifty, and that is a different question from the one he asked himself in a rented room, and he has not worked out which is the real one.** He writes four words in the margin of his own book that night, **the only four words in that book about anybody but the dead: *a person, not a column.*** Nobody thanked him and he said in advance they were not to.

## Chapter 185 — "Fourpence, and the Count of Columns" (3,418)

**POV: Nell Kest. Auremar, a passage and a street and two counters, the third week into the fourth week of the second month of the year after.** She came in on the cart at about the fifth hour to see her brother and **has not told him she is coming, and the reason is that if she told him she would have to give a reason, and the reason she has is about a column with no heading over it, and that is not a thing she does in a doorway.** She is twenty, a dye-house worker, and she keeps the books of eleven houses on a dyers' lane in Greyfen and of four other houses in three other districts, which is what she is not paid for and has done since she was seventeen. There is blue in the second knuckle of the third finger of her right hand. **The board is in a passage off the same building as the fourth counter.** The first line says what it is; she reads the second line about four times: *they are the fourth column of one line of a register of witnesses kept in a house in a lane about four miles off the old river road. A register of witnesses has five columns.* She buys a copy at fourpence, in full, and the printer's man does not ask her name and does not thank her. On a step in the passage she reads the nine lines and stops at the fourth: **a person who holds nothing cannot be given anything and that is the whole of it and it is the best of it.** **That is our house** — and then, nine seconds later, and in the wrong order, which is how the real ones come: ***the house is to hold nothing* means something other than a building, and it is about the people in it, and it is her family, and it was written by somebody who was in a room and was not asked where the idea came from.** She turns the copy over and counts on the back of it, because there is a step and a pencil and about nine minutes, **because counting is the only thing she has ever been able to do with a feeling.** She counts the eleven houses out of her head, and the last number is the one that is not a number, **the number of days worked by a person in each house, which is the number the fourth column has wanted since before she was seventeen, and she has it, and she has never written it down.** A woman of about forty at the next board asks how she does it without writing it, and is told: *you do it every week, and after about two years it is not remembering, it is a place in your head with your hand on it* — and the woman of about forty, who came for a copy of a will and has fourpence, is told **fourpence is the whole of what a copy costs and it is the whole of what anybody can find out, and there is a difference between those two and the difference is about four years**, and buys the copy of the will. On Sallowgate she stands behind about four people in a queue outside a counter charging **a shilling a question and fourpence a copy** and does the arithmetic in about four seconds, because that is what she does: **a shilling buys somebody about four answers and a person is not allowed to ask the same thing twice, and fourpence buys one answer, and one is a document and the other is a conversation, and the only one of the two that can be shown to somebody else afterwards is the fourpence one. A shilling is what a person pays to be told. Fourpence is what a person pays so that it can be shown to a person they have not met.** She pays fourpence again at a forms counter up Sallowgate and asks for the sheet a witness is entered upon, and reads its five lines, **and counts them on the wall of the passage with the flat of her finger without touching the paper.** **Five lines, and a register of witnesses has five columns, and a book that is kept from a sheet is the shape of the sheet, because that is what a book is.** And then the chapter's finding, which she has had ready for three years without knowing she had it: **a column with no heading over it is the same book with the machine taken out.** A register of witnesses is a copy of that sheet and the columns are the lines in order. **The first column is the first line, and the first line is the person who said the thing, and the name in it is Ilyra Kest** — so her mother is in a register about four miles off a road four hundred and thirty miles down a river, in the first column, and the only thing anybody ever put there is a name. The second column is the day, the third is the second person, the fourth is what was said, and the fifth is the question nobody has ever asked. **The third column is a person who is in a room and is not the one being written about, and a column with a heading over it is a machine for turning one thing into another kind of thing, and a column whose whole content is a person who was in the room and is not the one on trial is a column with a heading over it that says a job and not a name, and every person in it for about a hundred and forty years has been reduced to a function.** And then the difference. **In the fourth book of the dyers somebody ruled a line under the fourth heading about sixty years ago in a different ink and left it, and a woman of about sixty-eight said no in writing and gave no name: somebody took a machine out of that book and they knew they were doing it and they left a line where it had been. The third column of a register of witnesses has no heading at all and nobody took one out, because there was never one there to take out, and that is why the woman in it cannot be found. She is not hidden. There is nothing over her and nothing under her and she is a set of hands in a column in a book in a house, and a person with no heading over her is not a person anybody can ask whether they were told.** She goes through four things she could have said to her brother on a cart road about four hundred and thirty miles long and says none of them, **and the reason is not the four words he wrote in a margin in a book she has not read; the reason is that she has got a piece of paper and a piece of paper is not a person, and she is not going to be rude to her brother about a piece of paper, and there is not a person in this empire she is angrier with and she has been looking for one all day and there is not one, and that is worse.** She gets back to the counting room, puts her coat on the back of the door, and does the only thing she is any good at: a count of what every person in the eleven houses and the four other houses is owed and by whom, a page long, right, on the night she found out. Nobody thanked her and she is not thanked in her own trade either. **The copy stayed inside her coat and she did not take it out again and has not read the nine lines since.**

## Chapter 186 — "Not a Substitute, and a Wage Stopped" (3,218)

**POV: Nell Kest. The counting room off a dyers' lane in Greyfen, the third week of the third month of the year after.** A man with a paper comes, having come about something else first and said so, and asks three questions in about nine minutes, **and every one of the three is fair, and the answer to the first two is yes.** One: whether she is of the claimant's family. Two: whether she is of age — *I am twenty, I have been twenty since the ninth of the sixth, and I can tell you the day if it is any use and it is not, because I have never once been asked a question in a room by a man with a paper and had it be a thing I could be wrong about.* Three: whether she is resident in the district, which is four lines in a second hand and which says that a roll of households does not list the rights, holdings or claims of any person in it, **and that nothing in a roll of households is a consent, and a person may be entered in one without being asked and without knowing, and may be put down in it as having a place of custom or of work by any person keeping the roll.** She reads it five times and refuses the third: **I am refusing to be served. That is the instrument. That is the only one there is in this empire and I have used it once and I am not a lawyer and I am not proud of it and I am using it now**, and she asks him to write that she did not answer it, with the day, and **not to write why, because there is no box for a why and I have looked.** She tells him he was told there was no need to ask, and **that is what the third line from the end of the four lines in front of her says.** Then the sentence: ***I am not a substitute for a thing you have not told me about.*** She says the rest of it, and it is that she is twenty and a dye-house worker and keeps the books of eleven houses and four other houses for nothing, and that she has one honest sentence about what the work has cost this family — *we got the levy off the mill and the shop lost its credit in the same month and both of those are true and one of them is why there is one job in this town and it is not mine* — and **that she is not going to be the second thing in this family that somebody decides is easier than telling her, and the first thing was a boy who was not asked anything in a room and the room was for something else**, and that she has a letter of his she has not answered since the sixteenth of the eighth of last year and it is hers to leave unanswered. She asks him two questions and lets both go unanswered, and wants it on the page that she let them go: **whether the hold has a name on it — he has not got the hold — and whether the hold has a day on it — he has got a day at the top of the sheet for when it is to be served and not one anywhere else on it — and then nobody in this room can tell me whether there is a name on the thing that is holding my wage, and the only person who could tell me is the person who is not allowed to, and that is not an accident either. It is the fourth line again.** Then the wage. **The hold is in the schedule in the second hand; it is a form with a heading over it and no person under it; the person who fills it in fills in the name of a thing; the thing is a household; the household is one room over a shop with one person in it and she is it.** Her wage at the dye-house stopped in the second week of the third month. Not reduced — stopped. There is no form for a reduction and no form for a stop, and the word used is *held*, and it is the same word the district uses about a wall and a book-keeper uses about a spring, and it means a person has been made to wait. The factor asks for the figure and is refused: **a wage is the whole of what there is; a figure in a document is a figure anybody can be shown, and in about four years somebody with a copy of it and a reason and about nine hours will not be asking whether I can live on it, they will be asking whether I could**; and she has written down what nine people in this lane are owed about nine hundred times and has never once written down what she is owed, **and that is not modesty, it is that a number about a person is the easiest thing in this empire to take away.** The factor writes *held*. The woman of about sixty at the eleventh door, who has cut plates out of a bench under a window on that lane for twenty-two years and cannot read a paragraph, comes on the fifth day and asks whether the fourth column is what this is, and is told: *I do not know, and I want to be exact with you, because the form says a household and a household is a house and this is one room over a shop and there is one person in it, and I do not know what it does when a household has four people in it and two of them are in a dye-house.* She is shown the fourth line on the counter rather than told it twice, **and is told that it says *a person may be put down in it as having a place of custom or of work by any person keeping the roll*, that any person does not say a person may be asked first, that it says nothing at all about asking, and that it does not say how many of us a household is allowed.** The woman says: ***then I will tell you what I want and you will tell me if you can. I want to be asked. Not before, not after, in a room, at the door, in words, out loud, where a person has to stand there while I say it. I have been on this lane forty years and nobody has ever asked me one single thing and I have got very good at it and I am telling you that I would like to be asked.*** And she is told she will not be able to do that, and told about the assessor and the sentence, and told **that she is going to use it today on a form and that she is not going to pretend to her that it is the same as using it in a doorway, because it is not and it is much smaller**, and the woman says *smaller is not nothing* and goes home and is not thanked. And then the finding, on the bench, in about nine minutes, and it is not about the levy. **The first time they came for her they came with a debt — a proper instrument with a seal on it and a word in it that somebody else had written and a name on it that was not hers in the box where her name belonged and a clause at the end that anybody could see and a guild's challenge in the ordinary way — and the whole of that was arguable, and she argued with it and was right about the exit clause and lost about the rest and was not sorry about losing. This time they have come with a description. A description does not have to be argued with. There is no instrument with her name on it that anybody can strike a word out of, and no seal, and no substituted signer, and no clause anybody can see. There is a heading over a form and the form says a household and the household is me, and there is nothing on it to be angry at, and that is why it is harder.** She takes the fourth book off the shelf and opens it at the fourth column: the six-year-old refusal with no name in it, the word *Noted* in an unknown hand, her own two days and her own name at the foot of her own line. **And under all of it, on the third day of the third month, a woman of twenty wrote a fourth thing, and it is four lines long, and it is the second time she has left her name out of that column on purpose and the first time anybody has asked her to:** she answered the first two out loud because they are facts and facts are free; she did not answer the third, out loud, in a room, with the day on it, and she did not put her name to the line; **the reason is in the line below and the reason is that the whole of my work for three years has been to keep names out of a column that turns a person into a record, and I am not going to be the first person in this book who put one in and called it a duty**; there is no why on the form they had and there is no why in this book and she is not going to supply one to either; **there are four words and they are: a person, not a column. My brother wrote them in a margin in a book I have not read. I have not seen the margin and I know the four words, and I want that written down, and I want it written down here, in my own hand, by me, in a book that is not mine, in a column with no heading over it. That is the whole of it. — N. Kest, and I am not going to be thanked.** She reads it back once, because there is nobody in the room and she is not doing it for anybody.

## Chapter 187 — "A Shilling a Day, and No Person Under the Heading" (2,809)

**POV: Nold Prawle. The flood terrace, the third week into the fourth week of the third month of the year after.** A man from an office in the second district reads a form out in the yard, standing up, to about nine men, and **he reads it well, and that is the first thing to say about him and it is the thing that made it work.** The form holds the district works, being a household of the district, in the matter of a recorded claim entered and marked disputed, and in the matter of the works engaged in it. Asked which bit of them is us, he says the last bit, and that a clerk filled it in because the box says to, **and the box says the person, institution or thing engaged in the matter and a person fills a box the way the box is printed.** The yard does the rest of it, because that is what a yard is, in about eleven minutes. Prawle gets the list of works off the nail in the tool shed, with jobs against days and a name at the foot and **a day at the end of it in chalk and the same day in ink in a clerk's own book with no office on it**, and puts it on the bench by the mortar, and about nine men come over it. **The rate on a wall on that list is a shilling a day.** A man of about thirty from the second gang: **then the form has got the works in it. Not a wall. The works. And every man on that list is in the works.** Nobody says anything for a while and then about six of them say it at once, which is the only arithmetic a yard has ever needed. And Prawle: **it was never the wall, the wall is why I am here every day and nobody has ever once said the wall was in dispute; the form is not about the wall, the form is about the works, and a works is a thing, and the thing is what the box asked for.** The man from the office looks at the list twice and says **nobody told me that**, and asks it to be said in the yard, and is told: **say it again to your office, and if they ask you what the words mean, do not tell them you asked us. Tell them you were told by a mason. That is worth more than anything you could have found out in an office and it will last about four years.** A boy of sixteen on the list asks whether that means he is finished, and is told: **you are on a list of works with a day at the end of it and this form has got no name under it and no day at the end of it, and there is no way on earth for a form with no name under it to finish a boy who is on a list with a day against it — and I have to tell you that I cannot tell you that for certain, because I have been in an office for nineteen years and every single thing I have ever read there that had no name on it finished somebody.** Then the finding in a mason's mouth, said in the shed and not in the yard, about eleven days after: **a heading is a machine, a column with a heading over it is a machine, and a form with a heading over it and no person under it is a machine that runs on whatever is nearest, and if there is nothing else near it then it runs on the works, and the works is a thing, and a thing is a thing you can be held against without anybody being in it at all. I did not put my name in it. I put a wall in it.** About four days of a man's work in a fortnight are held; the rate is a shilling on a listed wall and three shillings on an unlisted one; **he has argued that with a man in a shed four times and lost four times and is not going to argue it a fifth time for nothing.** The cost in nine sentences in the yard, because he is not a man who says a hard thing quietly: four shillings is a fortnight of a boy's food and a fire and a barrow's wear, **and the barrow's wear is the part that does not come back at the end of a fortnight because the barrow is the same barrow and it has been up a wall four more days.** He has a boy of nine who does not know and is not going to be told, **and he is not going to be one of those men who tells his boy about the state of the district works; he will find out at some point from somebody who is not me, and that will be a different afternoon and it is not going to be this one.** And then: **I stood in a room for about twenty minutes on the second day of the twelfth month of next year with a lamp and a bench and ten entries read out loud, and I was not asked whether I would mind, and I said yes in five words. She told me beforehand how long I would be standing there, and that is the only time in about eleven years anybody has told me how long anything was going to take. I have not been thanked for that and I am not going to be thanked for it, and the day somebody thanks me for standing in a room is the day a person comes about the boy.** And the thing he is not going to say: **I am not going to tell anybody that it was worth it. It was not worth four days of a shilling and it was not worth four days of anything. A man who says a thing was worth it after it has cost him four days of a shilling is a man who has stopped counting, and I have counted every day of my working life in this trade and that is the only thing I have that my father did not have.** He went and found the clerk. **He did not ask her to fix it. He said one sentence in the ordinary way, the way a man says a thing he has said four times in a shed: the rate is a shilling and the district owes him for a wall. The form is not the wall.** Ivet Sarn read a definition out of the schedule to him standing in the corridor: *Engaged in the matter: having been asked to do a work of or about the matter, or being paid by a person who has been so asked, or being under the direction of a person who has been so asked. There is no column under this heading and this heading is not entered in any roll, and a person may be engaged in a matter without knowing that the matter is a matter.* He has it again: **then I have not been engaged. I have been standing where a wall is.** And she will not write it down, and gives the reason: **because I am in it, and because a thing written down at this window about a form is a thing a form can be answered with; there is no box for a why in any of this and I am not going to supply one in ink and find out in four years what it does.** Then the two of them work it out together in about nine minutes, standing in a corridor, and neither of them wanted to. **A form can hold anybody it likes as long as the person administering it is not asked what the words mean.** And the person administering it is a clerk in an office about nine miles away who is not a villain, **and she is a clerk; she opened a form, she read a box, she put in the name of a thing because the box asks for a thing, she did it correctly, and she is not going to be asked what the words mean, because nobody in this empire has ever asked anybody what the words mean, and that is not a failure of her, it is the condition of her.** And Ivet Sarn: **I have been at a window for nine years and nobody has ever come to this window and asked me what a word on a form meant, and I have been waiting for it, and it has not come, and I have gone on serving them out at the rail.** And he says: **then you are waiting for the wrong thing and it is not coming, and I have lost four arguments in a shed to men who are not villains either.** Nobody thanks him. **He wants it written down that he was not thanked more than anybody else in that building was, because a woman in that building had said the price of being a party out loud five times and a man of thirty-eight in a city four hundred and thirty miles up this river had put nine lines in a dead woman's hand on a board at fourpence a copy, and a mason of fifty who has lost four days of a shilling is not in the same market as either of them and would be insulted to be told he was.** He goes back to the wall and works a shilling's worth of a day on a listed wall, **which is a third of what the same wall is worth to anybody who is not on the list, and he said it this fifth time to nobody at all, in a yard, on his own, and nobody answered him because there was nobody there.** And the four days are still held, and he is not going to ask for them back, **and the reason he is not going to ask for them back is that asking for them back means asking a clerk what the words on her own form mean, and he has been in this trade for about eleven years and he has never once seen anybody do that and survive the doing of it.**

## Chapter 188 — "Forty-Five Pence a Day, and a Hold Against a Thing" (2,950)

**POV: Rennick Adley, thirty-eight, a book-keeper. The north bay and the store of a hired stone store off the Slade, the second day of the second week of the fourth month of the year after.** A form comes up the road with a heading over it and nothing under the heading, and **the whole of what it took him to see it was about four seconds, and the whole of what it took him to say about it was about nine minutes.** He has been keeping the books of the Slade Cut Company since the second month of next year; the Company's whole money is four shillings a year and all of it is the rent of the building. **In the second week of the eighth month of next year he refused, in about nine seconds, to rule a fourth column in that ledger, and the reason he gave was that a column ruled in a man's own hand is a heading over a page in about four years put there by a man who did not stand in the room. A clerk of thirty-four four hundred and thirty miles up this river has been carrying that reason for about a month and has never met him. This is what his reason was for.** His act: the box says the person, institution or thing engaged in the matter, and there is nothing under it. **Nold Prawle's is on a flood terrace a long way from here and says the district works; the mason who put a wall in that one wrote that a heading is a machine that runs on whatever is nearest, and a mason put a wall in it because there was a wall to hand and he had a boy of nine. Rennick Adley put the name of a building in it, in his own hand, in about four seconds, because there was nothing else to hand** — *the Slade Cut Company, of the hired stone store off the Slade, engaged from the first day of the fifth month of next year and continuing. — R.
