Adley, book-keeper, and no other person has signed this line and there is no other person in this empire who could.* When Doreth Ferrow asks what he has done, he says it is the worst thing anybody in this store has done since the spring bank, **and that it is the only thing he can do, and that he found the method out four hundred and thirty miles from here from a woman of thirty-four who has never met him and has been carrying his reason for a month; he has a choice of two things, and leaving the box empty means a clerk in an office fills it in and she will fill in a thing and it will not be a good thing and it will not be this thing, or he fills it in himself and then it is this and the roof is in a matter and he knows exactly whose roof it is because he has paid the rent out of the whole of it. It is four shillings a year and it is the roof over about forty books with no office on them and the bench the people stand at, and he put it in a box in about four seconds and would do it again tomorrow and would rather it was him than her.** Then he stands in the bay and reads it out. **He reads the names first** — not the form, the names, out of the third column, in the order they came on, every one, without hurrying the slow ones and without skipping the ones he had wanted to skip for about four months. **The third column is the one with no heading over it. It has had no heading over it since the sixth year and every one of the four hundred and something people in that book has gone into it, and about nine hundred and forty names are in that book and about four hundred of them are dead. It is the only column on this bank he is allowed to read a name out of, and the reason he is allowed to is that nobody has ever asked him for it, and a column with no heading over it is not a heading, and a person in a column that is not a heading has not been entered under anything by anybody.** Then the form, once: *Held against the Slade Cut Company, being a thing, in the matter of a recorded claim entered and marked disputed, and in the matter of the works engaged in it. The wages of the persons engaged are held at the same rate and for the same period as the sum held, and a person whose wages are so held is not to be paid that held sum by any person, on account of the person of that family.* **And then he reads it a second time, slower.** Nobody in that bay has ever asked him where he got that from, and he has been asked twice about the double reading by a woman of thirty-four four hundred and thirty miles up this river and has not told her and is not going to be asked, and **the first reading is for the words and the second reading is for the people who did not have them the first time, and he has never said that out loud to anybody either and it is written now and it is not going to be in his mouth.** Then the finding: **a hold on a rotation of about forty-one people holds every one of them and it has to name nobody, it has to name a thing, and the thing is a company, and a company is a roof, and the roof is four shillings a year** — and the part that ought to be frightening and is not: **the second season was never agreed to by anybody, never asked of anybody, began in the first month of the year after and it is about the length a season is, forty-one people are on it, nobody signed anything and nobody refused anything, and that is exactly why this is the cheapest hold in this empire. There is nothing to break. There is nobody to complain, because complaining needs a thing you were refused. There is no form anywhere that says a person may ask to be paid, and I have looked, and I know where the forms are kept and they are not there. If they had refused it, we would have had nine reasons in a book. Because they did not refuse it, we have nothing, and the nothing is what is being held.** About four people in that bay cannot read a paragraph: never asked once, not asked twice this week, **and there is no column for them and there is not going to be one, and the reason there is not going to be one is that a column for them would be a column somebody would have to fill.** A girl of seventeen is in the room at the back on a written engagement, at forty-five pence a day and four days a week, reading out loud. **She was not spoken to about the hold. She did not ask about it. A person who is paid to read is a person who can be told to stop**, and he has said that sentence out loud in this bay twice and has not sent anybody to anybody and is not going to, and she was not named, was not thanked, and is not going to start, and this is the last season in which anybody on this bank can ask her something and be answered for nothing. The chair of sixty-four in the bay says one thing, once, to him and not to the bay: **a carriage is not a wage; a thing that pays for a person to come and does not pay them for the day is not an offer, it is a way of counting how many rooms a person is in. I said that in this bay in the sixth month of last year to about thirty people and it was the truest thing anybody said that month and it has not been useful to anybody since, because being right about a thing is not the same as a thing being done about.** He then tells the chapter that the chair has another sentence he has not been given whole and has wanted for about four months, and is asked whether he is going to ask her, and says: **I am not going to ask her. The half I have is about a foreman throwing a paper with a heading on it away twice, and the half I do not have is on a slate in a counting room in a town about four hundred and thirty miles up this river, and a girl of twenty carried it up there on a cart and read it out in a lane, and I have never been in that lane and nobody on this bank has ever heard that half, and I am not going to be the man who says to a woman of sixty-four in a bay, please, what is the other half, because the day I ask her that is the day she stops saying the half she has got.** Then the factor's letter, on the bench since the third week of the third month, nineteen days old: *I am directed to require from you the name, place of custom and description of a person in the above works who may be served, together with the consent of that person to be served, and I am to say that without a name and a consent this office cannot proceed and will not proceed, and the matter will stand against the works until one is given.* **He has not answered it and has not thrown it away, and every day he does not send it is a day nobody has been entered, and when he does send it there is a name in a box with a heading over it, and the name belongs to a person who works about four hundred yards from that store, and the person will be served, and served is party, and party is a person a book can be true about for the rest of that person's life, and there is no form in this empire for taking a party back out of a box.** And: **we are all of us sitting on it, waiting for a letter neither of us is going to send — and I would like it minuted that I said the name of it out loud, and that about four people in this room cannot read the minute when it is written, and that I have read it out loud instead, and that the reason I have read it out loud is not kindness. It is that a fact said in a room with about thirty people in it is the only kind of fact in this empire that a person who cannot read a paragraph is also a party to.** He writes it in the bay's own ledger in the third column, with the day on it, in his own hand, and reads it back twice, once for the people who can see the words and once for the people who cannot, **and the second reading is the one he did not skip.** Nothing was thanked and nobody thanked him and he had said in advance that nobody was to. The hold is still in force; about nine men in three gangs are on a list of works with a day at the end of it; the factor's request is unanswered and is not going to be; and about nineteen people who said no with a reason in the first season are still behind that bank and are not going to be asked again by anybody in this stretch of it. And about four hundred and thirty miles up this river there is a board in a passage with nine lines in a dead woman's hand on it at fourpence a copy, and about seventy people had bought one by the end of that week, and there is no form for asking who bought them, and nobody asked.

## Chapter 189 — "Protection Is Not Secrecy, and It Is the Same Hand" (3,399)

**POV: Tamsin Rook. Her room four bays from a counter, the fourth day of the fourth week of the fourth month of the year after.** **On that day there was a conversation in a room and it had a day on it, and nothing else in the world did, and neither of the two people in it was going to be told anything afterwards.** The room is hers: a table, a press with about six hundred printed slips in it that say the fourth line is not to be completed by that office, a hard-backed book with no office on it, a lamp, and about nine feet of wall she does not use. Marek Kest comes in at about the seventh hour and has been up two nights and has a third fair copy of a thing that is already on a board. She says the price of being a party out loud, with the number, **and it is the seventh time, and four of the seven were about her, one was about a person who is not in the room and cannot be told and cannot be warned, and the seventh is not about either of them, and she has thought about why that is and has not worked it out and is not going to guess.** Then the other thing, said for the first time to him: **she is in four bays because a paper says so, and the paper is not the reason, and there is not one of those six hundred printed slips that she put there, and she has been good at it, and she has been the door in this building for about four months and it is not the reason** — and why on this day: **if I ever say a true thing out loud about why I am in a room, then that is who I am, and there is no form in this empire for a person to be who they are, and I have been hiding behind a paper for four months because the paper is a machine and a machine cannot be asked a question about itself.** She reads what she is about to say in the middle, and says so, and counts the sentences under the table where he cannot see her, and has never admitted to anybody that she does that. **"I am not going to comfort you." It is not coldness: a person who is being comforted has stopped being in the room. You have spent nine days deciding to hand a dead woman's method to a printer, and four weeks finding out you had been eligible for an office since you were a child, and about four months since finding out that your mother made you unservable so that she could not tell you, and you have not eaten properly since the second week of the second month, and you have a third fair copy of a thing that is already in type in your hand as though the fair copy were the part that mattered. And I am not going to be the person who takes you out of this room tonight. If I do that then in about four years there will be one version of the last four months and it will be the one where a clerk of twenty-four was kind to a man of thirty-eight, and that version has no sheet in it and no board and no woman of sixty-three in it and no third column.** Then the difference between protection and secrecy, **said in the middle, with the sentences counted under the table where he could not see her:** one of them is a thing you do to a person and the other is a thing you do about them; there is no form in this empire for the first one and everybody does it anyway; the reason everybody does it is that it works, and it worked. **His mother did it to him and it worked and he is not alive anywhere anybody can serve. He did it to a woman of sixty-three in the second month of the year after and it worked and she is not on a board in a passage and her name is not in any book anybody can buy.** And the part nobody has said to him: **she was in the book the whole time, and she is in about nine hundred of them, and there is no heading over the third column of any of them, and what is in that column is her hand and not her name.** So keeping her off a board did not take her out of a book and I want you to hear that before I say the other half. **A hand is findable, and it is the most findable thing there is. Anybody with a copy and about four years can put about four hundred hands side by side and find the one that is hers, and nobody is served anything and no name is said out loud and there is no form for it and no fee and no day at the end of it.** And a register of witnesses is not a copy anybody has, because the register does not travel and the leaf does not travel and the three things a leaf needs are all three required and none of the three has been had, so the finding is not free and is not available to anybody who wants it and is not refused either — **it is simply out of reach, which is the same thing as the whole of this matter and is not the same as a refusal, and there is no form anywhere that turns out of reach into a refusal.** So the act of protection wrote down the only sentence in the world that says where the books are, put it on a board at fourpence a copy, and told every buyer there are five columns. **Not printing the third one is the kindness, and telling the world there is a third one is the part that is not, and that is not a thing I have caught you doing. It is a thing the doing is.** I am going to say that it was the same act, and I am going to say it about your mother, and about your sister, and about you, and the same hand is not a figure of speech. The same hand is the point. It is one hand in one family writing the same sentence in one register and one margin and one form, and the sentence is always that a person is better off not being asked. And I do not believe any of you three decided to do it and I do not believe the woman of sixty-three decided to do it either, and I have watched about four hundred people in this city decide to do things and almost none of them decided.** He says he is not going to say his mother was right; she says **nobody is going to tell you she was kind, and if somebody does tell you that in the next year, you will want to know what they get for it** — and then **there is nothing in this room to forgive. I have said the word out loud twice this month in two rooms and I have not got a softer one for it. I have not done anything to you that needs forgiving. I have been a party, and I have been useful, and I have said the price of both out loud every time, and that is the whole of what I have done and I would do it again on the same day.** Then, mid-conversation, **the girl of about twenty-five at the intake desk puts her head in without knocking** and asks about the board: about seventy copies in nine days at fourpence, and the printer's man does not keep them and is right not to, and she has been three times to the counter with about fourpence of her own and has not been able to ask the man who wrote it. **Tamsin Rook gives four facts and refuses to help her.** One: there is no form anywhere that says a counter takes the name of a person for a copy, and that is not a rule anybody made, it is a trade, and it cannot be asked for without inventing it. Two: he has not asked her to buy one and he cannot ask her and he would not want to. Three: a printer's man at fourpence a copy is the only person in that passage who is nobody's clerk, and if he kept a list it would be a list of strangers. Four: **if you want to know who bought a fourpence copy of a printed sheet there is nothing in this empire that will tell you, and the reason there is nothing is that about four hundred people a year pay fourpence for a fact, and a great many of them would not care to be one.** And: **then say it to the next person who asks you, and do not say it to him, and do not ask me again, because I have just given you the whole of the answer and the second time I will have nothing to add and you will know that I have nothing to add and it will be worse.** Marek Kest stood four feet away through all of it and said nothing, and gives the reason: **she is a party to this room and not to anything of mine** — and she says **that is the correct reason and it is the reason I am going to say the next thing at all.** Then the one thing in the room he has not asked about: **you are not going to ask me and if you do then I will not answer, and it will not be a refusal to be served. It is a refusal to be asked, and I have never had to use that one and I would rather not learn tonight what it costs. There are four in it and one of them has been there since the first month of the year before last and it has not been sent and it has not been opened, and this is the seventh time in two years I have not thought about it, and I am not going to start now.** And the last of it, as a fact and not advice, **said standing up with her hand on the back of her own chair:** **I am not going to decide anything in a room on a day when one of us has been up two nights. I am not going to be told things. I have not asked anybody for anything since the day I was refused in a room and nobody has asked me for anything either, and those are two facts about the same week and only one of them is in a book, and I have made my peace with which one. And there is a form in this empire that makes a person a party, and there is no form in this empire that makes a person safe, and I have been the first of those since the last week of the seventh month of next year and I have said the price of it out loud seven times and nobody has thanked me once and I did not expect to be thanked once and I would like it written down that I did not, because in about four years somebody is going to read that I said the price seven times and they are going to assume somebody heard it.** Nobody had heard it. He put the third fair copy inside his coat, where four sheets of copyist's paper had been since the second week of the twelfth month of next year, and went out of the door and down four bays and along a corridor, and she shut the room, put the lamp out, and left the one thing in it alone.

## Chapter 190 — "The Last Week of the Fourth Month, and a Woman Who Was Not Sent" (3,012)

**POV: Marek Kest. Auremar, the last week of the fourth month of the year after.** The chapter opens as a reckoning in the plainest words there are and **none of it is a question and none of it has been answered by anybody:** a certification with a clerk of thirty-four's hand at the foot of it, nine seconds, price said out loud, **the second thing in this matter with her hand on it and the first one she chose**; a notice of a seat in six numbered lines and a foot, same paper, same hand, same device, the device a seat's own and not the fire-and-water mark, **a seal at the foot and no name under the seal**; a schedule in a second hand, unsigned, four definitions and a provision, one of which turns on a roll of households, **and one person in this empire fits that definition, and she is on a roll because a district cannot help it, and she has not been entered, and nobody has asked her to be**; a wage stopped in a household of one person by a form with a heading over it and no person under it, **and the person who filled the box in filled in the name of a thing, and the thing is a household, and a household of one is a person, and there is no column on anything in this empire that says which person a household is**; a refusal entered in the fourth book of an association of dyers in a furnace town about four hundred and thirty miles down this river, in a woman's own hand, with the day on it, **no name in it, and the reason the name is not in it is in the book in her own hand, four words long**; about seventy copies gone out of a counter in a passage at fourpence each in about nine days, no form for asking who bought them, nobody asked, and there is not going to be one. **A printed sheet on a board with nine lines in a dead woman's hand in it and a man's name at the foot of it and a heading that says what it is and where it came from, and the heading is the whole of why anybody can now tell there was a part. What is not in it: a third column with no heading over it, and a woman of sixty-three, and a man of thirty-eight who did not put her there and will not be thanked for it and has not called it a kindness.** Then the last movement, and **nobody sent her.** A printer in the town where the lane is set that sheet in type in the third week into the fourth week of the second month, **because a copy of a printed sheet is worth exactly what a form is worth, which is that anybody may have it for nothing, and a printer who does not set a sheet that is going round four hundred yards of a town is a printer who has decided to keep it, and there is no form anywhere that says he may.** A man who cuts kindling and sells at every door on that side of the water bought one at fourpence. **He can read. He is the only person in that lane who can, and he has never said so and nobody has ever asked him, and he read the whole of it standing in a doorway, and then he read the nine lines out loud in that doorway to a woman of sixty-three who cannot read a paragraph, because they are in her own hand and he did not know that and worked it out in about four seconds from the middle of it, and he read them out because there was a person in front of him who could not read them and he did not have a form.** He told nobody, has not been asked, is not going to be asked, does not want to be, is not named and is not in this, and fourpence is about four days of what a man makes selling bundles at doors, and nobody has told him and nobody is going to. And she got on a cart. He took a room for four days by the day above a shop in a street in that city, out of about forty-four pounds a year with no fund and no form for a fund, because he has a rented room with a bed in it and he is not having a woman of sixty-three find where he sleeps. She came up four flights at about the sixth hour on the second day, stood in the room she had not been asked into with her shawl on, did not sit down, and saw the fair copy on the table. **"There is my hand." "Yes." "Read it out." "No." "You read it out to me in a house in a lane in the second month of the year after, twice, the second time slower." "That was a different thing and I told you at the time that it was a different thing and you are not going to get it again, and there is nobody in this room who is going to read it to you a third time and not one of them is going to be good at it."** Then the question she came for: **is there more of me than nine lines.** **Yes.** There is more of her in about four hundred lines in a bound book in a house about four miles off a road, and in about nine hundred buildings in about nine hundred books that have never been compared with anything, and in every one of them there is a column with no heading over it and a set of hands in it that is hers. And then why he cannot tell her: **because the only instrument in this empire that can hand a person the rest of what they wrote is a question, and the question is on the fifth line of a printed form, and the fifth line has been done once, in pencil, in a kitchen, in about nine minutes, in the first month of the year after, by a clerk of thirty-four who is a party and therefore can be told and therefore is the only person in the room entitled to ask it, and she said the price of it out loud before she asked, and the price was that she can be served anything said in that room for the rest of her life, and she said it to a room. And she asked you, in your own kitchen, and you answered, and the girl of nineteen wrote it in pencil, and there is a sheet of paper in that kitchen with your name on it that is not the office's name. And that was the once. Nobody is going to ask you a second time. You are sixty-three and you are owed one question and you have had it, and there is no form in this empire for asking a person the same thing twice, and if there were one then the second asking would be about the first, and you would be asked in a room whether you remember, and a person remembering a thing and a person reading a thing back are two different acts and only one of them is evidence and I said that to you in the second month and I am not going to soften it now.** **Nobody asked her the fifth line again. Nobody has sent anybody and nobody is going to.** Then she asks about the girl of nineteen: will she be asked, by anybody, ever, and the answer is **by anybody, ever, and I made sure of that by not writing her down, and there is no form anywhere that says she was ever in that room, and she has a bundle of kindling and a story about a kitchen and that is the whole of what she has and it is not nothing** — and Bess Tarrant says *then it is not only me*, and he says **it is not only you. That is the half of the fifth line the clerk of thirty-four said out loud in that room and did not make a speech about, and I have not said it in a room to anybody in about four months. You are the wrong person to be told it and the only person in this empire who is owed anything and I could not think of a better one.** And she says that is a very odd sentence, and he says neither do I, and that was the end of it. Then the second question she is owed, asked in the same words she asked it in a doorway in the rain: *Will somebody tell her. That I wrote it down. That it is there.* And **Marek Kest gives her the same answer, in the same words, because there is only one answer and he had about four days to think of a second one and did not find one: a person in a house that is shut has no address. A person who is not told has not been erased. Those are two different things, and I have known the second one for about four months and I have never once been able to say it out loud without the first one coming with it. I am saying both of them now, and the first one is the harder, and I am not going to leave it out to make the second one easier.** She says it is a very cruel thing to say to a woman of sixty-three in a room; he says yes, it is. And she says: **well, I have come four hundred and thirty miles to be told it in a room, and it is worse in a room, and I would have had it in a doorway for nothing, and there is a bed in it and you have not offered it me and I am sixty-three and I am not going to ask you twice.** He says he is sorry; she says do not be, and gives the reason: **I did not come to be told anything by a man who has no career to lose and no office to be struck out of. I came because a man who cuts kindling stood in my doorway and read my own hand out loud to me for nothing, and that is the only thing that has happened to me in this that was not done to me, and I have had four months of things being done to me and one afternoon of a man reading, and I know the difference, and I have put it in a book in my own hand with the day against it, and there is no name in it.** And: **I have never once been asked whether I am a party to anything in my life and I am sixty-three and I have kept a house and I have never once been in one of them by name, and that is the only thing I have got and it is not nothing.** Then the guarantee, **printed whole and word for word identical to Chapters 0161, 0164, 0170 and 0180, and no child named**; the Lowcross bill at nineteen pounds three and fourpence, unpaid, nobody liable, about a penny a day, no line for a bridge in that fund and there has not been one in nineteen years, four hundred and eleven on the far side and three hundred and eighty-eight crossings, **and those are two figures and they are never the same**; a second season in its fourth month, agreed to by nobody, asked of nobody, **and the wages of about forty-one people on it held against a company whose whole money is four shillings a year and all of it is the rent of a roof**; about nineteen people who said no with a reason in the first season still behind that bank, not asked a second time, **and that is not this volume's last chapter**; about four people who cannot read a paragraph never asked once and now not asked twice, and no column for them and not going to be one; **The thirty-one of Mosswake are thirty-one.** And the last of it, **not a cliff and a name:** a form printed in about nine hundred buildings with five lines on it, the fifth asked once in pencil in a kitchen by somebody who said the price out loud first, and nobody going to ask it again. **A hearing is a room. A room is where records are asked for, and a record is what a person asks for when a person is going to do something with it**, and a clerk of thirty-four said that out loud at a counter in the second week of the first month of the year after, and **about four years later there is going to be a room in which a woman of sixty-three is asked whether there is more of her than nine lines. That room has a name. The name is a hearing. Nobody has written the hearing down yet.** And in a passage in this city there is a thing on a board at fourpence a copy, and it says, in a dead woman's hand, that it is to be done on a box and not on a paper, because a paper goes to a house and a box goes to a roll. **This is the first time in about four months that the paper has gone to a house, and nobody asked her to send it.**

## What Volume 04 Batch 0004 resolved, what it did not, and what it hands on

**Resolved:** a copy of a record bought at fourpence at a counter in the second week of the first month is now certified, in nine seconds, by that counter, with a clerk's hand at the foot of it, and the seal was not read out and the buyer's name is not kept. A notice of a seat with nobody's name on it has arrived in Auremar in six numbered lines with a seat's own device and a seal and nothing under the seal, and a schedule in a second hand with four definitions and a provision. The reading of ten entries is reported in four lines of a letter and its finding is that a hearing is not a document. Nine lines in a dead woman's hand are on a public board at fourpence a copy with a heading that says what they are and where they came from, and about seventy copies have gone out in about nine days. A wage is held in a household of one person and against a company whose whole money is the rent of a roof. A mason has four days of a shilling a day held and is not going to ask for them back. A book-keeper has put the name of a building in a box in his own hand and read the names out of a column with no heading over it. A woman of twenty has refused the third of three questions in a room, out loud, with the day on it, and has written a fourth thing in a book that is not hers with no name in it. The conversation about protection and secrecy has happened, as a scene of its own, with a day on it.

**Not resolved, and not this batch's to resolve:** nobody has been entered as a representative, and nobody has been asked; about seventy people now know there was a part and cannot tell which part; the answer Bess Tarrant is owed is still not payable and has now been given twice in the same words and does not pay either time; a clerk of thirty-four's own reading of her own price is on a page and nobody heard it; a mason is owed four days and a book-keeper is owed the whole of a second season's wage and neither is going to ask; the factor's request for a name is unanswered and the letter is on a bench; a girl of seventeen has not been asked anything and has not been contacted and has not been named; about nineteen people are still behind the bank and have not been asked again; the end of the run, the row, the striking-out, the column headed *by whose authority* and the name in it are untouched for the fifth movement running; the Ashfall bundle is shut and unnamed and what Ilyra Kest found is unanswered; no hearing has been written down; and the V4 half of the relationship milestone is still unpaid and is not paid by anything in these ten chapters.

## Chapter 191 — "A Date In A Minute Book, and a Name At The Foot Of It" (3,205)

**POV: Marek Kest. The building off the old river road where the office of a seat keeps its minute books, the first week of the fifth month of the year after.** **Two dates go into one minute book in one week and both of them have a name at the foot, and neither of the two names is the name of the person the date is about.** The minute books are on a shelf in a room on the ground floor with a window about two feet wide and a pane out of it, and there are eleven of them. **The woman at the table is Orla Denning, about fifty-five, nineteen years of minute books, not a lawyer, not a party, not a judge, and she has never been asked what any of it meant.** She says a copy is fourpence and **a shilling is a person, and there is no price in this building for a day and if there were one I would not know what to do with it.** He says **a date with nobody's name on it is not a summons to a person**, and she tells him he is the second person in four weeks to have said that to her, and she wants it noted that she noticed. **The first entry: the restitution hearing has a day — the third day of the third week of the fifth month, at the second hour, in a room with a rail in it** — and its notice is in six numbered lines with a seat's own device cut into the head and a seal at the foot and **nothing under the seal**, a second line asking that no inference be drawn from the absence of any name, and a sixth line that will not name the office's holder. She declines to say the name at the foot of the earlier notice, he did not ask her, and **she writes a line in the margin saying nobody asked her, and it is the first line she has written in nineteen years that is not a date.** **The second entry: a room, four years off, for a question — whether there is more of a person than nine lines — with the person described and not named, about sixty-three, and a line under it saying the person has been asked once.** The figure is the figure a clerk of thirty-four said out loud at a counter in the second week of the first month, entered on the day it was said and not in a minute book, and this is the first time it is in one. **She did not know what she was entering and entered what she was given, and says so in the room, and writes that down, and says that a clerk of nineteen years who says afterwards that she did not know is a clerk of nineteen years who was asked.** The finding: **a person who is not told cannot be told, and a person who cannot be told cannot be warned, and a person who cannot be warned cannot be asked whether she wants to be asked**; a date is findable and a person cannot be stopped from a date. **The only protection a person has against a day is to be told about it, and being told is a service, and being served is a party, and there is no way back out of a party.** He asks where she is: in this city, came up the road on a cart, stood in a room hired by the day for four days, asked him a question he could not answer, and has not gone home or has come back. Then: **the protection a name at the foot of an entry gives is fourpence of ink and about nine seconds of a woman's time, and it works in one direction — it makes the clerk answerable and it does nothing whatever for the person the date is about.** She writes down what he says because he asks her to and gives the reason, and says the part she does not have: **there is no column for telling anybody, and there is no column for it in any book in that building, and she has looked for nineteen years.** And then the ordinary machinery answers the date: **a third line with no day under it is a third line, and a third line with a day under it is a thing to be done, and what is to be done is a box printed in about nine hundred buildings, and a person fills a box the way the box is printed.** It went into a box on the fourth day of the third week of the fifth month in an office about nine miles from a counter, by a clerk who is not a villain, correctly, and nobody was asked and nobody was told and nobody knew, and **it was not done by anybody who wanted it done and was not done in a hurry and was done in about nine seconds by a person doing her job properly, which is the whole of what has gone wrong in this matter for about a hundred and forty years and is the reason nothing can be put right by anybody being found.** He does not go to the counter and ask to be entered, and writes down why: **a man with nothing enforceable behind him has no place of custom or of work anywhere in this empire to be entered, and he is the cheapest person in this empire for it, and the reason he is the cheapest is that his mother made him that on purpose, and she was right and he is not going to say so and nobody has told him she was kind.** He does not tell his sister. He writes both dates in a book with no office on it — *asked for by me and entered by a clerk who was not asked what it meant*, and *not asked for by anybody and entered anyway* — and **a book with no office on it is a thing a form cannot be answered with, and that is the only kind of record a person in this matter has ever had, and it has cost him nothing and it is worth nothing and he is going to keep it.** Nobody thanked him and he said in advance that nobody was to. And about four hundred and thirty miles down this river a foreman of fifty-one has never once in nine years been asked to read anything by anybody at the district works, and **nobody sent her, the same as nobody sent the woman of sixty-three, and there is no form in this empire for a person who comes on her own account, and the two of them are not compared and are not going to be.**

## Chapter 192 — "What The Fifth Line Is For" (3,127)

**POV: Marn Ottery. Auremar, the second week of the fifth month of the year after, the first sitting, the fourth day at the second hour, in a room with a rail in it.** She is thirty-four, eleven years at the fourth counter of the Notaries' Table, not a lawyer, a party to an instrument about a dead woman's name, and **the cheapest person in the building she works in and she says that out loud.** She was not on the bench and not on the rail; she was in the room because a counter is a thing a room asks about, **and because being asked is the one thing that has never happened to her and she had a fortnight to think about whether she wanted it.** The record of property and debt for a house in a lane of eleven houses about four hundred and thirty miles down this river is produced, wrapped, with a day on the wrapper, by a person who is not named. Four facts: **the seal on the paper the buyer produced is not the seal of this table and it was not read out**; the buyer's name was not asked for and is not kept at that counter; the copy was issued in full at the ordinary price to a person on a day; **and there is a certification at the foot of the request for it, written in about nine seconds on the seventh day of the first week of the second month, and she said the price out loud before she wrote anything — a document with her hand at the foot of it is findable in about four years by anybody with a copy of the right page.** There was no charge, **because the fee board at that counter has four things on it and none of them is time and there is no line on it for a certification of that counter's own book, because a table cannot charge a person for telling the truth about its own book.** Then a sheet is handed in and put on the table face up: the sheet a witness is entered upon, five lines, printed, in about nine hundred buildings, with a stack of them about nine inches deep on the table, **and not one of them has ever been looked at by anybody for any reason.** **There is no post in this empire whose job is to stand in front of a heading and ask, and on the fourth day of the second week of the fifth month somebody asked**, in four words: *what is the fifth line for.* She said the price out loud first, **because the answer is a thing she did and the thing she did is findable**: **from the day I was served I can be served anything about it for the rest of my life, and there is no form anywhere for taking a party back out of a box, and that is the eighth time I have said it out loud in a room** — four of the eight about her, one about a person who is not in the room and cannot be told, one about nobody in particular, one about neither of us, and this one about a sheet of printed matter. Then the answer, in the ordinary way, in about nine minutes. **The fifth line is a question, and it is the only instrument in this empire that can hand a person the rest of what they wrote** — not a copy, not a register, not a court — **asked in a room, out loud, by somebody entitled to ask it, before the thing is said, and written down with the answer on it.** The person entitled to ask is the second person, which is the person in the room who is not the person being written about, **and that is in a printed sheet in about nine hundred buildings and has been for about a hundred and forty years and it is the reason a register kept from that sheet has five columns and the third of them has nothing over it and what is in it is a hand and not a name.** Then: **then it is a form anybody could use.** No: **it is a form nobody has ever been entitled to use, and a second person cannot be served, and being served is what makes a person a party, and a party is the only person who can be told what a thing is going to be used for, so the fifth line asks a question of the one person in the room who by definition cannot be told, and it has been dead for about a hundred and forty years and nobody took it out and nobody ever found out it was dead.** And it was done once: in pencil, in a kitchen, in about nine minutes, in the first month of the year after, by her, who is a party and therefore the only person entitled to ask, who said the price out loud before she asked, and who asked a woman of sixty-three in her own kitchen whether she was a party to a thing about to be said in a room, and got *no*, and wrote the no in pencil on that woman's table, and a girl of nineteen wrote it out fair, and there is a sheet of paper in that kitchen with that woman's name on it and it is not the office's name. **It will not be done again on that woman: there is no form in this empire for asking a person the same question twice, and if there were one the second asking would be about the first, and she would be asked in a room whether she remembers, and a person remembering a thing and a person reading a thing back are two different acts and only one of them is evidence.** Two refusals: what the certification had cost her, given in the same instrument a woman of twenty used about a different figure four hundred and thirty miles away in a different month; and the name of the woman in the third column — **a person who is in a book in a house about four miles off a road and whose name is not in it, and if I say the name in this room then a person in a book becomes a name in a room, and the man who printed the nine lines of that woman's own hand at fourpence a copy did not print her, and I am not going to be the person who says it out loud.** The clerk of about twenty-five who took the minute wrote down without being asked that no form in this matter had ever been put to a person and been asked about, and that the reason a form printed in about nine hundred buildings had done what it did for about a hundred and forty years was that nobody had ever stood in front of a heading and asked what a word on it meant, and read it back to her before writing it, which is not the practice in that room, and asked to have *you are not the practice in this room* entered as well. Nobody thanked her. She took the sheet away because exhibits go back to the person who brought them, and it went into a book with no office on it on a page with the day on it, **and a book with no office on it is a thing a form cannot be answered with, and that is the only kind of record she has ever had, and it has cost her nine seconds and it is worth nothing and she is going to keep it.**

## Chapter 193 — "A Stub, And Three Times In One Form" (2,881)

**POV: Ivet Sarn. The Mosswake Roll Court, a flood terrace, the third week of the fifth month of the year after.** Thirty-eight, nine years at a window, a party as of the first week of the twelfth month of next year, four presses in the embankment corridor, a key on a string shortened twice by herself, and there is no form in this empire that makes a person be in charge of a thing. She is served on the second day of the third week, at the window about four feet off the ground, by a man who carries notices and who said the word *served* out loud, which he is required to do and which he said properly. **All four of the things are about a man called Pell Vey, and she is the only person in that building who has ever had to write any of them down, and she wrote them all down.** **Being served has stopped being a cost. Being documented is a different thing and it is not cheaper**, and she priced that out loud in the corridor about four minutes after he had gone down it, to nobody. One: a delivery stub, a slip the size of a playing card with a day on it, two numbers, and a line at the foot with a hand on it, **and a delivery stub is the one document in this empire designed to be handed to a person who is not the person it is about.** She put the hand beside four others within the hour and it took about nine minutes: **it is Pell Vey, head of the Notaries' Table, holder of the cabinet key, and there is not one document in that building with his hand on it that she has ever been able to read, and there is one now, and a man who puts his own hand at the foot of a thing that is going to be carried to a building four hundred yards from his own is a man who has decided to be findable, and in nine years she has not once seen an office do it.** **A hand identified by comparison is a hand nobody can deny, and that is the first time in this matter that anything has been a document against a person who is alive and in a building.** Two: a file kept in four places, on paper, in his own hand, and the list came to her on the fourth day with the same man and the same word at the sill. Three of the four lines are buildings she can name. **The fourth place is a back room off a corridor she has walked every working day for nine years, and she has never once been in it, and there is no list anywhere in that building that says who is allowed in it.** The man who carries notices says he does not know what is in it and is not going to tell her. Three: on three days, on a form with a question on it, the same person was asked the same question and refused, **and the words were fourteen words long and they were his own and they did not vary by a word.** **A refusal in one form on three days is a person being consistent, and a person being consistent is a document**, and the other half took her nine minutes: **a man in that building could have refused in four different forms and been unfindable, and he did not, and there is no form anywhere that requires a person to be consistent, and the fact that he was is the most exposed thing about him that anybody has found this year, and nobody made him do it and he cannot now unsay it.** Nobody asked her for that; she said so twice and wrote it down. Four: she went to the back room on the fifth day, because a file in four places can be produced and a file that can be produced will be asked about. There was nothing in it. **In nine years she has been able to say she did not know what the presses were for; she can now say she knows what the fourth place is for, and that it is for a person with a pen to sit at a table with, and a person with a pen at a table can put a thing into a column and take a thing out of a column, and both of those are the same hand and the same table, and there is no instrument anywhere that stops it.** What had been done there was in a margin, in a copy of a roll, in a hand that was not his, with a day against it — the fourth day of the fourth week of the ninth month of next year — correcting a line in which a body stood in a column headed for the person who did a work and putting a person's name there instead, and writing underneath why, and signing it. **It is nine minutes of work, it is the only thing in the whole of this matter that is a record on purpose and not a record by accident, and it was given away by a provincial archivist on the ordinary round with a box on her hip and a list of eleven stops, who came for four days and was not paid for it because nobody asked and there is no form for it, and who was not thanked and has not been thanked and nobody is going to thank her, and who said in that back room in words that it is not a crime and does not make her a good person.** **She does not know that her hand is in a fourth place of a file in a building about four hundred and thirty miles from her own office, and she does not know that a clerk of thirty-eight has spent about nine minutes in a corridor matching her writing to three other hands, and she does not know that a man is on a form three times in three days refusing in the same fourteen words because of a line in a margin.** The same surname is not a door and has never been one, and telling the man who carries notices would be a service and being served is a party. Then a scene at the sill: a man of about thirty-four with a fortnight's wage held, and **he is not on the form, and if he were he would be a person in a box with a heading over it, and a person in a box can be asked about for the rest of their life, and there is no form anywhere for taking a person back out of a box** — so the thing holding his wage has protected him from being findable and cost him fourteen days of a man's work, and both are true. He wants it written down twice; **she cannot, has looked for a form for it that morning and there is not one, and this is the first time she has wanted a form and not found one and it is the worst morning she has had there since she came**; she puts it in her own book with the day on it and her own hand, and that is a record of her saying it to him and not a record of him, and it is worth exactly what it is worth. He asked for the second reading and she gave it. Nobody thanked her. She wrote it all down that evening in her own book, read it back twice, the second slower, and did not read it a third time, and wrote at the bottom the reason: **a hand of hers is the only hand anybody is going to be able to put side by side in about four years, and she has now done this three times and the reason has not got any better and she has not stopped.** **The finding of it is not a man and it is not a woman and it is a hand: two of the four places have a name on the foot of them and one of them does not, and the one that does not is the one that is going to cost somebody something, and the somebody is not in this matter and does not know they are in it.**

## Chapter 194 — "The Roll Gets Checked" (3,145)

**POV: Nell Kest. The counting room off a dyers' lane in Greyfen, the fourth week of the fifth month of the year after.** Twenty, a dye-house worker which is what she is paid for, keeping the books of eleven houses on that lane and four other houses in three other districts for nothing since she was seventeen, wage stopped in the second week of the third month, the word is *held*, nobody has said the figure and she has not given it. The counting room is about eleven feet by fourteen with a bench, a window with a broken light, a stove she does not light until the ninth month, and about forty books on shelves made for taller books. **A district checks its roll of households because a district has to know who is in it, and the check is in the ordinary way and the ordinary way is what breaks it.** A woman of about sixty who has kept that roll for nineteen years comes down the lane on the second day of the fourth week with a sheet on a board and a basket, asks the fourth and the seventh in order, is told the room has not changed and is one person, and then turns the board round. **The something else said *representative in a matter*, against her name, with a day against it in a hand she did not know, and the day was the fourth day of the third week of the fifth month, entered in the office of a seat, and no further consent of the person required.** She reads it standing up and the woman says nothing, because a woman who keeps a roll for nineteen years knows what it is to stand in a lane and say nothing while somebody reads. Then: **I am not blaming you and you did not do it and you are the reason I can stand here and say what I am about to say out loud**; and if she had not come on the second day of the fourth week she would not have found out for a season, **and a season is about the length a thing can be held for without anybody deciding it is a season.** Then she says no, in a room, out loud, with the day on it, **which is the only place in this empire a no has ever worked**, and the woman of about sixty says she can put it in the fourth column of the roll and it will be there for nineteen years. **Write the day. Write that I said it out loud in this room with you in it. Write that I did not consent. Do not write why, and do not write a reason, because there is no box for a why on a roll of households and I have looked at the roll in your hand and there is nothing on this page for one.** And it did not work, and she had known it would not before she said it: **no further consent required. A room that writes a no down is not the thing that has the no in it.** She is refusing to be served, **the only instrument there is, used once already, not a lawyer, not proud of it, using it now**, and she asks that to be written down too. **The entry was made by a clerk about nine miles from a counter, filling a box the way the box is printed; she was not a villain and she was not asked and she did it correctly, and I cannot get at her and there is no form in this empire that lets a person produce a thing that is not in a book with a name on the spine.** The hearing is about four hundred and thirty miles up this river, on the third day of the third week of this month, **and I am going to it, and I am not paid to go and nobody is paying for me to go and I am not going to add it up.** The woman of about sixty at the eleventh door then says that the word *hold* has been used twice and that she has been left out of it twice, **and I told you in the second week of the third month that I would rather be asked than not, and you told me you would not be able to do that for me and that it was much smaller, and it was, and here it is again, and I have not been asked either** — and goes home, and is not thanked, and there is no form that requires it. Then the count. **The entry was made on the fourth day of the third week of the fifth month. That is a day.** A form that cannot be asked can still be filled in, and the day it was filled in is a day, and **the day is the only part of the whole thing that anybody can find.** She writes the day on the second clean sheet under the heading she wrote herself, and then stops and looks at it, and leaves it. **That sheet says what a person is owed, and by whom, and on what day, about the eleven houses and the four other houses and about nobody else**, and she started it because a column with a heading over it is a machine for turning one thing into another kind of thing and she wanted to see whether she could aim one on purpose; it is hers, nobody asked for it, no form, no fee, no column in that town will take it. **A day is a fact. A day on a sheet of her own with her own heading on it is a record of a person, and a record of a person is the easiest thing in this empire to make, and she has spent three years refusing to make one.** She does not tear it out; she leaves the day on the sheet, the first entry on it and the only one about anybody in her family. Then the weekly count, done out of her head in about four minutes, and **it has one line per house and has had for three years, and there is a second thing it could have now, which is a line for what that house is owed, and she has the figure for nine houses and not for the eleventh, because the eleventh is hers and she has never written down what she is owed.** She could have made it two columns in about a minute. **A column is a machine and a second column is two machines, and a person who has one machine and can see the whole of it knows what it is for, and a person with two of them has to choose which one she is looking at, and choosing is a thing she does not do in a book.** She leaves it one column, does not write the eleventh house at all, and says out loud to an empty counting room: **a book is a room, and I am not going to start filling one in on myself.** On the sixth day she writes a fifth thing in the fourth book of the dyers, in the fourth column, with no name in it, in about four lines, and says in the book that the reason the name is not in it is four words and they are the same four words as last time, and that she said them out loud to her brother in a street about four hundred and thirty miles away and has never seen him write them down, and **I want it written down as well, because a person reads a book after four years and not before, and in four years this page will say that a woman said no and will not say what the no did.** She reads it back once and not twice, because there is nobody in the room. And **a district clerk of about sixty walked down a lane with a board and asked her about a place of custom or of work, in the ordinary way, and got the ordinary answer, and wrote it down, and will do it again at the same time next year. There is nothing in that which anybody can be angry with and there is everything in it.**

## Chapter 195 — "About A Hundred And Thirty People, and a River Coming" (2,772)

**POV: Leda Rell. A hearing room in Auremar, the first week of the sixth month of the year after.** Fifty-one, nine years a magistrate of the Mosswake Roll Court and fourteen years a clerk of it, **and this is the first time in nine years she has sat down in a room that is not on a flood terrace.** She is about four hundred and thirty miles from her own district, with four files out of about a hundred and forty, and she said the number out loud in the corridor before she went in, because a number is findable and a person who says a number can be held to it. She is not a villain and has never sent a person to a jail. **She has a marble thing about a rule and about keeping people in roofs, and she gave it up on the third day of the fourth week of the fifth month, in about nine minutes, in front of a room, and what she gave up was not the rule.** They start with the four files. *Why four.* **Because I was asked what I could bring and I counted, and I chose them because I know which of them will hurt me and I have brought those.** Then the river: it was in the first of two, both in the same flood season, both chosen by hand, both with a day on them, **and she can name the year and cannot name the file.** **There were about a hundred and thirty people in front of me who could have been held. There was a river coming. I held about forty of them.** Chose forty out of a hundred and thirty. And why: **because a predictable claim in the right place stops an eviction in the wrong place** — said without any weight, read out exactly as written because *in about four years somebody is going to come in here and say a good reason was applied unevenly and I would rather the sentence were in the room than my memory of it* — **and the reasoning is the reasoning every flood authority in every district in this empire uses and has always used. It is not a bad rule. It is a good rule. That is not the thing that is wrong with it.** Then the witness, who had not come to be one: **Wren Ludd, about seventy-four**, who came because a paper with a day on it and a carriage paid for arrived, and **the carriage is not a wage and the paying of it is not a kindness and both of those facts are on the record.** He gives his name and the rest of it and watches her write it. *You are one of the ninety.* **I am one of the ninety. I had somewhere to go. That is the whole of the reason and it took her a flood season to work out which ninety and it took me nineteen years to be able to say this in a room.** The place was four miles up a lane on the low side and it belonged to a man whose ground had water standing in it from the second day of that week; he was on the high side of the same lane with a mother in the house and about nine feet of floor between the front door and the back. **He died in the fourth week. I have not said that in a room in nineteen years and I have said it to about four people on that lane and I am saying it here because she is in front of me and I am not going to make her say it first.** He did not know the man; he asks the reason be written as the reason he is sitting there and not as a reason about her, and she asks for it in those words. Then the finding. **In nineteen years I have enforced continuation clauses against about nine hundred and forty people in this district — not in one flood, in about a hundred and forty matters — and in the same nineteen years I have not enforced them against about four hundred.** The first category: about two hundred and ten who could not be found afterwards, and the service says they were served, and no court in this empire has ever gone back. The second: about a hundred and forty who are of a household, **and I entered *household* in the third line of about a hundred and forty files because there was a column for it and nothing else in the line would take.** The third, never written down until now: **about two hundred and forty people in front of me in the second of the two floods, and I held about nine of them, and I chose those nine because they were the nine who had water standing in their ground and everybody else had somewhere to go.** I chose, both times, by hand, on a day, in my district. Then: **a good reason applied unevenly by one person in a district for nineteen years is not a rule and cannot be defended as one. A rule is a thing that is applied the same way each time. This was not applied the same way each time. I chose, and the reason I chose is good, and the second four hundred are the reason the first nine hundred and forty cannot be defended as a rule.** She asks for it in those words, and for **I am not naming anybody**, and gives the reason again, the same reason as before and not a better one: **a person who names a body in a minute becomes a person whose minute can be asked about, and a minute that can be asked about is a document.** And then the thing she volunteers: **a finding entered against a person by that person on that person's own motion names no person, is appealable by nobody, and is not a discovery and is not a seam. It cannot be discovered, it cannot be unseated, it cannot be carried somewhere else and used. It binds me and it helps nobody, and I have made it mine so that it is here.** The court records it. Then the witness is asked what he wants, thinks about it long enough that the clerk stops writing, and says he is not owed anything; **that is the first time anybody has told him why he did not drown, and it cost her nothing to say it and it cost me the carriage and I would not have come without the carriage and I am not going to pretend otherwise.** He says four sentences and nobody writes them down because nobody asked him to, and goes. **The shift is in the record and it is not absolution and it is not a conversion, and the difference is that nothing in this room has made anybody safer, and she has not been forgiven by anybody and has not asked and there is no form that requires it to be entered that she has not been forgiven.** Nobody thanked her and she said in advance that nobody was to. And about four hundred and thirty miles down this river a foreman of fifty-one has never once in nine years been asked to read anything by anybody at the district works, and a seat's paper arrived with her name at the top of it in the third week of the fourth month, and she has not opened it, and there is no form anywhere that says she has to.

## Chapter 196 — "A Procedure Is Not a Person" (3,121)

**POV: Marek Kest. A room hired by the day above a shop in a street in this city, the second day of the second week of the sixth month of the year after, from about the sixth hour to about the eleventh.** He is the person who gave a dead woman's nine lines to a printer at fourpence a copy in the second month of this year and is not thanked for it. **The mark on the inside of his left wrist has not done anything since the fourth hour of the second of the fifth month of next year, when it was up for about nine seconds, and it told nobody anything, and it is not the price, and the wage is the price.** What he is doing is the thing nobody in this matter has been able to do: **you do not reconstruct a person by remembering her, you reconstruct a person's reasoning by walking it, step by step, in the order she would have walked it, out of the terms she had, and if the terms and the order both hold then the person is inside the reconstruction and not behind it.** **It can only be done by somebody who can hold four terms at once, and there is no form in this empire that says a person may do it**, and his only instrument is the two-inch line on his wrist that reads nothing. The reconstruction is the order of a day: a person in a room, a second person in the room, the question, the answer in a box, the day in the first person's own hand, the thing said, the first person not reading it back, the second person writing what was said and nothing else and not reading it back and not showing it. **He walked it eleven times and the results were the same eleven times.** Then: **A procedure is not a person. A record of what a person did in a room is a record of the shape of the room and the order the things were asked in. The order is knowable. The shape is knowable. What a person was in that room to do is in neither of them, and the reason she was in the room is the only part anybody has ever wanted, and it is the part a procedure cannot carry.** It is the part a form printed in nine hundred buildings was built to stop, **and the building of it was not done by a villain and was done in about nine minutes by a person filling in a box.** And the second half: **the procedure is not a machine for hiding the reason. The procedure is a machine for making sure the reason is not needed, and it does that by not asking, and the not-asking is in the first line.** Then he reaches for the other instrument and it does nothing: **it reads nothing, it decides nothing, it does not know where the ford is, it has never known anything, and there is no office in this empire whose business it is to ask it anything. It is a symptom.** The price is about forty-four pounds a year and five journeys and thirty days and three pounds and thirteen shillings and threepence gone out of it with no fund and no form for a fund. **He was not disappointed, and he wrote that down, because a man who is not disappointed is a man who expected something.** And then the day went, in the middle of the ninth of the eleven walks, and nobody took it and nobody noticed it go. **The sixth day of the third month. He was eleven. His mother put a sheet of paper into a box on a kitchen table and told him to leave the room, and he has written it down twice and told it to four people, and it is the first thing in a book with no office on it that has four pages headed *What the blankness is for* and a second heading *Written by a person it was done to, who was not asked*, and it is the whole of what he knows about where the idea came from.** **He can say the date and he can say he was eleven and he can say there was a kitchen and a table and a box, and he cannot say whether he left the room or stood in the doorway. He told that story in a rented room in the fourth week of the fourth month, out loud, to a woman of twenty-four, and it is gone, and it is not coming back, and there is no form anywhere in this empire for a person to have a day back.** He noticed it at about the ninth hour by going back to the fourth page and finding a line about the district works in his own handwriting and no memory of writing it. **Nobody comforted him.** She was in the room for the whole of it and there are two reasons and **they are two instruments and they have never been the same instrument**: a paper, made in a form, in four days, with a day on it, requiring her in any room he is in, producible by anybody holding it; and a watch, a separate instrument, requiring only that a person who is not from the office that cannot be named be in any room he is in. **Both of them require her.** A person who is safe because nobody can instruct her and useful because somebody needs her standing in a room is a person with two boxes filled in on the same form, **and she wrote that sentence down months ago and has not said it out loud to him until this month and she is not going to say it tonight.** She did not stop working: a bundle of about four hundred forms on the corner of the table going into a second order because somebody asked for a second order, and she went on going through them. He picked up a sheet — the sheet a witness is entered upon, the same five lines read out in a hearing room in the second week of the fifth month by a clerk of thirty-four who is a party — **and he is not going to read it out again because he has it by heart and there is nobody in this room who needs it**, and she tells him, without looking up, that he has checked that sheet eleven times since the second month in a corridor and in a rented room and once in a bay four hundred and thirty miles down a river with a lamp behind her, **and that about four hundred forms compared fifth line against fifth line with not one difference is the most thorough piece of work anybody has done on that document in about a hundred and forty years, and it is work a person with a good eye and a lamp can do and no instrument whatever, and he has never once been thanked for it and he is not going to be** — and then: **you did it for your mother and you have been doing it four hundred times since and the two are not the same, and a fact said in a room with two people in it at the eleventh hour is not the only kind of fact this empire has.** She gives him a fact when he asks: the price of a party out loud, **the ninth time, eight of the nine about a person, this one about about four hundred forms, and she has not said it since the fourth month and has not missed it**. And then the fact that is about him: **a day of your own memory is not evidence. It is not in a copy and it is not in a hand anybody can compare and there is no form in this empire for producing it, and the one thing you had that no document in this matter has is the one thing that can be taken out of a book with a pen and a good reason. And there is a book in this matter with about four hundred lines in it about four miles off a road, and it has more of your mother in it than you are going to have again, and you cannot go and get it this week and you have not been able to since the second month.** **Nobody comforted him, and Tamsin Rook did not put her own work down** — she finished the second order at about the eleventh hour, wrote the day against the top sheet in her own hand, and did not show it to him and did not read it out. Then the finding, written out fair and read back twice, second slower, nobody in the room to hear either: **the reconstruction is possible, out of a procedure and out of nothing else, and it will give a shape and not a woman, and that is not a defect in the method, that is the method. I am going to do it anyway. A man who does a thing that cannot give him what he wants is doing a thing that is not heroism and is not cowardice and has no name on any form in this empire, and I have looked, and there is no form for it, and I am going to do it on the fourth day of next week.** Nobody thanked him.

## Chapter 197 — "In One Breath, and In That Order" (3,149)

**POV: Orla Denning. The hearing room, the last sitting, the fifth day of the fourth week of the sixth month of the year after, from about the seventh hour to about the ninth.** About fifty-five, nineteen years of minute books, not a lawyer, not a party, not a judge. **She entered a date four years off in the first week of the fifth month and did not know what she was entering, and she has never once been asked what any of it meant.** She was asked on the second day of the third week, in four words, by a person with no office in this matter; she said yes; she was asked again on the third day and said yes again; and on the fourth day a person asked her whether she understood what she was writing down, and she said she was going to find out and report. The two sentences, in this order, with nothing between them: **the witness status of a person is restored, the record having been wrongly kept, and the restoration is entered with a day on it and a name at the foot of it, and the name goes on a roll, and there is no way in this empire to put a name back a second time.** **An act done by a person who was not heard cannot be undone by a court that has no power over her and no standing to make one.** The first is a thing a court can do because the court found the record wrong. The second is a thing no court in this empire can do, and the reason is not unwillingness and not lack of power, it is that **the person is not alive to be heard, and there is no form anywhere in this empire for a person to be heard after, and the not-hearing is the finding and it cannot be got round by anybody in this room by any instrument anybody has.** And before she reads them: **I am going to read two sentences in this order and I am not going to stop between them, and if anybody in this room thinks the first one makes the second one better then they should leave now, because they will be here for the rest of it and there is nothing in the rest of it either.** Nobody left. Then the act, described without a word for it: **a box on a form printed in nine hundred buildings, filled in by a person with authority to fill boxes, in a room, with a second person in it who was not a party and could not ask anything; nine lines in a woman's hand, on the page whole in a public document at fourpence a copy with a heading that says what it is and where it came from and a man's name at the foot of it and no date and four lines arguing why there is no date; and the last of the nine says it is to be done on a box and not on a paper, because a paper goes to a house and a box goes to a roll.** **The box went to a roll. That is what happened to it and it is the only thing that has happened to it, and there is no instrument in this empire that can be asked what it was for by anybody who was in the room, because the only person who was in the room and was not the person being written about is in nine hundred books under no heading at all, and nobody is going to ask her again.** Then the roll itself: **a bound book about four inches thick with a marbled board and a clasp, in a press in that building for nineteen years; it is a roll of persons; a name goes onto it when a record about that person has been found to be wrongly kept; about nine hundred names have gone onto it in about a hundred and forty years; this is the first one in nineteen years.** She asks for a different pen because the first had been in a pocket, and writes the name in her own hand in the ordinary place with the day against it, and does not hurry and does not go back over it. **Nobody in that room had seen a name go onto that roll in about nineteen years, and a name only goes onto it when a court has found that a record about that person was wrongly kept, and there is no other door into that book, and a person who was never entered as a person in any record has nothing to be restored to.** She reads it back once and not twice, and somebody at the back says *the rule is twice*, and she says, without turning round, that it is a rule of a bay about four hundred and thirty miles down this river that a girl of seventeen made in the second week of the fourth month and nobody decided, and she is not going to decide it in a room with a rail in it, **and the day is in it twice anyway, once in my hand and once in the margin.** Tamsin Rook asks whether it is findable: **it is on a roll in a press in a building in a city and anybody with a copy of the page and about four years can put a hand of mine side by side with about four hundred others and find it. Findable is not a consolation. Findable is what a name on a roll is, and there is no other way to put one back, and a court that has found that a record was wrongly kept has got one instrument and it is a pen, and I have used it, and I would like the room to understand that I have used it and that nobody in this room is going to be thanked for it and I am not going to be either.** Then the refusal, entered with a reason so the not-entering is on the record and is not a silence: **there is a question in front of me about whether a seat of this empire gave an order in this matter. I cannot answer it. Nobody in this room can answer it, and it is not going to be answered in about four years by anybody, and the reason is not modesty and it is not caution. It is that the only document that would bear on it is a document that cannot be produced by anybody.** Asked what document: **a notice of a seat in six numbered lines with a device cut into the head of it and a seal at the foot of it, and under the seal there was a name once.** It is in that building, and she is not going to say the name, describe the hand, or say which of the two notices it is, and she asks for it to be entered that she declined and was asked and was not pressed. And the reason for the whole of it, on the table since the second week of the second month and never read aloud: **a document arrived in that building about four hours before a second one did, and the second one had a seal and nothing under the seal, and it asked in its own second line that no inference be drawn from the absence of any name. The arrival of the second document is the proof.** That is the whole of what the name at the foot of the first one was for, and it took one year and a printer and a piece of paper at fourpence a copy, and nobody did anything wrong in either of them. Nobody thanked her. Then her own sentence, nineteen years long, never said out loud: **a seat is a thing in a room without being a person. I have written nineteen years of minutes about a seat and I could not tell you one single thing about what a seat is, and I have never been in the same room as one, and there is no post in this empire whose business it is to be in the same room as one. I am the only person in this room who cannot be examined, and I am the only person in this room who is paid nothing, and those are the same reason and nobody has ever put them together.** And: **the finding is about a record and a roll and a name. The seat is not in the finding. Naming a thing in a room does not put the thing in the room, and there is no form in this empire that makes a document a person, and a document that names an office is a document and not an office.** Then a question is named.
