A question had been put to a court in this city about nine years ago, in a room with a number on the door, and the court still exists and sits on the same ground. **"The Cinder Clause," said Orla Denning**, once, correctly, and stopped, and the court recorded that the question exists. **The question exists. It was asked nine years ago by the court that asked it. It has not been answered in nine years by the court that asked it**, and nobody in the room has been asked it and nobody is going to answer it, and she says not one word about what it means because she does not know and there is nothing in the eleven books in that building that says. Entered in those words, and: **a document is findable, and I am going to put it in a minute book with the day on it and my name at the foot of it, and that is the only protection a question has ever had in this empire.** Then Tamsin Rook, who is in the room and is not a witness and cannot be examined and is not on any roll of anybody in this matter, and both instruments require her: the price of a party, **the tenth time**, nine of the ten about a person and this one about a name on a roll, **which is the only thing she has ever been in a room about that she cannot get out of by leaving the room**, with the number, four years and a hand of hers and about eleven weeks of standing in a corridor. Told she is not on the roll: **the woman who is not on the roll is sixty-three and she is in this city, and she cannot be put on that roll by this court or by any other, because the roll is a roll of persons and she was never entered as one.** The court rose at about the ninth hour. **A name was restored to a roll with a day on it and a name at the foot of it, and it is findable, and there is no way in this empire to put a name back a second time. An act done by a person who was not heard was not undone, and cannot be, and the not-undoing is entered with a day on it and a name at the foot of it, and it is findable too. And there is no way in this empire to un-undo one either, and that is the half of it that nobody is going to write about, and a reader is going to be left with two facts and no way of telling which of them this is about, and that is not an accident of the finding and it is not a defect in the record. It is what a room is.** Nobody thanked anybody, and about four hundred and thirty miles down this river a second season is in its fourth month and has not been asked of anybody.

## Chapter 198 — "The Hearing She Is Owed" (2,726)

**POV: Halla Wray. The tool shed at the Slade end, the first week of the seventh month of the year after, the second day.** Fifty-one, foreman of the Slade Cut, **an office with no office in it: a thing nine families agreed to about eleven years ago and did not write down and cannot produce, held the way a person holds a job nobody is going to ask her about.** Her term ran out in the third week of the third month. **She has put her own name at the foot of three lists of works and it is the first name at the foot of anything on that cut in sixty years.** **She can read. That is not in dispute and has never been and is in nine years of a shed nobody's business, and it is the other thing about her that is not in dispute: nobody at the district works has ever once in nine years asked her to read anything.** The paper came up the road in the third week of the fourth month on a cart with a boy and not with anybody who knew what was in it, with a seat's device cut into the head of it, no office on the wrapper, **her name at the top of it in the ordinary way**, and it sat in a box on a shelf in that shed for about eleven weeks. The shed is about nine foot by eleven, with a door that shuts, a bench along the north wall that four men can sit on, and a lamp not lit until about the seventh hour. **About nine men came in on the second day of the first week of the seventh month because somebody put a word in the yard and not because anybody asked them, and two of them came late on purpose.** She knew why, said so afterwards in the yard to the man who had come down the lane and to nobody in the shed: **they said no in the first season, both of them, at the gate, in the same words anybody uses, with a reason, and the reason went in the book in the place where the no is, and they have not been asked since and they are not going to be asked. They came late because they wanted to hear what I said before they decided whether to still mean it. That is not a thing a person is supposed to be able to do and they have done it and I am not going to make them explain.** And: **if they say it again it is because somebody asked them again, and nobody is going to ask them again until the season comes round, and when the season comes round somebody is going to have to. And that somebody is going to be me, because I hold the list, and the day somebody hands me a season to ask about is the day I am asking a person who has already said no once.** And: **forty-two years on this bank and nine years holding the only job on it that is written down nowhere, and there is no form in this empire that makes a person be in charge of a thing, and the nine families agreed it out loud about eleven years ago in a shed and it cannot be produced, and there is nobody in this district who would know how to write it down.** He had not got a book; she said to tell it to the man of thirty-eight, who will write it down for nothing, and she is not going to thank him; and: **everybody on this bank has got his name. That is the whole of what a name at the foot of a list is.** Then: **nobody sent her, nobody asked her, there is no form in this empire for a person who comes on her own account, and the whole of what she wanted was to be asked something in a room where she had to stand there while she said it.** She says before anybody has said anything that she has been asked about the bank five times this year and said no five times and every one was right, and has said in that shed that she would rather be asked than not, and has been asked twice and said yes twice, and has refused to be asked a third time without being asked. The man who came down the lane says he cannot arrange it and is not going to pretend he can: **the reason I am in this shed is that a thing happened in a city four hundred and thirty miles up this river and I have read about it, and I cannot get there, and I am not going to send anybody.** So they ask her. It took about four minutes to arrange and was arranged by a man who had never arranged anything in his life, out loud, in front of about nine men. **A foreman of fifty-one, in a shed, being asked, out loud, in a room she has to stand in, for the first time in nine years.** She answers in about four minutes, as arithmetic, with no speech in it: the bank is not mine, it is a thing nine families agreed to and it is not written down and cannot be produced, and that is why there is nobody to sue and that is why she can be the whole of it and is not a person anybody can be angry with; the form came with a heading over it and nothing under it and the person who filled it in filled in a thing, **and nobody has ever been asked what the words mean and there is no post in this empire whose job is to stand in front of a heading and ask; I have been on this bank since I was nine and I have never once in nine years been asked to read a word of anything, and a man in a city has now found out the rate on a wall and I have known the rate on this wall since I was seventeen.** A man of about thirty from the second gang says she could have told him, and she says she could have and did not and is not going to now, **because a person who is paid nothing can be asked, and a person who is paid nothing is also the only kind of person in this cut who can be told no by anybody. If I start telling, then in about four years there is a piece of paper in this shed with a sentence of mine on it and a day on it and a name at the foot of it, and I have watched a man of thirty-eight do exactly that with his mother's handwriting and I have read what it cost him, and I am not starting at fifty-one with a boy at home.** Then the other three things, flatly, in order: the second season began in the first month of this year, about the length a season is, about forty-one people, nobody agreed it and nobody refused it and nobody signed anything, wages held against a company whose whole money is four shillings a year and all of it the rent of a roof — **that is the cheapest hold there is and it is not a villain's hold and it is an ordinary hold, and it is cheap because there is nothing in it to break**; a factor's letter on a bench in the store up the road, four lines, nineteen days when it went on the bench and about forty now, wanting the name of a person who may be served and that person's consent, **and it is not going to be answered, and every day it is not answered is a day nobody has been entered, and I know what a day of that is worth and I am not going to be the one who spends it**; and about four people in that bay cannot read a paragraph, never asked once, not asked a second time, **and there is no column for them and there is not going to be one, and the reason there is not going to be one is that a column for them would be a column somebody would have to fill.** Then the sentence she has been carrying since the sixth month of last year: **A carriage is not a wage. A thing that pays for a person to come and does not pay them for the day is not an offer, it is a way of counting how many rooms a person is in. I said that in that bay in the sixth month of last year to about thirty people, and it was the truest thing anybody said that month, and it has not been useful to anybody since, because being right about a thing is not the same as a thing being done about.** Told she has said that before: **I have said it once, and I have not said it to this room, and there is a book-keeper on that bank who has wanted the other half of it since the third month and is not going to ask me for it, and the reason is that the day he asks is the day I stop saying the half I have got.** Told she has never given him the other half either: **no, and I am not going to, and it is not in this shed, and I have had it since the third month and I use it about four times a season, and it does not go into a room that writes it down, and you can put that in whatever you keep and I will not be asked about it again.** Nobody thanked her; she said in advance that nobody was to, and the man who arranged the asking did not thank her and said afterwards in the yard that he had wanted to and had been told not to and understood why. Then she got the box down off the shelf, because it was in her way, and there was nothing in the world that had ever told her to open it. She opened it: one side of a sheet of good paper, not printed, a seat's own device cut into the head, six numbered lines and a foot, the foot a seal and **nothing under the seal**, and the second line asking that no inference of any kind be drawn from the absence of any name, and **her name at the top of it. Not at the foot. At the top**, in the ordinary way, and nobody has ever asked her whether she wanted it there and there is no form anywhere in this empire that requires anybody to ask. The third line she read twice, the second reading slower, with the men who had not gone standing at the door: *where a recorded claim is entered and marked disputed, and the family of the claimant holds no enforceable asset, the person of that family who is of age and resident is the family's representative in this matter, is to be entered as such in the office of the seat, and no further consent of that person is required.* **That is me, and I am not a person of any family and I have never been in a book of anybody's, and that is because the job is not written down. A company of nine families and forty-one people is a family, and the only one of us with a place of custom or of work in a book is the one they cannot write down either. I have been that for about eleven years without knowing it, and I have been unfindable on purpose, and now I am findable by accident.** Asked who put her name on it: **nobody put my name on it. Somebody put a class on it and the class has got one member, and there is a woman in a city four hundred and thirty miles up this river who is a member of the same class, and she found out in the fourth week of the fifth month by a district clerk walking down a lane with a board, and she said no out loud in a room with a day on it, and it did not work.** She put the sheet down on the bench, face up, where anybody who came in could read it. **Nobody has been asked. There is no form anywhere in this empire for a person to be asked, and there is no form anywhere in this empire for a person to be let out of a thing that does not need them, and the word for what she has just been put into is the same word the mason's four days are under and the same word the wage of a dyer of twenty is under, and the word is *held*, and a person who is held cannot get up and go.** Halla Wray got up and went, and left the sheet on the bench, and shut the door, and it is a quarter past the seventh hour and the lamp is not lit.

## Chapter 199 — "Two Boxes Filled, and a Third Thing With No Box" (3,002)

**POV: Tamsin Rook. A room four bays from a counter, the third week of the seventh month of the year after.** **Nothing had happened for three weeks, and that is the whole reason there is a scene.** The finding is entered and findable and nobody has thanked anybody; the day a man of thirty-eight lost is three weeks old and is not coming back and nobody has come to see; the paper with a seat's device on it went to a shed on a bank in the first week of this month and there has been no letter about it, because there is no form that requires one. She is in four bays because a paper says so and the paper is not the reason; she is a party; **there are four of a certain kind of thing in her own rooms, one of them there since the first month of the year before last, and she has not thought about them in about two years and did not think about them tonight.** She said in advance, in a room, with the reason: **I am not going to decide anything in a room on a day when one of us has been up two nights.** Neither of them has been up two nights, it is the day, and **the sentence is the reason there is a scene here and not an apology.** He comes at about the seventh hour; she makes him sit; he says nothing for about a minute and a half. Then she puts a book on the table: **a hard-backed book with no office on it, hers, her own hand in it in about nine places**, opened near the back and turned round, with **two boxes ruled on the page in her own hand with a straight edge and a pen, and neither of them had ever been filled in.** It is not a form, not printed, never sent anywhere, not a copy of anything; she ruled it about eleven weeks ago because she could not get the sentence she wanted out of her head onto a page; she has not shown it to him and has not thought about it in about nine days. **Both of them are you. Not you the person. You the two instruments.** And the two instruments, kept apart in the order she has kept them apart for about a year: a **paper** — a court order made in a form in four days with a day on it, requiring her in any room he is in, producible by anybody holding it, produced four times, every one of them producing her in a room in front of about thirty people, the last in the fourth week of the sixth month, and she was in it and could not be examined and was not examinable and was in it anyway — and a **watch**, a separate instrument that does not name him and does not name her, requiring only that a person who is not from the office that cannot be named be in any room he is in. **It does not say who. There are about four hundred people in this city who could satisfy it, and it has been satisfied four times, and three of those four times it was me**, and the fourth was a girl of about twenty-five at an intake desk who opened a wrapper because she was going to open it anyway. So it is not about you and it is not about me and it is about a room — **and that is the part that has taken me about eleven weeks to write down: a person who is safe because nobody can instruct her and useful because somebody needs her standing in a room is a person with two boxes filled in on the same form.** She puts the pen down. **That is not a complaint. It is not a thank you. It is a description of a person**, she has been that person since the second month and has nobody to be it with, because everybody she knows is somebody's clerk; **it has taken me eleven weeks to work out that the sentence is about me and not about the arrangement, and about nine days to work out that I do not mind**; and she says both out loud because **my third line forbids advice and my fourth line says a fact is not advice, and I have said the words of both of those lines in this room tonight and I have never said them out loud in a room before.** He says there is a third thing; it has no box and there is no form anywhere in this empire that makes one and she has looked. He asks her to say it so he can write it down; she says no, and it is the first time anybody has refused him anything. **He tries four of them, out loud, standing up, in the way a man who has spent this spring learning to say a hard thing in a room tries a sentence and finds out whether it is true.** The first: that he could not do this without her — no, in four words. The second: that he would be careful — **that *careful* is a word for a person who is going to do a thing and it is not a thing and it goes in a book.** The third: that he had thought about it for about eleven weeks and could not make it into a sentence about the two of them — **the first of the four that was true, and it was not enough.** The fourth he does not finish. *You have stopped.* **I have stopped because I have got to the end of what I prepared and I have not prepared any more of it, and I am a man who prepares things, and there is nobody in this empire I would rather have stopped at the end of a sentence than in.** **Then that is the sentence. You have got to the end of what you prepared. That is what the third thing is, and it has no box because there is no form in this empire that will hold a sentence a man has not finished, and I am not going to help you finish it and I am not going to ask you to.** And: **that is not a thing anybody can be a party to.** No — **and that is the first good thing anybody has said in this matter since the first week of the fifth month, and I have written it on nothing.** And the shape of the third thing: **a thing this empire can put in a book is a thing this empire can ask about, and there is one thing in this room that is not going in a book** — not because it is unimportant, but because if it is written down then in about four years a clerk can hold it up and read it out and ask them both the same question, and a person remembering a thing and a person reading a thing back are two different acts and only one of them is evidence. Then the rule: **the rule of the twelfth month of last year is there, on the table, in both our heads; either may put a choice in writing with a day on it and the other must answer in a room, in words, with a date; it has been used six times, and it could be used tonight in about nine seconds and it would be the correct instrument, and it would be a document, and there would be a day on it, and a name at the foot of it, and about four years.** *Are you not going to use it.* **We are not going to use it and a correct non-use is as good as a use and it is entered as one.** Then she fills in the two boxes in her own hand with the day on it and reads them back twice, the second slower, and he does not read it, does not ask to, and does not touch the page. *Two names that are the same name.* **Two boxes and one name in each, and they are the same name, and that is the honest fact. It is why I ruled them by hand instead of writing one out and drawing a line under it**: a line under one name would have made it look like a single thing, and it is two things that happen to land on the same person four times since the second month. Then the other two sentences, because the page would be dishonest if she did not: **the undertaking of the fourth of the first month is live and has not been retired and has not been amended and has not been exercised tonight, and I am not going to exercise it tonight, and it stands**; and *I know. I have not put it in front of you once since the fourth month and that is not an oversight and I have thought about it every week.* *I do know why.* *Say it.* **Because there is nothing in it that I have got a reason against, and if I put it in front of you and you gave me a reason, then I would have to act on the reason, and the reason would be in a room, and I have watched about four hundred people in this city be careful in about four hundred rooms and I am not going to be the four hundred and first, and that is the whole of why I have not put it there and it is a bad reason and I know it is a bad reason.** It is a bad reason, **and it is the reason I have not asked you for it, and we are both hiding behind the same bad reason and neither of us is going to say so out loud, and that is the third thing and it has no box.** Then he says she is not going to say the price of it, and she says **I have said it ten times in a room and I am not going to say it an eleventh time in this one, and I am not saying it because it would put a number in a room and the number is the only part of me that anybody can be held to and I have had enough of being held to.** And that she has never once asked him for anything. And the one thing she is going to ask: **I am asking you not to thank me.** *I was not going to.* **I want it written down that I asked and that you said you were not going to, and that there is no form anywhere that requires it**, and there are four of them in her rooms and one has been there since the first month of the year before last and has not been sent and has not been opened, and she has not thought about it tonight and is not going to start. Then the lamp, and the door, and the two of them standing. **In the fourth week of the fourth month of this year he left at about the ninth hour and she shut the room, and that is written down, and it is not going to be unsaid, and he has not asked her about it and she has not offered.** **On the third day of the third week of the seventh month of the year after there is a lamp that is still lit at about the ninth hour and a door that is open and nobody shuts it**, and the difference between those two facts is the whole of what the last three weeks were for, and **there is no form anywhere in this empire that requires a door to be shut, and there is no column anywhere in this empire for the two boxes being filled, and the whole of what either of them has done tonight is the first thing either of them has done that no form in this empire requires.** It is not entered. **About four hundred and thirty miles of road is what it would cost anybody who wanted to come and see it, and there is no fund, and nobody is going to be told, and the reason is not privacy. It is that a fact said in a room with two people in it is the only kind of fact in this empire that is not evidence of anything, and they would rather have that.** And the thing left standing, in her mouth, not a comfort and not a reward and not about the hearing and not about the mark on his wrist and not about the day he lost: **The third thing has no box. That is what the whole of it since the second month has been for. I have been the woman with two boxes filled in on one form, and I have been the most dangerous person in this matter, and I have been the person nobody in it can protect, and those three things have been true at once since the second month of this year, and I did not know it and he did not know it, and it has now been said out loud in a room, and it is not going in either of our mouths again.** Nobody was thanked. Nothing was forgiven. **There is nothing in the room to forgive and she has said that in a room before and said it again tonight in different words**, and he did not say his mother was right, and nobody told him she was kind, and the day is a day and the door is open and nothing has come through it yet.

## Chapter 200 — "A List Of Works, and Nineteen Who Say No Again" (3,115)

**POV: Rennick Adley. The north bay and a hired stone store off the Slade, the fourth day of the last week of the seventh month of the year after, from about the sixth hour.** Thirty-eight, keeping the books of the Slade Cut Company since the second month of next year, whose whole money is four shillings a year and all of it the rent of the building; the man who put the name of that company into a form in about four seconds on the second day of the second week of the fourth month because the box says the person, institution or thing engaged in the matter and there was nothing else to hand. **The second season was asked for on the fourth day of the last week of the seventh month, in a bay, standing up, by a man who said out loud before he started that he had been asked to ask and had not volunteered.** He has a factor's letter of four lines on a bench that has not been answered and is not going to be answered, and **about nineteen people who said no with a reason in the first season are still behind that bank, and this is the first week since the first month in which any of them has been asked anything at all.** The list of works was read out and **a man was first on it.** He had asked, on the fifteenth of the seventh month of a year that is not this one, to be asked last, and he was written first, and he has never corrected it, because a list of works is read out and a name at the top of it is the one everybody hears, and he wanted to hear it. **Kem Ostry is a carter.** He works the Slade to the mill wall and back with a cart of no particular description, has no employer of record, and has been paid at a guild rate of **one shilling and sixpence a day for a barrow of stone, a man and a boy**, since the fourth month, and his name has been in nobody's column anywhere. He said no at the gate in the first season in the same words as about sixty other people and gave a reason: **a name at the foot of a list of works means somebody comes and finds out whether it is working every fortnight for a season, and he had been the one watching since the fourth month and would like it stopped.** He was not argued with and not asked a second time; the reason was entered **because a person is entitled to have the reason they gave written down in the place where the no is, and not in a letter.** He was not asked a second time either, and **that is the finding: nobody had asked him, so nobody had to ask him again, and the reason nobody had asked him is that a person who is owed a wage cannot be asked about a season, because asking is a conversation and a conversation with a person whose wage is held is a conversation with a person who is losing money by having it.** *You have not asked me once since the first month, and I have been waiting for you to.* **Noted, and I did not ask you because I am not allowed to, and I am not allowed to because I am the one who put a roof in a box on the second day of the second week of the fourth month, and a man in an office read a definition out to a mason in a corridor in the third week into the fourth week of the third month, and both of those are the same sentence said by two people in four hundred and thirty miles, and I have carried mine since the second day of the second week of the fourth month without anybody to hand.** He said it again in the same words; about nine men in three gangs heard it; **the reason went in the book in the place where the no is.** Then the rest, one after the other, out loud, in a bay, in about four minutes, and **about nineteen people said no again.** Every one gave the reason they gave the first time, none of the nineteen reasons was the same as any other, and none was a reason about the weather or the mill or money; he wrote all nineteen in the third column of the bay's own ledger with the day on each, **and read the whole page back twice, and the second reading was slower and was the one he did not skip.** **Nobody in that bay has ever asked him where he got the double reading from, and he has been asked twice about it by a woman of thirty-four four hundred and thirty miles up this river and has not told her and is not going to be asked; the first reading is for the words and the second reading is for the people who did not have them the first time.** Then the nineteen reasons, read out, not the names, **because a name in a room is a thing that can be carried out of a room**: a boy on a list of works with a day against it and somebody coming to look at it every fortnight; *I am the one who holds the book and I will not hold a book that has a season in it*; *I have not been asked anything in nine years and I am not going to be asked in the first week*; *I said no once and the reason went in a book and nobody argued with me, and I would like that to happen twice*; *I am paid by a man who has not got four shillings a year and he would have to find it out of me*; *the last time there was water in it I was the one who went out on the low side with a rope and I am not doing it on a paper*. And the nineteenth, a woman with two children who had come down the lane in the rain, in four words: **I have to be home.** *That is not a reason.* **That is a reason. A person is entitled to have the reason they gave written down in the place where the no is, and not a second question, and not an opinion from the back of a bay. I have been keeping books since the second month of next year and I have read every form in this store and there is not one page in any of them that says a person has to give you a better reason than that one.** She went home at about the seventh hour; her name is in the third column with a day on it and no reason attached beyond the four words, **because the four words were the reason.** And: **a refusal is a thing a person is entitled to make once and have it kept and not be troubled about it again until the season comes round, and the season came round and about nineteen people said no again and they are still behind the bank.** About four people in that bay cannot read a paragraph: never asked once, not asked on the fourth day of the last week of the seventh month, no column and none going to be one, **because a column for them would be a column somebody would have to fill.** A girl of seventeen at the back on a written engagement at forty-five pence a day and four days a week doing the thing she is paid for; **not spoken to about the season, did not ask, and a person who is paid to read is a person who can be told to stop**, which he has said out loud in this bay three times and has not sent anybody to anybody and is not going to; not thanked, not going to start, **and nobody asked her to read anything that carries a rule, because there is no rule in that bay to carry and there has not been one since a man of fifty refused to rule a fourth column in a ledger in the second week of the eighth month of next year in about nine seconds.** Then the hold, read out: against the Slade Cut Company, being a thing, in the matter of a recorded claim entered and marked disputed, wages held at the same rate and for the same period, and a person whose wages are so held not to be paid that held sum by any person. **The guarantee, printed whole, word for word identical to Chapters 0161, 0164, 0170, 0180 and 0190, and no child named.** A bill at Lowcross of nineteen pounds three and fourpence, unpaid, nobody liable, about a penny a day the real cost, no line for a bridge in that fund and none in nineteen years, four hundred and eleven people on the far side, three hundred and eighty-eight crossings, **and those are two figures and they are never the same.** **The thirty-one of Mosswake are thirty-one, and there is a name and a door against every one of them in a returning officer's own hand, and there is no form anywhere in this empire for asking a returning officer what he wrote down after he had walked it.** The factor's letter of four lines on a bench since the second week of the third month, requiring the name, place of custom and description of a person who may be served together with that person's consent, saying that without both it cannot proceed and will not proceed and the matter will stand against the works until one is given — **it is not going to be answered, and every day it is not answered is a day nobody has been entered.** Nobody thanked anybody; nothing was forgiven, nothing paid back, nothing in that bay reversed. Then the last of it, four hundred and thirty miles up this river, in the plainest words and none of it a question. **The fourth counter of a notary's table, a sheet of printed matter with three ruled boxes on it, an oak slab and a rail and a fee board of four things and none of them time.** Box one: a name whose witness status was restored in the fourth week of the sixth month with a day on it and a name at the foot of the entry, on a roll, findable, with no way in this empire to put a name back a second time. Box two: a name entered as the representative of a family on the fourth day of the third week of the fifth month by a clerk filling a box the way the box is printed, and that person said no out loud in a room with the day on it and it did not work. **Two of them are filled with the names of two people who are not the clerk.** Box three is a description, and the description says **that there is a person in this matter who has not been asked and has not been found** — and it does not say a name, does not say a hand, does not say a lane or a county, and says two facts that are both findable and neither of which is a person. **There is a fourth space on that sheet with no heading over it, where a heading would go, and nobody has ever put one there, and about two hundred and forty people have never known it is there.** On the fourth shelf of a received room in that city there is a bundle marked *damaged, four items, uncollated*, there about twelve years, **not opened, not named, and it is a location and it is not a discovery**, and there is no form that requires a person to go and look at a bundle because they have found out that it is there. And the door of that room is a door and it is open and **nothing has come through it yet**, and a person may now ask for a thing in a room, and about four hundred and thirty miles of road is what that costs, and there is no fund. **The entry was read back twice and the second reading was slower. A girl of seventeen about four hundred and thirty miles down a river made that the rule of a bay in the second week of the fourth month, and it is now the rule of a counter, and nobody decided to make it the rule of a counter, and that is what a rule is.** There was one person in that room: a clerk of thirty-four, eleven years at that counter, not a lawyer, a party to an instrument about a dead woman's name, who has said the price of it out loud in a room ten times and nobody has thanked her once and would like it written down that she did not, **because in about four years somebody is going to read that she said the price ten times and they are going to assume somebody heard it.** Nobody had heard it. And at about the sixth hour, alone, at a counter with a rail on it, in a room with a pane out of the window, she said out loud, to nobody: **A person who is not told has not been erased. A person in a house that is shut has no address. Those are two different things and the first one is the harder one, and I have known the second one since the first month and I have never once been able to say it out loud without the first one coming with it, and I am saying both of them now and I am not going to leave one out to make the other one easier. This has been about the second one for about a hundred and forty years and it is about the first one since the first month, and a form printed in about nine hundred buildings has been asking the wrong person for about a hundred and forty years, and the only time it got asked at the right person it was in a kitchen with a pencil, and the person who asked it said the price out loud first.** Nobody thanked her. **And about nineteen people said no again, and they are still behind a bank, and about four hundred and thirty miles up this river a door is open and nothing has come through it yet.**

## What Volume 04 Batch 0005 resolved, what it did not, and what it hands on

**Resolved:** a hearing has a name and two dates, and both dates are in one minute book with a clerk's name at the foot of them, and one of the two is four years off. A form printed in about nine hundred buildings has been asked what it means, and the fifth line of it has been put in a room and read out and answered in nine minutes, and it is the only instrument in this empire that can hand a person the rest of what they wrote, and it has been used once. A court asked a clerk and a magistrate whether a woman of sixty-three is on a roll and she is not and cannot be. Pell Vey's hand is documented by comparison, his delivery stub is in a clerk's hand at the foot of an entry, his file is in four places and one of them is a back room, and he refused to answer in the same fourteen words on three days. A woman of twenty has found out in the ordinary way, from a board and a basket, that she has been entered as a representative, and has said no in a room with the day on it, and the no has not worked. A magistrate has given evidence about a river, named no person, and entered a finding against her own practice in a room with a witness in it, and it is not absolution and it is not a conversion. A man of thirty-eight has attempted a reconstruction out of a procedure, has failed, and has lost a day of his own memory that is named as a day and is not coming back. A name is restored to a roll with a day on it and a name at the foot of it. A question has been named for the first time anywhere in the manuscript and has not been answered and is not going to be. A foreman of fifty-one has been asked, out loud, in a shed, for the first time in nine years, and has answered in arithmetic. Two boxes on a form have been filled with the same name on the same night, and a third thing with no box has been said out loud in a room and has not been written down. And the second season has been asked for and about nineteen people have said no again.

**Not resolved, and not this batch's to resolve:** the act done by a person who was not heard is not undone and cannot be; nobody can prove whether a seat gave an order and the name that would prove it is not going to be said aloud; the question about a clause has never been answered in nine years by the court that asked it; a woman of sixty-three is not on any roll and cannot be put on one because she was never asked; nobody was entered that anybody entered was asked about first, and two people now are; a wage is held in a household of one and about forty-one wages are held against a roof and a mason's four days are held and a book-keeper's factor's letter is on a bench; a date four years off cannot be unscheduled; the forty-one forms have been checked and not thanked; the end of the run, the row, the striking-out, the column headed *by whose authority* and the name in it are still not read out; the Ashfall bundle is shut and unnamed and what Ilyra Kest found is unanswered; the two sealed pages are shut with two refusals between them and no third; and the volume's own next question — if the office was meant to be temporary, who changed it into an inheritable one, and why are dragons themselves bound by the altered compact — is not asked in this batch and is not going to be asked in the next one either.

# Volume 05, Chapters 201–210, Batch 0001

## Chapter 201 — "The Form With Her Name At The Foot Of It" (3,109)

**POV: Orla Denning. The office of a seat, a building off the old river road, a room on the ground floor with a window about two feet wide and a pane out of it, eleven minute books on a shelf, the second day of the first week of the ninth month of the year after.** About fifty-five, nineteen years of the books, the first four of them in a hand that is not the one she is using now, not a lawyer, not a party, not a judge, and **she has never been asked what any of it meant.** A bundle comes up on a tray because a thing that has been heard gets a file and a file with no heading over it cannot be found, and this office finds its own things twice a year. **The head of a file is a printed label with four things on it and one of the four is a box: *Matter. Place. Day. The person, institution or thing engaged in the matter.*** The other three she can do standing up. She cannot fill the fourth, and she fills it with the thing the roll gave her, and the thing is a household, and the matter is a claim about a Kest house about four miles off the road with nobody in it. **A return is one printed sheet with that column on it, filled in at this end and sent out, and a keeper of a roll copies it into her own book, and that has been the ordinary way for about a hundred and forty years and there is no form that requires a keeper to be asked whether the column is right before she copies it.** She goes down the bundle and is not looking for anything on purpose: in about nine of the returns the column holds a household, in about four a company, in two a company of watermen, in one a chapel, and in one there is a line through the column where a name had been, struck out with a pen and not a rule. **Not one of them had a person in it, except one.** That one is dated the fourth day of the third week of the fifth month, for a district about four hundred and thirty miles up this river, and the column says a name, and she knows the name and has not said it out loud in that room and is not going to. **So the office asked a roll of households for a person, and a roll of households gave it one, and the office wrote the one down, and the office did everything correctly and the person said no and the no did not work.** Her own name is at the foot of that return, in her own hand, in about nine seconds, and she has not been asked and nobody has been asked, and she has thought about those nine seconds every week since the fifth month and has told nobody. **A form which cannot be asked cannot be un-filled, and it cannot be un-filled by the person who filled it.** That is the whole of what she has got out of nineteen years and a tray and it is not in any of the eleven books and she has looked. She writes *household* on the file head and the day and the place and the matter, and then she comes back to the fourth line and writes a second line under it, in the same hand, in about nine seconds: **I am asked to state the person, institution or thing engaged in the matter. There is no person engaged in it. There is a household of nine doors about four miles off the road, empty, and a claim, and a finding on a page. Nothing in this bundle is a person except one line, and the one line is a person of twenty about four hundred and thirty miles from this desk, and I did not choose her and I was not asked about her and I entered her in the fifth month, correctly, in the ordinary way, and my name is at the foot of that sheet and it is the second thing in this matter with my hand at the foot of it and the first one I did not choose.** Then the thing that has no form behind it: **a file with two lines under a box is a file that will be asked about, and in about four years a person with a copy of the right page can put it side by side with the return and ask a clerk of this office to explain the difference, and she will have to explain it, and she cannot.** So she says out loud to an empty room that there are two ways and the second one is hers: write the one line, put her name at the foot, carry the tray down the corridor and say nothing, and in four years there is a file with a household in it and a clerk in it and a day on it, **and that is the whole of the protection and it is worth fourpence of ink** — and the other way, which is that a person who writes the second line cannot be asked to produce the first one, because she will produce it gladly, and say out loud in whatever room she is in that she filled that box on the fourth day of the third week of the fifth month and that nobody asked her and that she did it correctly, in the same breath with the finding that the no did not work. **A clerk who takes a file out of the ordinary course has not done anything a form forbids, because no form in this empire has a line about it, and there is no form anywhere that requires a clerk to put a sheet in a press, and that is why it is hers to decide and why it is hers to be shown.** Then the corridor. An unnamed carrier who has carried trays for about nine years puts his hand on it and stops, because there are two lines on the head where there is one. **Who fills that one in — the person, institution or thing? I have carried more of them than I can count and I have never once seen anybody stop to read that one.** She answers him out loud, in a corridor, in about four minutes, and tells him what the box is and where the words come from and that the office is the only place in this empire that fills it in and does it right, and that what goes in that column is a household or a company and that nobody has ever asked which of the two a thing is, and she tells him the definition and the roll and the four miles of road and the day in the fifth month, **without once saying the name.** **He asked because he was going to say something about the trays, and she answered because he was standing there, and neither of them chose it, and she has thought about that since and it is the reason the answer was any good. A room wants a record. A corridor wants a tray gone. Neither of those is a reason to ask a question and both of them are why one got asked. A form does not get asked anything by a man with a tray. A woman does, and the woman answered, and there is not going to be a post for it.** He asks whether to put it down as usual. **Put it down as usual and read the head of the file to the man at the counter on the second floor, out loud, both lines.** I want him to hear the second one and not only the first, and I am not going to say why and you are not to ask me. *That is not usual.* **And I would like it noticed that you asked me who fills that box in, and that nobody in nineteen years has asked me what the words on it are for, and that you did not ask a form anything. You asked a woman standing at a counter, and I answered you because I was standing there.** He reads it out on the stairs, both lines, which is not usual, and she hears him from the bottom and does not go up. Last: **There is no post in this empire whose job is to stand in front of a heading and ask what it is for** — not in that building, not in that city, not in any of the four hundred and thirty miles between that desk and a district where a woman of about sixty walks down a lane with a sheet on a board and a basket once a year, **and she does not know what the fourth column of her own roll is for either, and she never will, and nobody is going to ask her, and it is four hundred and thirty miles and there is no fund.** The file is on the table with two lines on the head of it and it is not in the press and it is going to stay not in the press for as long as she is the clerk who keeps the books.

## Chapter 202 — "Fourpence And Nobody Writes It Down" (2,822)

**POV: Marn Ottery. The fourth counter of the Notaries' Table in Auremar, an oak slab, a rail, a fee board of four things and none of them time, the second day of the second week of the ninth month of the year after.** Thirty-four, eleven years at that counter, the one for scale instruments and it has been for a hundred and forty years, come to it from the second counter where estates are, not a lawyer and does not want to be one, **and a party to an instrument about a dead woman's name who has said the price of that out loud in a room ten times and whom nobody has thanked once and who did not expect to be thanked once and would like it written down that she did not, because in about four years somebody is going to read that she said the price ten times and they are going to assume somebody heard it. Nobody had heard it.** A woman of twenty has been up to that counter three times; the third time is the time, because the first two times she stood at the rail and looked at the board and went away, and a clerk notices that the way a clerk notices everything, which is to say she notices it and does nothing about it for about eleven days. **You have not asked it twice. You have looked at the board twice. The board does not have your question on it and it is not going to, and there is no price on that board for a question.** The woman puts a sheet of her own on the slab with a heading she wrote herself and one day on it and nothing else. **That is yours.** *Yes.* **I am not going to write anything on it, and here is the price of what I am about to do.** A document with my hand at the foot of it is findable in about four years by anybody with a copy of the right page, and I have said that number out loud twice in a room and I am saying it again because a number a person has said can be held to. A question about a box is worth a question at a notary's table, a question is a shilling there, and here there is nothing, **and the nothing is why I can do this and the nothing is also why you had to come three times.** Then the answer, in about four minutes, without a single word twice: **A representative is a person the machinery can act on.** That is the whole of the word and it is a box's word, not a lawyer's, and about four hundred people a year come up to that counter wanting a lawyer's word and there has never once been one on the board. **Being in that box is the only way anybody has ever found of making you a party**, and it did it without asking you, and the third line of the notice says in its own words that no further consent of the person is required, **and that is not a wicked sentence. It is a sentence written by somebody who needed a form to go out in a week.** What it lets them do: **Nothing you would recognise.** It lets a form put your name in a place where a name is a thing that can be asked about. There is no hand behind it. There is no man behind it. **The wage of yours that is held is held under a heading with nothing under the heading, and this box is the same, and the two of them are the same act done by the same machinery in the same year, and about four hundred and thirty miles apart.** *And can it come out.* **No.** *Write that down.* **I cannot.** **Then say why not, and say it out loud, and I want it in the room.** Marn Ottery puts both hands flat on the oak, which she does about twice a year, and says: **There is no form in this empire for a document about a person who did not ask to be in one. That is the reason and it is the whole of the reason and it is not a matter of taste and it is not caution. A form is a thing that happens to a person.** Every one of them is printed, every one of them is filled in by somebody else, **and not one of them in about a hundred and forty years has had a line on it for a person to put a question on and get an answer in writing, and the reason is that a form about a person is the thing the person cannot get out of.** And she has looked, at that counter, in the book of forms under it, in the ordinary course of her job, and it is not there and never has been, and the last time this empire came close was about a hundred and forty years ago, and what it had then was a fifth line that asked the second person whether she was a party before anything else was said, **and that line is dead, and it is dead because the person it asks cannot be told that there is a question.** The woman of twenty: **So the answer exists, and there is nowhere to put it.** **The answer exists and it is in your head now and it has a day on it because you asked it on a day,** and the only place in this empire it can go is a room with a person in it, and a room is not a form, and a room writes down whatever it likes and can be asked about it. Then a blank out of the box, where there are about four hundred, bought and not filled in: **That is fourpence and I am not charging you fourpence and I am not going to pretend that is a kindness, because it is the ordinary trade of this counter and I would have sold it to anybody who asked for it. Take it. It is proof that you asked.** The woman does not take it. **It is about an instrument, and I am not in an instrument. I am in a box, about four hundred and thirty miles from where I was standing when you said that, and if I take that sheet off this counter it will be a sheet in my hand that says nothing about me at all, and I have got one of those already and I made it myself.** *Take it anyway.* **No, and I am going to tell you why, and it is because a person who takes a piece of paper off a counter is a person who has been helped, and I have been helped four times this year and I can count them, and a person who is helped is a person who owes, and I have not got a figure for what I owe and I am not going to be the one who starts.** Marn Ottery writes the day on the slab in pencil where it will come off, because that is what a counter does, and says **That is not a record.** *I know what it is.* Then the rule, said standing up: **The only thing standing between you and the rest of your life is somebody asking a question out loud in a room. That is it.** There is no other instrument in this empire and there has not been one since the second person stopped being a person. And there is no post in this empire whose job is to ask — no post, in about nine hundred buildings, in any of the four hundred and thirty miles between that counter and that lane, in any office, at any counter, at any window, in any court, whose business is to stand in front of a heading and ask what the words on it mean. **Ask for a form for it. Go round all nine hundred of them. It is not there, and it has never been there, and in a hundred and forty years there has been one asking of a word on a form, and the one was a person asking another person in a room that wanted a record, and nobody chose it, and it will not happen again by itself.** *And you. You have answered me. Why.* **Because you were standing here and I have had eleven years, and because I am a clerk, and a clerk is a person who can be asked things, and about nine people a year find that out, and I say so at the counter before anybody asks me. A foreman can be sent for and a clerk cannot, and I have not been sent for and I have not been protected and I have never been asked whether I wanted to be in a room and I have never been able to leave one and nobody has ever had the manners to notice the difference.** A man of about fifty comes up, says four words, pays fourpence for a copy and goes; **That is about four hundred of them a year, and every one of those men has walked out of this room with a piece of paper in his hand and a thing in it that they could not get before they came in. And not one of them was asked what the fourth line means, and about nine in eleven years have stood at that rail and looked at the board and gone away, and two of them were you.** *That was not the same.* **It was exactly the same, and the reason it was not the same is that I am a person and a counter is not, and the whole of what is wrong with this room is that a person stands in it on more days than the forms do, and there is a form for the counter.** And then, at the rail on the way out, turning round, which nobody at that counter does: **You said a room writes down whatever it likes and can be asked about it.** *That is what I said.* **Then write this down and put your name at the foot of it. Not for me. I do not want it and I will not carry it. Write it and put it in your own book, and in about four years I will not know you did it and you will not be able to give it to me, and that is not a kindness either, it is the only shape the thing has.** And Marn Ottery, exactly: **That is the first thing anybody has asked me for at this counter in about eleven years, and I am not going to be able to do it, and I want to be exact about why, because you will not ask me again.** *Then say it.* **There is no form for it, and I have been a clerk long enough to know that a clerk who puts a sentence of her own into a book with no office on it has made a document, and the whole of what I have been afraid of since the second month is a document with my hand at the foot of it.** Out on the street: **There is a day, and I am not going to send it to anybody, and I am not going back down that road with nothing, and I have been in this city since the third week of the fifth month and I am not going home until somebody asks me a question in a room.**

## Chapter 203 — "A Class Nobody Can Count" (3,036)

**POV: Marek Kest. A rented room with a table in it, a book with no office on it and about four feet of a wall he does not use, the third day of the third week of the ninth month of the year after, with Tamsin Rook in it.** Thirty-eight. **He has no office and no fund and no register and nothing in this empire he could certify anything with, and a bar of his own that came off him on the twelfth of the ninth month of last year on an application of one line which he wrote himself. There is a line about two inches long on the inside of his left wrist. It reads nothing. It decides nothing. It does not know where the ford is.** She is in the room because two instruments require it and the two instruments are not one instrument and neither of them merges them: a paper made in a form in four days with a day on it, and a watch that requires only that a person who is not from the office that cannot be named be in any room he is in. The thing he could not do was count, and he had spent nineteen days failing to do it in about nine different ways, and on the third day he stopped, **and the stopping was the finding.** The office of a seat keeps eleven minute books, and a minute book takes down what a room did, on a day, with a clerk's name at the foot, and eleven of them on a shelf is a complete record of a thing nobody looks at twice a year. **An entry is not a minute.** That is the whole of the difficulty and it took him nineteen days because he kept trying to make the books into a register, and they are not a register and never were, **because a book that takes down what a room decided cannot be made into a book of what a room did to a person, because the second thing does not happen in a room. It happens in an office about nine miles from a counter, in about nine seconds, in a hand, on a sheet, and the sheet goes out.** **So the office of a seat has a shelf of what was said and no shelf at all of what was done.** Then the engine, in his mouth and then hers: **A roll of households does not say a person is of age and resident. It says a household is at a door.** The office asks a district for the person of a family who is of age and resident, and a district has got nothing in the world that answers that, and so the office asks the next question, **which is the only question there is an answer to, which is who is on the roll.** Said again in the other order: **A roll of households does not list rights, holdings or claims. That is on the face of the third line and it has been there longer than I have been alive.** So a district can tell the office where a person is and can tell it nothing else whatever — not what they hold, not what they are owed, not whether they are of age, **and not which of the people at that door the office is asking for** — and the office is asking for a person and is putting the answer in a box that says the person, institution or thing engaged in the matter. **And a roll of households has a household in it.** *That is the answer to something.* **That is the answer to a question nobody asked. That is how a company of nine families got into a box with a heading over it, and how a foreman of fifty-one got into one, and how a chapel and a poor-box and a company of watermen got into about four hundred returns in a bundle in about nine hundred buildings.** And then the sentence he has not said out loud in about two years, and says in this room: **The third line catches anybody of age and resident of a family that holds nothing enforceable, and it catches them by finding them on a roll of households. My mother made sure there was no Kest on any roll in this empire, and that was the right thing to do and was done in a room in about nine minutes by a person who was not asked, and it is the reason there is no Kest on the roll of that district four hundred and thirty miles up this river, and the roll is the only thing in this business that could have found my sister, and she is on it, and she is found, and the finding is what got her in. The same hand is not a figure of speech and I have said so before in another room and I am not going to improve it. One family, one act, and it made two of its children unfindable and findable in the same year.** Nobody says anything for about a minute and a half. Then the count, and the counting is the discipline: two are known; he writes the two in his own book on a clean sheet, looks at them for about a minute, **then takes the pen and puts a line through both of them and writes *two* against them instead.** *You have destroyed it.* **I have taken two names out of a book with no office on it, in a rented room, with nobody in it, and there is no instrument anywhere that stops me, and I did it before the ink was dry on the line I had struck through, and that is not a record of anything. That is a man tidying.** The sheet is for the questions: **One line per question in this matter that nobody has asked. I have got eleven and most of them would take a person about four minutes to ask and about four years to answer,** written down in the order they ought to be asked, and there is no order, and the day is against the sheet and not against the lines. *There is a twelfth.* **There is a twelfth line and it is empty and it is going to stay empty.** *Then write on it what it is.* **If I write on the twelfth line who is going to ask the questions, then I have appointed somebody, and there is no post in this empire whose job is to ask, and a person who appoints somebody to a post that does not exist is doing the thing the whole of this is about, which is filling in a box the way the box is printed. I am not going to do that and I would like it noticed that it took me nineteen days not to do it and that I was certain about it by the time I had the pen down.** He reads the eleven out because she asks: what a second person is on a witness form; whether a roll of households can say a person is of age; what a company of nine families is inside a definition that says a family; what a room wants when it asks a question; whether a minute book with a clerk's name at the foot of an entry protects the person the entry is about. *That one has an answer, and the answer is no, and it was given by the person who wrote it, out loud, in that room, and it protects the clerk and nothing else, and I would have struck it off the sheet.* **I have not struck it off.** **Do not strike off the things that have been answered. A list of questions with the answered ones still on it is the only honest list there is, and the moment it is tidy somebody will believe there is less to do.** Then: whether a person can be un-entered; what a hold on a household of four does; who wrote a line in a margin in a hand that was not his; whether a company that cannot be served can be said to have refused anything; whether a person who is in a house that is shut has an address. *That one is a finding, and it is in a minute book with a day on it and my name at the foot of it, and you did not ask it, I answered it in the first week of the fifth month, in a room, and you were in the room, and it is on your list as though it were still open.* *Then I will put a day against that line as well.* **Put the day against it, and not my name, because if you put my name on eleven lines then in about four years that sheet is a list of things a clerk of twenty-four has been asked, and I am a person who cannot be instructed and I am not going to be a document about a woman of twenty-four who was in a room.** He writes the day against the tenth line and leaves the name off it, reads the sheet back once and not twice, and the eleventh line is the one neither of them says out loud. Then the rule, used once, in a hand and not a form: *Marek Kest's choice, the third day of the third week of the ninth month of the year after. Either I go to the office of a seat and ask a question out loud in a room, or I do not. If I go, I am a person who has asked, and a person who has asked is answerable for what he is told. I am not asking for an answer. I am asking to be a person who has asked. — M.K.* She confirms the rule and the date and answers no, in words, with the date, and gives the reason as a fact and not advice, using her third line and her fourth line: **The office of a seat puts more people through that room in one year than there are lines in any of the eleven books on that shelf. It does not remember them.** It has no book of them, because a book of them would be a register and that office does not keep a register, **and that is the entire structural reason the third line works and the entire structural reason nothing can be done about it in a room.** And a clerk of about fifty-five in that office is a person who has written about four thousand entries in nineteen years and has never once been asked to remember one of them, and that is a good life and it is not anybody's fault. And: **if you walk in there and ask what the fourth line of a form means, then you are a person that office remembers, because you are the first one, and you will not be remembered as a man who asked a question. You will be remembered as a man who came in about the fourth week of the ninth month and wanted to know what the words on the boxes were for.** And in about four years somebody will come back to that room to look at a return, and the clerk will not remember him, and the room will, **and one question from you teaches that room a thing it does not know, which is that the question can be asked, and a room that knows a thing can be asked stops being a room you can ask.** *That is a good reason.* **It is a fact. It is about what rooms are for. I have not advised you and if you take it as advice you are a man who has been advised in a rented room by a woman who is a party and cannot leave it, and I would rather you did not.** *You know what I did with it.* **You wrote it in order to be refused.** *Yes.* **And you got refused, and the refusal was a real answer, and it was given in about forty seconds by a person who had already thought about it, and you did not argue. That is the first time I have believed a document you wrote. Every one of the others was true and every one of them was a man getting a thing ready so that somebody would catch him at it, and I have caught you more times than I can count and I have never once wanted to catch you again, and this is the first one where I did not want to.** He puts the sheet in the book at the back after the four definitions and shuts it: **That is the rule used once, in writing, with a day on it, and it is the only instrument either of us owns, and it is the first one where the answer is a thing I did not know in the morning.** Then his wrist: it told him nothing, it has not told him anything since the fourth hour of the second of the fifth month of next year when it was up for about nine seconds, and it does not know where the ford is, **and it does not know that a roll of households four hundred and thirty miles up this river has a woman of twenty in its fourth column.** **There is no office in this empire whose business it is to ask me what that is for, and I have got about four feet of wall and a table and a rule I used once and a list of eleven questions with a day on the sheet and an empty twelfth line, and I am not going to write anybody's name on the twelfth line, and I would like it read back to me now, in this room, in words, whether you think that is cowardice.** **It is not. It is the first thing you have done since the sixth day of the third month that is not a way of making yourself expensive to look at, and I am not going to soften it and I am not going to be thanked for saying it, and nobody is going to thank me, and there is no form anywhere that requires a person to be thanked.**

## Chapter 204 — "A Refusal With Nothing To Refuse" (2,758)

**POV: Halla Wray. The tool shed at the Slade end, about nine foot by eleven, a bench along the north wall, a lamp not lit until about the seventh hour, the third day of the fourth week of the ninth month of the year after, in front of about nine men.** Fifty-one, foreman of the Slade Cut, **an office with no office in it: a thing nine families agreed to about eleven years ago out loud, and it was not written down, and it cannot be produced, and she holds it the way a person holds a job nobody is going to ask her about.** On that bank since she was nine. **She can read. Nobody at the district works has ever once in nine years asked her to read anything.** And: **a person who tells a shed beforehand has asked the shed for a hearing and a hearing is a party.** She has the six lines in a book of her own with a day against them, and she has read them to herself about nine times and to nobody at all, **and there is a difference between the two and nine men in a shed are not going to be shown the difference.** What is on the sheet is a notice of six numbered lines and a foot, a seat's own device cut into the head of it and not the fire-and-water mark, **her name at the top of it, in the ordinary way, in the hand of whoever sent it, and nobody has ever asked her whether she wanted it there and there is no form anywhere in this empire that requires anybody to ask.** The second line asks that no inference of any kind be drawn from the absence of any name. The third line is the one that has her in it. **The sixth line declines to name the holder of the office of the seat at all, which makes it the first document in this matter that names an office instead of a person.** She announces it: **I am going to say the two lines that nobody has ever said out loud in this shed, and then I am going to do a thing, and I would like the nine of you to understand that the thing is not for you and is not about you and I am not asking any of you for anything.** The second line first: **It says that no inference of any kind is to be drawn from the absence of any name. Forty-two years I have been on this bank and I have never been in a book of anybody's, not a roll, not a return, not a list of works with a head on it, nothing, and I have been proud of that in a way I have never said out loud to anybody about anything, and I have just read a piece of paper that instructs anybody who reads it not to draw any inference from the fact that there is no name on it. That is not a threat. That is a man telling the world in advance not to look.** And I have been doing it for forty-two years without a piece of paper and he has now put mine in writing, and he could not have known that, and it would not have mattered, because the sentence is about him and not about me and I am the only person in this shed it can be said about. Then the sixth line: **It declines to name the holder of the office. So the thing that put me in this cannot be named.** It refused, not answered, not produced, not held to. Named by nobody, in a document, in a hand, with a seal at the foot and nothing under the seal. **A man wrote a line that says *I am not going to tell you who I am* into a piece of paper he is sending to a foreman on a bank, and he sent it to me, and I cannot do one thing about it, and I have wanted to say that out loud in a room for about eleven weeks.** Then the refusal, and it did not work, and she said so in advance and did it anyway: **I am refusing to be served. That is the instrument. It is the only one there is in this empire and I have never had to use it, and a woman about four hundred and thirty miles up this river used it in a room with a day on it in the fourth week of the fifth month and it did not work there either, and I am going to use it now, in this room, out loud, with today on it, and I would like one of you to write it down, and I do not care which.** **Nobody wrote it down.** One of them said afterwards, in the yard, that his hands were cold and that he had wanted to, and that nobody had given him paper, and that he had not thought to fetch any. **It has not worked, and I am going to say why, and the why is the reason I have had since the seventh month and have not said, and it is not the same why as hers, and I would like that noticed, because if the two whys are the same then it is a bad system, and it is not a bad system. It is the worst system anybody has ever written down and it works. A refusal to be served requires a service. That is all it is. It is a door you put your back against, and there has to be a door and there has to be somebody knocking. And nobody knocked. I was not served. I was entered.** I was got at by a class, and a class is not served on anybody, and there is nobody in this to knock on, and **a person who has not been served cannot refuse to be served, and the only instrument this empire has for a person to say no has just been found to be no use at all to me.** And: **that is not a hole anybody has left in it. It is a sentence written in about nine hundred buildings by somebody who needed a form to go out in a week, and it says that no further consent of the person is required, and it says that about me, and it is right, and there is no second instrument, and I have looked for one since the seventh month in every form in this empire I could get hold of and there is not one and I am the first person to have had to look.** A man of about thirty from the second gang: **And you have said it in here.** **Nothing.** That is the answer and I have had it since the first week of the seventh month and I have been carrying it about like a stone. **You do nothing, and the sheet goes on being on the bench, and there is no procedure in this empire for a person to be let out of a thing that does not need her, and I have looked for one, and the reason there is not one is that in about a hundred and forty years nobody has ever needed to be let out of one.** *You are in a box.* **I am in a box by a class, and a company of nine families and about forty-one people is a family inside the third line's own definition, and the only one of us with a place of custom or of work in a roll of households is the one whose job was never written down. That is me. I have been the reason I could not be found for forty-two years, and I have never once chosen it, and I was nine years old when it started, and a child does not choose anything.** And the fifth time, said once and not listed: **That is the fifth time, and I have worked that out this week and I am not going to list them in here, and the reason is that a list of five is a list of five, and the people in the other four are not in this shed, and every one of you has a family up the road, and I am not going to read five names out in a room with men in it. The protection and the catch are the same act, and it has been the same act five times, and nobody chose it, and the reason nobody chose it is that the people who were protected and the people who were caught were never in a room together and could not have known about each other.** Then the thing with no form behind it, which took the better part of a quarter of an hour and is the first thing she has done in nine years anybody in this trade will be able to find: she takes out a sheet and writes the six lines, all of them, in her own hand, and the device, and the foot, and the seal, and the fact that there is nothing under the seal, and the day against it in the corner, **and she does not write her name anywhere on it.** Told *that is not any use without a name on it*: **It is not any use at all without a name on it, and that is the point, and you will not understand it for about four years and I am not going to explain it to you now. A record of a document is not a record of a person.** I am going to write down six lines and a seal and nothing under the seal, and that is a thing in a room and not a woman on a bank, and in about four years a man with a copy can go and hold it up beside the one on the bench and ask somebody to say whether the two are the same, and the two will be the same, and the somebody will have to go and look at a roll, and the roll is four hundred and thirty miles up this river, and he will have to go and ask the woman who keeps it, and she is not going to know what the fourth column is for either, **and that is where it stops and it stops about four hundred and thirty miles from here with a woman of about sixty holding a board and a basket and no idea what she has in her hand.** And my hand is at the foot of it, and my hand is the only part of this anybody cannot take off me, and I have known that since I was seventeen. Then why, and not for the record: **I have said in this shed that I would rather be asked than not, and I have been asked twice and said yes twice, and I have refused to be asked a third time without being asked.** I have said that a person who is paid nothing is the only kind of person in this cut who can be told no by anybody, and I have said that a carriage is not a wage, and I have said it twice now, and I am not going to say it a third time. And the other half of the reason, which is the half she has not got, and which she uses about four times a season, and which does not go in a room that writes it down: **the day this book-keeper asks me for it is the day I stop saying the half that I have got**, and she has said that in that shed before and every man in it heard it and one of them wrote nothing down because there was no paper. Then the last of it, to her face: **I would like to be found. I have spent forty-two years being unfindable and it is the reason I am standing in this, and if it had been any other way I would be standing somewhere else with a worse thing on me, and I am not going to be embarrassed about saying that out loud at fifty-one in front of nine men. What I am not going to do is be the reason four other people get found**, and there are four of them on that bank who cannot read a paragraph and have never been asked once, and the season is coming round again, and I have thought about it since the seventh month and this is where I have got to, and I have not told a soul until now and I am not going to be thanked for it, **because there is no form anywhere in this empire that requires a person to be thanked, and I have said that in advance and I mean it.** She puts the sheet on the bench face up beside the other one and the two of them lay there for anybody who came in.
