Then the thing the chapter is for: there was a man at the back of the shed who had not said anything for about nine minutes, with a book under his arm, who had not sat down, and whom she had known since the second day of the first week of the seventh month and had never once said so in a room. **He did not ask her for the other half.** He stood at the back and looked at the two sheets on the bench for about a minute and a half and then went out into the yard and shut the door behind him, which nobody else did. Afterwards, to nobody at all, in the yard, at about the eighth hour, with the dark coming up off the water and the door open behind her: **He did not ask.** Nobody answered, because there was nobody there, **and there is no form anywhere in this empire that requires a person to be answered when she says a true thing to an empty yard, and she had said it out loud because a thing a person says to a yard is not evidence of anything, and it is the only kind of saying there is that nobody can take off you in about four years**, and she has known that since the sixth month of last year and has used it about four times a season. Then she lit the lamp, which is a quarter of an hour later than it ought to be, and did not shut the door.

## Chapter 205 — "What The Roll Had" (2,872)

**POV: Ivet Sarn. The clerk's window of the Roll Court on a flood terrace, the embankment corridor behind it, four presses, a back room off that corridor she has walked past every working day for nine years and has never once been inside, the first day of the first week of the tenth month of the year after.** Thirty-eight, nine years at that window, and about nine people a month ask her for a book in the wrong form and she admits it and tells them what it will cost them. **She is not hiding anything. Her caution is partly justified: the last time a docket was reopened it cost that district a winter of aid, and there is a paper about that winter in a drawer in her own room and she has never told the court why.** A return comes up the corridor in a bundle and it is not going into a file, it is going into a register, **and a return going into a register is a return that has to be copied, and a return that has to be copied is a return somebody is going to read the column on before they copy it.** The column is headed for the person, institution or thing engaged in the matter, filled in in ink in a hand that is not hers, dated the fourth day of the third week of the fifth month. **There is nothing to copy. It is done.** That is not a reason to put a sheet in a press; it is a reason to look at it, and she looked at it for about four minutes. **The date on the return is the day the column was filled in and not the day the return was sent, and there is no space on the sheet for the second day.** The office of a seat had asked that court, in the ordinary way, for the person of a family who is of age and resident, **and the court keeps a roll of households of that district for the water, and the roll has got no answer to that question in it, and about nine hundred buildings print a form with a box on it for the answer, and the office had filled the box in itself.** **So the box is not asking us anything. The box is the office's own column coming back to us with a day on it, and we are to copy a thing we did not find.** Then the man at the window, at about the ninth hour on the third day of the week, about thirty-four, moved in the second week of the ninth month from a street with a shop on it to rooms over a yard four streets off inside the same district, and told nobody at the counter because there is nothing at the counter that asks him. **What does resident mean. On that. Not on yours. On the return. It is on the return and it is a word and I have looked at it for a fortnight and it does not say whose word it is, and I am not asking you as a favour, I am asking you because you are the only person in this building who reads the forms, and I have a wife and a boy and I would like to know whether a word is going to be used about us.** And she says the price before she answers, and did not know she was going to until about a second after she had said it, **and that is how it happened: I am going to answer that in a room, out loud, in about four minutes, and there is no charge on the board for it, and I am not going to write it down for you, and here is the price of answering it: a person who asks a question about a form in a room becomes a person somebody has answered, and there is no instrument anywhere in this empire that takes that back off him. I am telling you that now, at the start, before I say the words, because you have a fortnight of not knowing and I am about to take it away, and I would rather you had the price first.** *I have not asked you to take anything away.* **Nobody ever does. Ask.** Then the answer, in about four minutes, without a word of it twice: **A roll of households is not a register of persons. It is a list of doors.** This court keeps one because the water has to know how many houses there are on a bank, **and the fourth column of mine has had no heading over it for nine years and I have not filled it and nobody has ever asked me why, and that is a different fourth column from the one on your return and I am not going to stand here and pretend the two of them are one thing.** **A return like that one goes out to a district, and this empire has about nine hundred of them, and the office sends one to every one, and each one asks the only question this empire knows how to ask a district about a person, which is *where is that person*, and each one comes back in a column with a heading over it with whatever the district had.** A district's roll of households has a household in it. It does not have a person in it, and it certainly has not got a person of twenty in it, and it has not got consent in it, and it has not got a claim in it, **and the form on your sheet says in its own words that the roll does not list rights, holdings or claims.** **So the answer that came back is correct. The answer is a household. The box wanted a person and a household is what the roll had, and the office wrote the household down because the alternative was writing nothing, and a person who writes nothing in a box is a person who has been struck out with a pen and not a rule, and I have seen that on about four hundred of these in nine years and I could not tell you one of the people who did it.** And the word itself: **And the word resident means what it has always meant, which is *on the roll at a door*, and it does not mean living there, it does not mean paying anything, it does not mean anybody has agreed to anything, and a man can be resident on four rolls in four districts in this empire and be on none of them in the sense he means.** *That is not what I asked.* **It is exactly what you asked, and you asked it well, and I would like it noticed that you asked it because you were afraid, and not because a room wanted a record.** She turned the return round on the sill so it was facing him. **Nobody has ever asked one of these in this building. I have been at this window nine years and the only person who has ever asked me what a word on a form means is a man who came in afraid about his own household, and he is not a lawyer and he is not a clerk.** And it is the second time in a hundred and forty years that anybody has asked another person what a word on a form meant, and the first one was a room that wanted a record, and neither of the two of them is a plan. *I would rather not have asked.* **That is the correct answer, and I want to say to you that it is the correct answer and it is also the answer a woman of twenty did not give about four hundred and thirty miles up this river, and she said no in a room with the day on it and it did not work, and you have just said the same thing in about four words and yours is going to work better than hers did, and I would like you to sit with that for a minute before you go.** *I have not got a minute.* **Then take it on the walk back, and understand what you have done, because almost nobody does and it is the whole of the cost. You have not learned a thing about the water. You have become a person who asked a question about a form in a room, and in about four years a man with a copy of the right page can put a line under your name saying that a clerk of this court told him what the word resident meant, and you will not be able to say that you asked about your own household and not about anybody else, because the form does not have a place to put that, and there is no form anywhere in this empire that has a place to put that, and I have looked.** He went. He did not say thank you and she did not want him to, and there is no form anywhere that requires a person to be thanked, and she has never once in nine years asked for it and is not going to start. Then the ordinary thing with the return: a return that is copied goes into the register and a return that cannot be copied goes in a basket under the sill, because it has nothing in it that this court is the person to copy, and the form says so and has said so for about a hundred and forty years, and the basket is a shallow one of wicker about nine inches deep and sits under the sill where everybody who comes to the window can see it. **There are returns in that basket. There have been returns in that basket in every year of the nine. She has never thrown one away. She has never shown one to anybody. She has never told anybody what is in it, and it is nine sheets deep**, and every one of them has that column and every one of them is the only document in the world that says how a box got filled, **and the form that the basket comes from calls them rubbish.** The corridor is about a hundred and forty feet long, the floor of it is wet from about the eighth hour, there is a lamp at the north end that is out, and the door of the back room is on the left about halfway and was open a couple of inches, which it has been every working day for nine years. She went past it. She has been past it about two thousand times. **A person who opens a room nobody has asked her about is a person who has given herself a duty, and a person who has given herself a duty cannot stop.** She has got enough of those in nine years and one of them is the reason she has a paper in a drawer about a winter. She had been in that room once, in the fifth week of the fifth month, on a matter that is somebody else's, and there was nothing in it, and she has said in her own book that she knows what the presses behind her are for, and that a person with a pen at a table can put a name into a column and take a name out of a column, and that there is no instrument anywhere that stops it. And then, to the window, with the register under her arm: **I have been sitting on the answers for nine years, and there is no post in this empire whose job is to ask me what is in the basket, and if there were one it would not be a clerk of this court, because a clerk of this court is paid and a person who is paid can be told to stop.** The man had gone by then and there was nobody at the sill. She did not show him; she had thought about it while he was standing there, in about nine seconds, and the reason was not caution and she said so to an empty window afterwards, in the ordinary way, at about the tenth hour: **because a clerk who shows a man her basket is a clerk who has given the man a reason to be interested in it, and a man with a reason to be interested in a thing cannot be left alone with it, and about four years from now a person with a copy of the right page is going to come along that corridor and ask me what the basket is, and I am going to have to say a thing about it, and there is no form anywhere in this empire for a person to say *I have had those sheets for nine years and I never asked what they were* without that sentence being the answer to a question he came with.** Then she wrote it in her own book with no office on it, in her own hand, with the day on it: that a return had come, that the column on it was filled in at the other end in advance, that the day on it was the day the column was filled and not the day it was sent, that no space existed on the sheet for the second day, that a man at the window had asked her what the word *resident* meant, that she had answered, and why she had given the answer for nothing. She read it back twice, the second reading slower, and not a third time, and at the bottom she wrote the reason, which is the reason she has written eleven times in nine years and which has not got any better: **A hand of mine is the only hand anybody is going to be able to put side by side in about four years, and I have now done this for the eleventh time and I have not stopped and I am not going to.** Then the return went in the press with the other returns and she copied nothing, because there was nothing in it she was the person to copy, and the fourth column of her own register was where it has been for nine years, which is empty, and she went and stood in the embankment corridor for a minute and a half and did not go into the back room, **and there is no form anywhere in this empire that requires a person to be told she has a duty about a room she has never been inside.**

## Chapter 206 — "The One Way Of Reaching Four People" (2,784)

**POV: Rennick Adley. A bay at the Slade end and a hired stone store off the Slade, the second day of the second week of the tenth month of the year after.** Thirty-eight, keeping the books of the Slade Cut Company in a hired stone store off the Slade since the second month of next year, **and the Company's whole money is four shillings a year and all of it is the rent of the building.** Not a clerk. He can count and he has a fair hand, **and the book he keeps has no heading at the top of it and a name at the foot of every line of a list of works.** The second season was asked for on the fourth day of the last week of the seventh month and about nineteen people said no again, one after another, out loud, in a bay, in about four minutes, **and every one of the nineteen reasons went in the third column of that bay's own ledger with the day against each one, and the reasons were read out and the names were not, because a name in a room is a thing that can be carried out of a room.** It is now the second week of the tenth month; the season is running; nobody agreed it and nobody signed anything, and the wages of about forty-one people are held against a company whose whole money is four shillings a year. The ordinary things first, on a day: the count of the works, which takes about four minutes and which nobody has ever asked him for and which is the only thing he is paid for; the water, which is at about the third-of-the-way mark and is not coming up to the second week of the tenth month and which he wrote down because he writes everything down; **the bank, which is about four hundred and forty foot long and which he does not have a figure for and which he is not going to invent.** Then he read the third column back, all nineteen, out loud, in the bay, in the ordinary way, the second reading slower, nothing skipped, **and the second reading is his own rule and he has had it since the second week of the fourth month of this year and nobody decided it and that is what a rule is.** Then again on the fourth day of the week, **because a person is entitled to have the reason they gave written down in the place where the no is, and a person is also entitled to hear it said out loud in a room once a season, and there is no form anywhere in this empire that says so, and he has read every form in that store and there is not one page in any of them that says a person has to give you a better reason than *I have to be home*.** **They are still behind that bank, and the reason went in the book in the place where the no is, and the book does not go anywhere, and the bank does not go anywhere, and both of those are the same sentence and I have not been able to improve it since the seventh month.** Then the arithmetic: about forty-one people on this cut, about nineteen of whom have said no to this season with a reason in the right place **and they are owed nothing and they have been asked once and not a second time, and that is correct and I am not going to touch it**; and **about four people in this bay who cannot read a paragraph. They have never been asked once. They were not asked in the first season and they were not asked on the fourth day of the seventh month and they were not asked this week, and there is no column for them and there is not going to be one, and the reason there is not going to be one is that a column for them would be a column somebody would have to fill, and nobody has appointed anybody, and there is no post in this empire whose job it is to be appointed.** *Then ask them.* **I have.** He puts the ledger down and his hand flat on the third column, which is a column of nineteen reasons and a day against every line of it, and the names are in a different book with about nine hundred and forty of them in nine hands over about sixty years and a day against those too. **I have worked out how. That is what I have been doing for nine days instead of counting the works, and I counted the works this morning first, because I am not going to let a thing I have thought about all week get in front of the water. There is a person in this bay who reads.** She reads better than I do, she does it for forty-five pence a day and four days a week, and she is here because she is paid to be here, **and if I asked her to read the fourth column out to those four people, in this bay, on a day with a day on it, then four people who cannot read a paragraph would know what the hold is and who is holding it and what it does to a week's money, and that is the whole of what a person is owed in this matter and I have got it worked out in about nine seconds and it is the correct thing to do and I am not going to do it.** *Why not.* **Because a person who is paid to read is a person who can be told to stop.** That is the whole of the reason and I have said that sentence out loud in this bay and I am saying it again and I am not going to improve it. If she reads a hold to four people then in about four years a man with a copy of the right page can stand in a room and ask her whether she read it, and read it to whom, and on what day, and in what words, and she will not be able to say no to any of it, because she will have done it, and because she was paid, and because a person who is paid is a person who cannot refuse. And I am not going to spend that. Not hers. It is not mine to spend, and it is not the four's, and I have not got the standing to spend it and there is no form anywhere in this empire that would give me the standing and I have looked for one in about nine hundred buildings and there is not one. *So we sit here.* **Nothing. We do nothing and I am going to write down that we did nothing, and the day, and the reason, and I am going to read it back twice, and the second reading is the one I am not going to skip, and I am not going to put a name at the foot of it, because a name at the foot of it makes the four people on that line findable and I am the man who put a roof in a box in the second day of the second week of the fourth month of this year and I have not stopped being that man.** And the finding, in his own hand, with the day on it: *Asked on the second day of the second week of the tenth month of the year after, in this bay, out loud, whether the four persons here who cannot read a paragraph are to be told what the hold is. There is one way to tell them and it costs a person of seventeen who is paid to read, and a person who is paid to read is a person who can be told to stop. Not done. Not this season. The four are not asked. That is the finding and it is mine and I am not going to hand it to anybody. — R. Adley.* **Nobody thanked him. There is no form anywhere in this empire that requires a person to be thanked, and he has not asked for it, and he is not going to.** Then the rest of it, standing up, at about the seventh hour, because a bay is a room and a room gets a day and he had a list: **a guarantee stands offered on this bank and unanswered, on four hundred and forty foot of it, and about sixty children under sixteen are inside it, and inside a guild's blank list, and inside a rotation they have not been asked about and have been told about none of it. It is not going to be taken up and I have not got the terms of it in my head and I am not going to read them out in a bay at about the seventh hour.** A bill at Lowcross is nineteen pounds three and fourpence and is unpaid and nobody is liable, and there has not been a line for a bridge in that fund in nineteen years, **and I am not paying it and nobody in this bay is paying it and I am not going to stand here and ask any of you for a penny.** A factor's letter of four lines is sitting on a bench in that store since the second week of the third month and it wants the name of a person who may be served and that person's consent, and it says without both it cannot proceed and will not proceed, and the matter will stand against the works. **It is not going to be answered, and every day it is not answered is a day nobody has been entered, and I know what a day of that is worth and I am not going to be the one who spends it.** And: **And the thirty-one of Mosswake are thirty-one.** He said that last one and moved on, and it is another district's figure and it is not his to explain, **and about nine men in that bay do not know whose it is and are not going to be told, because there is no form anywhere in this empire for a book-keeper of a company to explain another district's number to a bay full of men who have never crossed it.** Then, alone in the bay with the ledger open: **There is a foreman of fifty-one in a shed up the road who has put the words of a document in her own book and has refused to put herself in it**, and Rennick Adley heard about that the way everybody on that bank hears about everything, which is from a man who was in a shed, and he has thought about nothing else since the fourth week of the ninth month. **He did not go up the road. He has not gone up the road. He is not going to ask her for the other half of the sentence, and the reason is the one he gave in the seventh month out loud in front of nine men, and the day he asks is the day she stops saying the half she has got, and he has wanted it since the third month of this year and has not asked, and there is no form anywhere in this empire that requires a person to ask.** Then a carter came into the bay at about the eighth hour, which he does not do. *Are you going to ask me again.* **No. Not until the season comes round, and not by a second person, and not in a letter, and not by anybody but me, and I will come to the gate and I will ask you in the same words I asked you in the seventh month, and you may say the same words back, and if you say something different I will write down what you said and not what you said last time.** *You have not asked me once since the first month, and I have been waiting, and I said in the bay that I wanted it noted that I had been waiting, and you wrote it down and you read it back twice, and you did not argue with me, and I have thought about that every day since.* **I wrote it down. I read it back twice, and the second reading was the slower one, and that is my own rule and nobody decided it, and it came to me off a girl of seventeen who is paid to read and is not paid to think, and that is the whole of where it came from.** *Then write this one down, because I am going up the road for the winter and I am not coming back to this bank for the asking, and I am telling you that as a fact and not as a threat, and I would like it in the place where the no is, and I would like it to say the day.* He wrote it in the third column with the day and read it back twice, the second reading slower. **That is in the place where the no is, and it is a yes and it is a no in the same line, and both of them are in my own hand and neither of them is a name.** *You have never put a name at the foot of anything in that book.* **The same name is at the foot of three lists of works in that book and it is not mine, and a man at a gate who asks to be asked last and is written first has decided once what he wants to hear, and the day he stops being able to hear it is the day somebody in this bay is doing him a kindness he did not ask for, and there is no form anywhere in this empire that would let me do that to him.** The carter put his hat on and went out into the wet and did not say thank you and was not thanked, and the ledger stayed open with nineteen reasons in the third column and a new line under them. The last of it: **The season is still running. About nineteen people are still behind the bank and about four of them in this bay have still never been asked anything, and he has written down on a page in a bay's own ledger, in his own hand, with the day on it, that he decided not to, and he read it back twice, and nobody thanked him, and the girl of seventeen was at the back of that bay until about the eighth hour and then she was not, and nobody spoke to her about the season, and she did not ask, and nobody thanked her and nobody is going to, and she is not going to start doing the rest of it for nothing, and he has not asked her for anything in nine days and is not going to, and the door of the store is open and about four hundred and thirty miles of road is what it costs anybody who wants to come and look at a page in a ledger and there is no fund.**

## Chapter 207 — "The Fifth Time She Brought Him A Sheet" (2,863)

**POV: Tamsin Rook. Four bays and a press and a corridor, the second day of the third week of the tenth month of the year after.** Twenty-four, a party to an instrument about a dead woman's name. **Two instruments require her in any room he is in and she has never once merged them and he has never once merged them, and a form gets merged by being inconvenient**: the first is a paper made in a form in four days with a day on it, and the second is a watch that does not name him and does not name her and requires only that a person who is not from the office that cannot be named be present. About six hundred people in this city could satisfy the watch, **and she has satisfied it every time it has been called for and nobody has ever paid her for it. Both instruments require her and neither of them says anything about her.** The bays have a press in them and a corridor, the press has about six hundred printed slips in it that say the fourth line is not to be completed by this office, and there are about four hundred blanks in a box under the counter four bays along; she has a desk of her own and a hard-backed book with no office on it and her own hand in it in about nine places, and the book is not the court's and has never been in the court. **Read that before it goes. Read it in front of me. And if you have a reason against it, say the reason in a room and out loud and not on a page.** He read the four lines four times, the last standing up, in about a minute and a half, and did not sit down. It is a copy of four definitions, set out in ink on foolscap in a copyist's hand which is hers, with a heading that says what it is and where it came from, **and no date on it, and about four lines under the heading arguing why there is no date**, and it is going about six miles to a household at the end of a lane, in a hand and not in a wrapper, at fourpence a copy, **and nobody is being paid to carry it because the person carrying it is walking it and has agreed to walk it.** *I have a reason.* **I know you have. Give it.** **I gave it in the second month of this year and you said no and it went anyway, and that was the arrangement, and the arrangement is mine and not yours, and I put it in a book on the fourth of the first month at about the seventh hour and told you it was worse than the rule we made. The reason is that this is the first sheet in eleven weeks that says out loud what a household is inside a definition, and it is going to the one household in this matter that has a person in it who cannot read a paragraph, and the woman who keeps that house is hard to find and has been for sixty years and has never once been asked anything and is never going to be, and a sheet is the cheapest way in the world to a house and there is no form that asks a house's leave.** **And I am going to tell you that you are right. That is the arrangement. Say the rest of it.** The rest of it: **the woman who keeps that house is not my mother's sister and is not in this matter and has done nothing that anybody can be shown, and about four years from now a man with a copy of this page can put it on a table in front of her and say *this is about you*, and she will not be able to say one word about it, and there is no form anywhere in this empire in which she can be told first, and that is the whole of the cost and it is a small cost because she is a person who is hard to find and has been for sixty years, and I am not going to pretend it is not a cost just because it is small.** She writes *agreed* and the day under his reason in her own hand. **That is the fifth time the undertaking has been done, and it is the second time you have given no reason against one word, and I am going to say the number out loud because a number a person says can be held to and I would like this one held to. And the rule of the twelfth month of last year has not been used today and I am entering the not-using as a use, because a correct non-use is a use and it is the only kind either of us gets right.** Then the ordinary counter: a man came into the bays at about the ninth hour for a copy of a form at fourpence and she had to serve him and it took about two minutes, **and about four hundred of those blanks are bought and filled in in a year, and the buying is done at the fourth counter four bays along, and nobody at this counter and nobody at that one has ever been asked a question by anybody.** He did not ask her anything, and **she has never once in this matter had a person stand at a counter she was serving and ask her a question, and there are about four hundred of them a year, and the number is not the point.** The point: **this counter is a room. A room gets a day. A person can come up to it, and be served in it, and ask in it, and walk out of it, and there is nothing on the board under the rail and no fee and no form that says what may be asked at it and none that says what may not. It is the only counter in this city where a person can come up, stand in a room with a clerk in it, and the clerk is a person and is not an office. And in the whole of the time this counter has stood nobody has asked at it, and the reason nobody has asked is not that they do not want to know.** It is that there is no post, and a person who wants to know something at a counter does not come to a counter, they come to a counter to buy fourpence worth of paper, **and they would be ashamed to stand there and use up a minute of a clerk's time for nothing.** And, to the counter after he had gone: **I have thought about that for about eleven days, and the honest shape of it is that the room is there and the asking is not, and the two of them have never once been in the same place at the same time, and in the fifth month of this year, in a room with a rail in it, a clerk of thirty-four who works at the fourth counter four bays along was asked one question out loud, and there were about four hundred blanks in a box under that clerk's own counter at the time, and that is the only time in about a hundred and forty years the two of them were in the same place, and it was an accident, and it was because a room wanted a record.** Then the reason she had actually come to the desk with: **I have a fifth version of the sentence you did not finish. I have had it since the third week of the seventh month and I have not said it out loud and I have not written it down and I am not going to write it down, and I am telling you that it exists and that is all I am going to do about it.** **The reason I have not written it is not privacy and it is not the third line.** It is that **a sentence a man has not finished, written down, is a sentence a clerk can read back to him in about four years and ask him whether he meant it, and a man asked whether he meant a thing has to say what he meant, and what he meant is a thing about two people, and there is no third person in this empire who could be made to hold a version of it that is wrong.** And so it goes in nothing, and it stays in the room, and I have said that out loud in a room to you and it is the fifth time and I am not going to improve on it and I am not going to be thanked for it, because I have asked you in advance, in the third week of the seventh month, not to thank me, and you said you were not going to, and there is no form anywhere that requires a person to be thanked and there never has been one in this matter or in any other. *You have the two boxes in your own book. Both of them filled. Both of them the same name.* **They are two boxes and one name in each and they are not the paper and they are not the watch and they are not this. I have not ruled a third and I am not going to, and a person who rules a box for every thing that happens to her in a year has turned a book into a form, and I would not be the first clerk in this city to do that and I would like to be the last.** Then her hand on the sheet, because it was the only object in the room going six miles to somebody's house: **You have been asking me for about nine days who is going to ask the questions on your sheet, and I have been not answering you, and I am going to answer it now in a room and I am not going to write it down afterwards, and both of those are deliberate. It is not you. It is not me either, and that is the part that has taken me the whole of these nine days, because a woman of twenty-four in four bays with a book with no office on it is the cheapest person in this city to send, and I know that, and I have known it since the second month, and nobody has sent me and nobody is going to and I have made sure of that myself and I would like it written down that I made sure of it myself. You cannot be asked, because you have no office and no fund and a bar that came off on the twelfth of the ninth month of last year on a line you wrote yourself, and there is nothing anybody can instruct you about and nothing anybody can pay you for and nothing anybody can thank you for, and that is the reason you are the most dangerous person in this matter and it is also the reason nobody in it can protect you, and I have said both halves out loud in this room and I am not going to soften the second one.** **So it is going to be nobody, and here is the part that is worse than that, and it is a fact and not advice, and my third line forbids advice and my fourth line says a fact is not advice:** a person who asks a question in a room about a form becomes answerable for the answer. Not the person the question is about. The one who asked. A clerk of thirty-four in this city has said the number out loud twice, which is about four years, **and a clerk of thirty-eight in a building four hundred and thirty miles down this river has found a thing she wanted to write down and could not and has said that wanting a form and not finding one is the worst morning she has had at that window since she came.** **And I have said the price of being a party out loud ten times and nobody has thanked me once and I did not expect to be thanked once and I would like it written down that I did not.** And I know exactly what a room does to the person who says a thing in it. **And I am four hundred and thirty miles from that bay, and I am not going to be sent, and nobody is going to ask me, and if anybody in this matter ever asks me to go and ask a question in a room on that bank, I am going to say no, and I am saying now that I will say no.** He did not argue with it, and she watched him not argue with it, and about nine days ago she would have found that flattering and about four hours ago she had worked out that it is the only evidence she has ever had of anybody's judgment and she has not decided what to do with it. **Say one thing for me, and say it in words, and I am not going to write it down and you are not to either, and if either of us writes it down then I will know that one of us is going back to being careful and I would rather have the sentence than the caution.** **There is no post in this empire whose job is to ask. It has now happened twice, and the first time was a room that wanted a record and the second time was a man who was afraid about his own household, and neither of those is anybody's plan, and two is not a plan either, and in about four years there is going to be somebody at a counter who is going to be asked what a word on a form means, and they are going to say the same thing you would say, and I want you to have heard me say it before that happens.** He said it, in about four seconds, flatly, and then asked one question and the question was not about the sheet. *Are you going to be all right.* **No. Nobody in this matter is going to be all right and I would like it noticed that I have never once been the person who said that, and I have said it now, and there are four of them in my rooms and one of them has been there since the first month of the year before last and it has not been sent and it has not been opened, and I have not thought about it and I am not going to start.** Then she carried the four lines down the corridor herself, put them in the hand of a woman who was going to walk them six miles for nothing, did not watch her go, and shut the door, **and it is not the door she does not shut on the third day of the third week of the seventh month of this year and the two are not the same door and she is not going to be told they are by anybody.**

## Chapter 208 — "The Woman Who Cannot Be Asked" (2,795)

**POV: Bess Tarrant. A room hired by the day above a shop in a street in Auremar, a lane off it about four miles further on, the third day of the fourth week of the tenth month of the year after.** Sixty-three, keeps a house at the end of a lane about four miles off the old river road, **can write and cannot read a paragraph, and has never once in her life been in a room by name, and those are two separate facts and she has never joined them up until the ninth month of this year.** She came up the road on a cart in the second month and has not gone home, or has gone home and come back, and the hiring is done by a woman who comes up at about the eighth hour with a slate. **Nobody sent her. There is no form anywhere in this empire for a person who comes on her own account, and she came on her own account, and that is the only instrument she has ever had.** The day: she gets up before it is light because the room has one window and the light comes in sideways off a wall; she does not go out before about the ninth hour because there is nothing open and she has not got the money for the eating places; she goes out at the ninth hour and walks, **and there is about four miles of it she can walk in a day without being asked anything by anybody, and she has got it to a wall at the end of a street that is not long, and she stands at the wall for about an hour and a half, most days, and goes back.** **She cannot do anything else. There is no work in this city for a woman of sixty-three who cannot read a paragraph, and she has looked, and there is no form on which she can write *I cannot read a paragraph* and hand it to somebody, and there is no form anywhere in this empire for a person to say what they cannot do. There is a form for what a person is. There is not one for what a person cannot do, and that is the whole of why a woman of sixty-three can come into a city in the second month and go to the fourth week of the tenth without one question being put to her that she cannot answer.** The second object a person can hold is in her coat: a copy of nine lines, **in her own hand, which she has not read and cannot read, and which she has not had anybody read to her since a doorway about four miles off the old river road where a man who cuts kindling stood and read the whole of it out loud because it was in her hand and he worked that out from the middle of it and he did not have a form.** She took it out once, in a room above a shop, in the fourth day of the week of that month. **She knows what it says. She wrote it.** Knowing what you wrote and being able to read what you wrote are two different things, and the gap between them is a person's whole life, and about a hundred and forty years of this empire is the width of it. **You can write a thing and not read it back. I have known that since I was about nine. And nobody has ever asked me about it, and nobody is going to, and there is no post.** Then the woman who hires the rooms, about thirty, does about nine rooms on that street, has never once asked Bess Tarrant anything and is not going to, comes up with the day on the slate and puts it against the doorframe the way she puts it against nine doorframes, and says the figure. *I have not got it.* **That is all right, I have got it on the slate.** *Then read me what it says.* The woman stops. It is about four words on a slate, four days and a figure, **and it is not a form and it is not a receipt and there is no office on it and it is scratched on with a piece of chalk because the woman cannot afford ink for nine rooms.** *Four days, and so much.* *Read it again.* **I have just read it.** *You have told me two numbers and a word.* **That is not reading it to me.** That is telling me the answer. I have been in this room since the second month and I have never been able to say the difference out loud to anybody and I have just said it to you, **and you are the first person in this city who has been asked a question by me since the second month, and it is about a chalk mark on a slate.** The woman read it again, slowly, with her thumb under the line, and the two of them stood in a doorway for about a minute and a half. **There, that is what it says. And that is everything, and it took about ninety seconds, and it has taken you ninety seconds and me nothing, and I could have done it in the second month and you have been here ever since.** Then the thing she had worked out in the ninth month, said in the doorway to a woman of about thirty who hires rooms by the day: **Asking works.** That is what I have got wrong since the second month and it has taken me until the fourth week of the tenth month to say it and I am saying it to you because you have read me four words off a slate. It works on a person. It has always worked on a person. **A man stood in a doorway about four miles off this road and read nine lines of my own hand out loud to me and I have not been the same since, and there was no form and no fee and no day at the end of it.** And it has been asked once since the ninth month of this year. I do not know who asked, and I have been told that much and no more, and that is not a conspiracy and it is not a plan either. **It is two accidents about four hundred and thirty miles from each other, in rooms that had nothing to do with one another, and a person who wants to know why nobody asks forms anything has now got the start of the answer and it is that it keeps not happening to the same person.** And: **it does nothing whatever to a piece of paper. You can ask a person until you are hoarse and the paper does not change. And a form cannot be asked at all, and I have been sitting in this room since the second month waiting for a form to change its mind, and there is no post in this empire whose job is to ask one, and the first time anybody asked one in about a hundred and forty years it was because a room wanted a record and a person happened to be in the room.** *And you have tried it on paper.* **I have tried it on paper since the second month. You cannot put a question to a form. You can only fill it in, and filling it in is what it is for, and there is not a line on any of them, in about nine hundred buildings, that says a person may ask what the words mean, and I have looked at a great many of them since the second month of this year and I cannot read a paragraph of any of them and I have had that looked and read to me and that is a different thing and it does not count.** Then the woman in the room below, about twenty-eight, who comes up at about the tenth hour with a chair she has to carry up two flights and who stays about four times a week. *Read me this.* The woman looks at it and puts it down face down. **No.** *You have not looked at it.* **I have looked at the first line of it. I know what it is. It is a thing you have written for yourself and you want read back to you, and I am not going to be the one who reads it.** *Why not.* **Because you are not paying me and that makes it worse, not better, and I want to be fair with you about that, because everybody says the paid one is the one who can be stopped and it is the unpaid one who cannot say no at all. A woman who is paid to read is a woman somebody can tell to stop, and she can be shown the day she read it. A woman who is asked as a kindness in her own time by a woman of sixty-three she has lived above since the second month is a woman who has said yes in a room with nobody in it but the two of them, and if anybody ever comes and asks me what I read for you, I have to say yes I read it, and I have to say it to a person, and I have no slate and no day and no figure and nothing to point at.** *You have me. You can say that I asked you and that I wanted to know.* **I can say it and it will not help me, because you are sixty-three and cannot read a paragraph and in about four years that is going to be the only thing anybody knows about you, and I am twenty-eight and I will be able to read a paragraph for another forty years, and I would rather not be a thing a person above me was heard asking for.** She sat in the chair for about a quarter of an hour and they did not talk about it again, and when she went down she took the salt and left the chair, which she always does. Then what Bess Tarrant is going to do, told plainly, with the reason: **I am going to go and stand in a room where boxes are filled in. That is the whole of the plan.** There is no more of it than that and I have had since the second month to make a better one and there is not one, and I am sixty-three and I cannot read a paragraph and I have no money and I have a house about four miles off this road that is not shut and that I am the only person who knows is not shut. And I have worked out, this week, why nobody ever came to find me, and it is not the reason everybody thinks. **There is a line about me in a third column with no heading over it four hundred and thirty miles down this river, and it has been there since the sixth year, and my name is not in it and it is not a name, it is a description, and I have been unfindable on purpose, and I have been proud of it, and I have said in rooms that I was the only one of us nobody could find.** And I was wrong, and I was wrong in the most stupid way a person can be wrong. **The machinery does not need me. It needs a person who writes.** There is a woman in an office about nine miles from a counter who has written nineteen years of minutes and about four thousand entries in them and has never been asked what a box on a form is for, and she is the one the whole of this runs through, and she is the easiest person in this empire to find, because she is at a desk every day of her life in a building with a door on it. **So the arrangement did not keep me out of the way of the thing that was going to happen. It kept me out of the way of the only thing that was never going to happen, and being unfindable is the reason I was never asked and it is not the reason I was safe, and I have had those two the wrong way round for nine years and it has taken me until now to turn them over.** *You could have written and asked for the room. I do not let rooms to anybody I have not had a word with.* **Then that is what it is for. It is not for the room.** It is so that a person who cannot read a paragraph is a person somebody has had a word with, and that is the only thing I have wanted since the second month and I could not have said what it was and I have said it now in about ninety seconds on a step. Then she paid the day out of what she had, which was most of it and not all of it, and shut the door and stood in it with her coat on. There was a copy of nine lines in the coat and she did not take it out. **Nobody asked her anything that day and nobody asked her anything the next day, and there is no form anywhere in this empire for asking a woman of sixty-three the same question twice, and the first asking was in a doorway in the second month of the year after and it was done by a man who cuts kindling and who has told nobody since and is not going to be asked and does not want to be.** And last: **the date four years off that is in a minute book in a building about nine miles from a counter in this city is about her and she does not know it exists, and there is nobody who could tell her, and she is going to go and stand in a room where boxes are filled in and she is going to find out nothing about that either, and she has decided to go anyway, and that is the whole of what she has decided.**

## Chapter 209 — "The Third Asking, At A Desk" (2,898)

**POV: Nell Kest. The office of a seat, a building off the old river road about nine miles from a counter, a room on the ground floor with a window about two feet wide and a pane out of it and eleven minute books on a shelf, the second week of the eleventh month of the year after.** Twenty, a dye-house worker, which is what she is paid for, **and she keeps the books of the eleven houses on a lane in a furnace town about four hundred and thirty miles up this river and of four other houses in three other districts, which is what she is not paid for.** Her wage stopped in the second week of the third month and it is stopped now and the word for it is *held*. She has a sheet of her own with a heading she wrote herself and one day on it and she has told nobody about either. She has been in this city since the third week of the fifth month, and has been to four offices and two counters and one hearing room with a rail in it, **and after the fourth office she stopped going to offices.** A woman of about fifty-five is at a table, and she is not a lawyer and she is not a party and she is not a judge, and she has never been asked what any of it meant. She stood in the doorway for about a minute and a half before she said anything, **because she had come about four miles across this city to that door and she had rehearsed it the whole way and about a third of it had gone out of her head in the last stretch.** *You filled a box.* **I did.** **On the fourth day of the third week of the fifth month of this year. And the box was for the person, institution or thing engaged in the matter. And you wrote a name in it, and the name was mine, and I did not know there was a box and I did not know there was a day, and about four hundred and thirty miles up this river a woman of about sixty walked down a lane with a sheet on a board and read it off a roll and told me, and I said no out loud in a room and it did not work.** *Yes. All of that is correct. Sit down if you want to sit down.* **I will not sit down. I have come about four miles to ask a question and I am going to ask it standing up and I am going to be standing up when you answer it, and if I sit down I will be a person being received and I have been received by a great many people this year and I have not been asked one question by any of them.** Then the question, and it is the third time in about a hundred and forty years that one person in this empire had asked another person what a word on a form meant, and the first time anybody had asked on purpose. **How did the box get filled. Not what it says. Not what a representative is, a clerk of thirty-four told me that at a counter in the second week of the ninth month and gave it to me for nothing and would not write it down, and I have it. I want the other half.** I want to know how a person of twenty about four hundred and thirty miles away got into a box in a building she has never been in, by a hand she has never seen, out of a book she has never had, and I want it in a room and out loud, and I have been about six weeks working out that there is exactly one person in this empire who can tell me and she is about nine miles from the counter I stood at in the ninth month. Orla Denning put her pen down and answered it in about four minutes, standing on the other side of a table with her hands flat on it, and she did not sit either. **A return. A return is one printed sheet with a column on it and the column is headed for the person, institution or thing engaged in the matter, and it goes out to a district, and the district keeps a roll of households, and a keeper of a roll of households copies the column into her own book where a person can see it. The column is not filled in by the district. The column is filled in here, in this room, at this end, in advance, out of a roll, because a keeper cannot invent a person and cannot be asked what a word on a form means.** When the office asks a district a question the district has no answer to, it gets back the only answer there is, and writes the answer down in a box with a day on it, and sends it, and the keeper copies it into a roll. **The question the office asked your district was: the person of that family who is of age and resident. A roll of households does not say a person is of age and resident. It says a household is at a door. So what came back was a household, and the household that came back was yours, and the entry for it says a place of custom or of work and it does not say which of the women in it, and there is no box in this empire for the difference between a person and a trade.** *And you took the household, and you put a person in it.* **I took what came back and I put it in a box that takes a thing as well as a person, and I did it in about nine seconds, and I was not asked, and nobody was asked, and I have written on the head of a file in this room that I did it and that nobody asked me and that I did it correctly, and the file is not in the press, and there is no form anywhere in this empire that requires a clerk to put a file in a press.** *Why is the file not in the press.* **Because a file in the press is a file that a person can be told about, and being told about it is a service and being served is a party, and there is no way back out of a party. And I have been a clerk in this room for nineteen years and I was not in a party before the fifth month of this year and I would like to stay out of one for as long as this building lets me, and that is a reason and it is not a good one and I have not improved it.** Then the question she had come four miles for, which she had not said yet. *How many of them are there.* **I cannot tell you.** *You are the office. You are the only office in this empire that does this. You must be able to tell me.* **I have kept eleven minute books for nineteen years and I have entered about four thousand things into them and every one of them is a thing a room decided, and a thing a room decided does not record the thing that was done to a person in about nine seconds in a box. The office keeps no register of them. That is not carelessness.** A register is a book of persons and this office has never kept a book of persons, and it never needed one, because the persons were in other districts' books and this office never had to look at them. **So the number is not lost. The number has never been anywhere.** It is in a roll of households in every district in this empire, and every one of them is about four hundred and thirty miles from this desk, and not one of them has a keeper in it who has been asked what the fourth column is for. And I would say to you, as one clerk to another, and I have never said anything of the kind to anybody in nineteen years, that there are two of you that I know of and that is not a number, it is a memory, **and a memory of two is worse than a figure of none, because a figure of none is a thing a man can look for and never find, and a memory of two is a clerk of fifty-five in a room with a pane out of the window.** Then the price of the next four minutes, and the price is the truth and it is not about her. **You have just asked a question about a form in a room, out loud, and you are twenty, and you are not a party to anything, and nobody is going to serve you with this, and there is no instrument anywhere in this empire that will let anybody tell you what I am about to say you cannot have. A person who asks becomes answerable for the answer. Not you. Me.** In about four years a man with a copy of the right page can put this room side by side with a sheet of my hand and ask a clerk of this office why the column was filled in at this end in advance, and she will have to answer it, and her name will be at the foot of it, and the answer will be that she was not asked in about nine seconds in the fifth month of this year, and there is no form anywhere that asks her whether she was asked. **You have moved a thing from a book with no name on it to a room with two people in it, and that is the whole of what you have done,** and the two people are a woman of fifty-five who has written nineteen years of minutes and a woman of twenty who cannot read a paragraph and has been in this city since the third week of the fifth month, and neither of us can be protected and you have not gained anything at all except the four minutes. *I know that. I priced it in the fourth week of the fifth month to a woman of about sixty holding a board and she wrote it in a column and there was no box for a why and I have looked. I came four miles to be answerable for a question. That is the first thing anybody has ever let me be the price of and I am not going to be coy about it in a room.* Then she did not hand over the sheet. *You want to see it, because a day is the only part of it anybody can find, and you have a day, and you have been holding it since the fifth month, and you have not told me about it and I am not asking.* **You are not asking.** **A person who is not asked has not been given a duty, and I have known that since about the seventh month of next year and I have never been on the wrong side of it until this year.** *Keep it. I am not giving it to anybody. It is a sheet of my own with a heading I wrote myself and there is one day on it and the day is the only part of the whole business that can be found, and the minute I give it to an office it becomes a record of a person in an office, and I have spent three years refusing to make records of people and I am not starting with myself.* Then what she had come to say, and it is a decision, and it is hers. **I cannot get out of the box. You have not told me I can and I did not think anybody could, and I have asked four offices and two counters and a woman at a hearing and not one of them said the word *out* once. And I am twenty, and I am about four hundred and thirty miles from a lane with eleven doors on it, and my wage is held, and the only person who can tell me what the fourth column of that roll is for is a woman of about sixty who walks it once a year with a board and a basket, and nobody is going four hundred and thirty miles to ask her and there is no fund and no form for a fund, and I have said I was not going to add it up and I am not going to now.** **So here is what I have decided and it is the only decision I have and I have had it since the ninth month. I cannot get out of the box, and I am going to be the person who knows how it was filled, and I am not going to be a person who knows it alone.** In this city there is a counter where a clerk of thirty-four told me what a representative is and would not write it down. Four hundred and thirty miles up this river there is a lane with a roll of households on it. About nine miles from here there is a man with a book and no office on it and eleven questions in it and a twelfth line he has left empty because there is no post in this empire whose job is to ask. **That is three, and there is a fourth, and she is a clerk of thirty-eight at a window on a flood terrace about four hundred and thirty miles down this river, and she has never been asked anything either, and I am going to be asking four people instead of one**, and there is no form for that and nobody is going to help me and I am not going to be thanked for it, because there is no form anywhere that requires a person to be thanked and I have said that out loud too many times this year. Orla Denning did not write any of it down, and she said so. **I am not going to write that down either, and I want to be exact about why, because you will think it is kindness and it is not. It is that a woman of fifty-five who writes a woman's plan in her own book in about nine seconds has done to you the identical thing that was done to you in the fifth month of this year, and I have had the two of them side by side since about the fourth week of the ninth month and I have not been able to put them down again.** **The thing that happened to you was a document. If I write your plan down then you have been got at twice by two people who were not villains, and one of them is standing in front of you on the other side of a table.** *That is the answer to the question I have not asked you yet.* *What question.* **Whether you are frightened of having written the two lines on that file head. You are. And it has cost you about four hundred and thirty miles of nothing and a tray, and you did it anyway, on a day, in a room, with nobody in it, and I have not got a word for what that is and I am not going to make one up at the end of a four-mile walk.** **I have a word for it, and the word is *expensive*, and you are twenty and you have not got the four years I have got, and I would like you to go and be asked four questions and not one of them here.** **Sit down if you want to sit down. The room is not going anywhere and neither am I, and I have a few minutes before the tray comes down this corridor, and there is a chair on that side with nothing on it.**

## Chapter 210 — "A Bay, And No Post Whose Job It Is" (2,865)

**POV: Halla Wray. The Slade end, the shed and the bay, the third day of the last week of the eleventh month of the year after.** Fifty-one, foreman of the Slade Cut, an office with no office in it, on that bank since she was nine. **She can read and nobody at the district works has ever once in nine years asked her to read anything, and in the fourth week of the ninth month of this year she read six numbered lines out loud to nine men in that shed because she had decided to and nobody asked her, and it is the first time in her life that anybody in that shed has heard her read anything.** There is one sheet of her own hand in a book of her own, with the day against it; it is the words of a document and not the document, and **it has no name in it**, and she put it there on purpose, and she has read it since and has not added her name and is not going to; and the notice it was copied from is on the bench and has been since the seventh month, so the two of them are two sheets and not one. The second season came into its last weeks, the water was at the third-of-the-way mark, and about four hundred and forty foot of bank stood behind it with about nine men on it who had come because a word had been put in the yard and not because anybody had asked them. She did the ordinary things, **because a foreman who stops doing them is a foreman who has begun to make a speech of her own job**: the count of the works, which takes about four minutes; the water; the hold, which is against a company whose whole money is four shillings a year and all of it the rent of a building, **and which has not moved since the fourth week of the fourth month and is not going to move because a foreman is fifty-one and has a boy at home**; the factor's letter on a bench up the road, four lines, wanting a person who may be served and that person's consent, **and it is not going to be answered, and every day it is not answered is a day nobody has been entered.** Then the nineteen reasons, in a bay, in about four minutes, and not the names, the second reading slower. **They said it in the seventh month and they have said nothing since, and that is correct, and nobody is going to ask them again until the season comes round. A person is entitled to make a refusal once and have it kept and not be troubled about it again, and there is no form anywhere in this empire that entitles anybody to be troubled twice.** Then the four, in the open, standing, with the men looking at her, **none of them understanding that this is the fourth time in a year she has said it and the first time she has said it in a room with nobody to answer her**: **About four people on this cut cannot read a paragraph. They have never been asked once. Not in the first season, not on the fourth day of the seventh month, not in the second week of the tenth month, and not today, and there is no column for them and there is not going to be one, and the reason there is not going to be one is that a column for them would be a column somebody would have to fill.** And, crediting him and not taking it: **A book-keeper on this bank worked out the one way of reaching them in the second week of the tenth month and wrote down that he was not going to do it, with the day on it, and read it back twice, and he did it because a person who is paid to read is a person who can be told to stop. That is correct and it is the whole of the argument and I am not going to improve on it and I am not going to say it as though I thought of it.** And the other half, which is hers, and which she has been carrying since the third week of the seventh month and uses about four times a season: **I have been the reason I could not be found for forty-two years. Forty-two years on this bank and nine years holding the only job on it that is written down nowhere, and a child of nine did not choose any of it, and a foreman of fifty-one is in a box because of it. And I would like to be found.** I said that in this shed in the fourth week of the ninth month and some of you heard it and not one of you wrote it down, and that was correct, and there was no paper and nobody thought to fetch any. **So we have a woman on this bank who wants to be found, and four people on this bank who have never been asked anything, and one of those four is about the same age as the years I have been unfindable, and that is not a coincidence and I have not got a speech for it and I am not going to make one.** Then the question the whole of it turns on, asked out loud, standing up, in front of them, with it said in advance that nobody is going to answer it: **Who asks.** **That is the whole of the question and it has been in me since the ninth month and I have not said it in a shed because a shed is not a room that wants a record and I have spent nine years in rooms that do not want anything.** **So here it is in a room. A woman of twenty in a furnace town got put in a box in the fifth month and I got put in a box in the seventh month, and neither of us was asked, and there is no form in this empire for asking either of us, and the only instrument anybody has ever found for saying no to a box is a refusal to be served, and it did not work on the woman of twenty and it cannot work on me at all, because I was not served anything, I was entered by a class, and a class is not served on anybody, and a person who has not been served cannot refuse to be served.** That is the fifth time the protection and the catch have been the same act and I am not going to list them and I am not going to count them again, and nobody chose it, **and the reason nobody chose it is that the fifth time it happened it happened in this shed to me, and the four people it is about are not in this shed and have never been in a room together either.** **Now. There is no post in this empire whose job is to ask. I have been told by two people in the last six weeks that it has now been done three times about forms, and that two of the three were accidents and nobody chose either of them.** One was a room that wanted a record. One was a man who was frightened about his own household. And one was a woman of twenty who walked about four miles and stood at a desk and asked how the box got filled, and that one was on purpose, and nobody sent her, and I have not been told who she asked. **So three, and no post, and no plan, and I have asked nine men in a shed in the last two minutes and not one of them has said a word, and I did not expect one and I want it entered that I said in advance that I did not expect one, because a woman who asks a question in a room and then says afterwards that she expected nothing is a woman who has been in a room before.** And what she has got, and it is not a speech and it is not in a book: **Somebody asks, or nobody asks. And I do not know which, and neither do the three of them, and the only thing I have found out this year is that it happens to people who were not going to do it.** It happened to a room that wanted a record. It happened to a man who was afraid about his own household. It happened to a woman who was twenty and had come four miles. **There is no post. And that is the whole of the answer, and I have been waiting since the first week of the seventh month for somebody to stand in this shed and tell me what happens instead, and nobody is going to, and I am not going to ask them twice.** The shed stays quiet for about a minute and a half and then a man of about thirty from the second gang: **So you want one of us to do it.** **No. I do not want one of you to do it and if one of you offers I am going to refuse you, and I am telling you that now, in a room, in advance, so that none of you is a hero about it in about four years.** Here is my reason and it is the reason I have had since the fourth week of the ninth month and it is not a good reason and I know it is not a good reason and I am saying it anyway. **The moment one of you asks those four people, they are found. Not by the district and not by a seat. Found.** By whoever comes asking next, and there is always somebody who comes asking next, and I have watched a woman in a furnace town get found by a box and a day and a hand in about nine seconds by a person who was not a villain. **And I have been the one that could not be found, for forty-two years, and I have said in this shed that I would like to be found, and I have meant it, and I am telling you both of those things in the same breath and the second one is the one that decides it. So I am not going to be the reason four other people are found. If the four stay unasked this season then that is a decision and it is mine and I have made it and I am not going to be talked out of it by a man in a shed who thinks he has found something to do.** She put the book with the two sheets in it on the bench and left it there, and it stayed there all night, and in the morning the shed was open and about nine men came in and looked at it and none of them asked about it and none of them will. Then, at about the sixth hour on the second day, in the middle of it: a man of about fifty-five who has been on that cut for about thirty-three years, which is nine years less than she has, and who came the year after her and has never once said so, **and he is one of the four.** Halla Wray knew which one of the four he was before he was through the door, **and she knew it in the ordinary way a foreman knows the face of a man on her own bank, and there is no form anywhere in this empire in which a foreman's memory of a face is a record, and there never has been, and she has relied on that for nine years.** *Can you look at my drum. The chain has gone stiff and it wants oiling and I have brought it up here because the smith is at Lowcross and Lowcross is a bridge and the bridge is shut and I am not going over it for a chain.* **The chain wants the third link out and a drop of something in the bush. That is the whole of it and you could do it yourself with a nail.** *I have not got a nail.* That was the whole of it. It took about two minutes and he stood at the bench with the drum on it and she told him about the third link and about the oil, **and every man in that shed watched a foreman do a perfectly ordinary thing to a man who cannot read a paragraph. And she did not ask him.** Not about the hold. Not about the season. Not about the nineteen reasons or the two sheets of paper with a seal and nothing under the seal lying on the bench where anybody who came in could read them. She had asked the room in the last two minutes whether they knew who fills in a box, and she had said in advance that nobody was going to answer, and she had meant it as a kind of honesty, **and a man of fifty-five walked in about two minutes later who is one of the four people it is about and she did not ask him one word.** She thought about it for the rest of that week and has not got a better account of it than that and has not told it to anybody. **He would have said yes.** That is the part she cannot get round, and she is a woman who has been right about the rate on her own wall since she was seventeen and she is not a woman who is comfortable with being right. **He would have said yes, in a shed, out loud, in about two seconds, and then he would have been a man who had been asked, and a man who has been asked can be asked again by whoever comes next, and she would have started it. And that is not a reason, and she knows it is not a reason, and she gave it out loud in a shed in the second week of the eleventh month to a room as though it were.** **It is a bad reason. I have said in this shed that I would rather be asked than not, and about the bank I have been asked five times and said no five times and about this I have not been asked once, and the reason is that nobody has thought of it, and I have thought of it, and I have not asked, and that is the whole of what I have done in a year of standing in rooms. I would like somebody to put that on a slate and read it back to me**, and there is nobody here who is going to, and I am not going to ask one of the four men in this shed to do it either, for the reason I have just given, and I know exactly how that sounds. Then the water went down about a foot before the end of it and the second season came to its end with about nineteen people still behind that bank, and about four of them in that bay never having been asked anything, and a guarantee under the fire-and-water device standing offered and unanswered with about sixty children under sixteen inside it, and a bill at Lowcross unpaid and nobody liable and nobody paying it in a shed either, and a factor's letter on a bench wanting a person who may be served. **Nobody sent anybody anywhere.** The lamp went on at about the seventh hour, which is later than it ought to be, and the door of the shed was open, and **there is no post in this empire whose job is to ask, and three accidents are not a plan, and the woman who has the most reason in the world to be asked about a thing has still not been asked, and a foreman of fifty-one has decided, out loud, in a room, in front of about nine men, that she is not going to be the reason four other people are found, and that is the end of the season and it is not the end of anything else.**

## What Volume 05 Batch 0001 resolved, what it did not, and what it hands on

**Resolved:** two people are shown in a box and neither was asked, and the ordinary way each of them finds out is on the page in a clerk's own hands — a woman of twenty from a counter, a woman of twenty from a board and a basket, a foreman of fifty-one from a shelf in a shed. A clerk of about fifty-five has discovered that the entry in the box is in her own hand and that she was not a villain and was not asked, and has entered it, with the day, on a file head, and has taken the file out of the press and it is not going back. The rule this volume turns on is stated on the page in three pieces by three people and is not compressed anywhere: **a form which cannot be asked cannot be un-filled, and it cannot be un-filled by the person who filled it; the only thing standing between a person in a box and the rest of their life is somebody asking a question out loud in a room, and there is no post in this empire whose job is to ask; and a person who has not been served cannot refuse to be served, so the only instrument there is is no use at all to a person entered by a class.** The reason the machinery got the foreman is said in her own mouth and it is the fifth time the protection and the catch have been the same act and nobody chose it. A clerk of thirty-four has given the answer to what a representative entry is, out loud, at a counter, for nothing, and has not written it down, and the reason there is nowhere to put it is that there is no form in this empire for a document about a person who did not ask to be in one. A clerk of thirty-eight has answered a question about the word *resident* at a window and has said the price out loud before she answered, and the finding is that what goes in the box is whatever the roll has, and a roll of households has a household in it. A book-keeper has worked out the one way of reaching four people who cannot read a paragraph and has not used it and has entered the not-doing with the day on it and read it back twice. A woman of twenty-four has exercised the undertaking of the fourth of the first month for the fifth time, has refused to write down a sentence a man has not finished, has said the price of a party out loud ten times and been thanked zero times, and has said in advance that she will say no if anybody ever asks her to go and ask a question in a room on that bank. A woman of sixty-three has worked out that being unfindable is the reason she was never asked and not the reason she was safe, and has decided to go and stand in a room where boxes are filled in, on her own account, and nobody sent her. And a foreman of fifty-one has asked the room the question the batch exists to ask, out loud, and has not got an answer out of nine men, and has decided that she is not going to be the reason four other people are found, and has said the reason out loud and then said that the reason is a bad one.
