**Not resolved, and not this batch's to resolve:** nobody is going to say who is going to ask on purpose; the woman of about sixty who keeps the roll of the district about four hundred and thirty miles up the river is unnamed and unasked and there is no fund and no form for a fund; the class cannot be counted by anybody and two of its members are known; the two who are in the boxes stay in the boxes; the act done by a person who was not heard is not undone and cannot be; the date four years off is in a minute book and cannot be unscheduled and the woman it is about does not know it exists; the guarantee stands offered and unanswered with about sixty children under sixteen inside it and no child is named; the bill at Lowcross stands at nineteen pounds three and fourpence, unpaid, nobody liable, no line for a bridge in that fund in nineteen years; the thirty-one of Mosswake are thirty-one; about four people in a bay who cannot read a paragraph have still never been asked once and a reader of seventeen has still not been thanked and is not going to start; the two sealed pages are shut with two refusals between them and no third; the Ashfall bundle is shut and unnamed; and the volume's own question — if the office was meant to be temporary, who changed it into an inheritable one, and why are dragons themselves bound by the altered compact — is not asked in any of the ten chapters and is not going to be.

## Chapter 211 — "A Man Reads It Aloud And Nothing Goes In A Book" (3,116)

**POV: Rennick Adley. The Slade end, the hired stone store off the Slade and its bay, the second day of the first week of the twelfth month of the year after.** Thirty-eight, keeping the books of the Slade Cut Company since the second month of next year, **the Company's whole money four shillings a year and all of it the rent of the building.** The season is shut; there is not much to do; the factor's letter of four lines is on the bench, **not going to be answered, and every day it is not answered is a day nobody has been entered.** Ordinary things first: the count of the works, the water, the hold, and the nineteen reasons in the third column read out with the second reading slower. Then a man of about fifty-five, **one of the about four people in that bay who cannot read a paragraph, and who Rennick Adley has known and never said a word about**, comes to the end of the bench at about the ninth hour with a printed district slip. It has a heading, a day under it, four lines, a line for a name and a space for an officer's hand, and the heading says the water at four houses is to be shut a day and a night for cleaning a main, and any house without stored water will be classed as a complaint, and a complaint has to be made in writing by the person of the house, and the district cannot do it for anybody. **And there is no box on it anywhere, and the person of the house is a person and not a household and not a trade, and somebody wrote that down on purpose, which is more than a form has ever done, and the man cannot read a word of it and did not know it was a favour.** *I have got the whole of it in my hand and I cannot tell whether the four is mine or the next one along, and I am not going to put my name under it until somebody has told me what is on it.* **He could have said no.** He thought about it in about four seconds and the reason is that **a man who has been read to in a bay is a man who has been seen**, and a book-keeper who reads a slip out loud in a bay in front of nine men is doing to four men at once what a foreman of fifty-one refused in the second week of the eleventh month to do to one; so he walks out of the yard with the man, reads the heading first, then the four lines, in about a minute and a half, and is stopped twice, both times at a figure, both times to have it said again more slowly. **The line for a name and a man who cannot sign: I can put it down and you can make a mark under it, and I will read the mark back to you so that you know which one it is, and I will not write anything else and there will be no book.** A mark is made with chalk off the yard wall and read back twice, the second slower. *You are not going to write it down.* **Neither of them is going anywhere and that is the correct arrangement and I would like it noticed that I worked it out in about four seconds and that the four seconds were about you and not about the works.** Then the finding, said to the man and not to the two other men: **Nobody asked anybody what a word on a form means, and I want that said, and I want it said by me and not by a clerk, and I am the wrong man to say it and I am saying it anyway. A man came to the end of my bench with a slip in his hand and asked me to read him his own paper. That is not a question about a word on a form. That is a man asking a man to read him a thing that is his. It is not one of the three and I am not going to let it be counted as one of the three, because a count of what has been asked about forms is a count of people and that is the only thing that count is.** And: **it is the only one of the three that has ever been done, and it is the only one of the three that has cost nobody a thing.** Then the whole of the hold and the guarantee standing offered and unanswered on four hundred and forty foot of it with about sixty children under sixteen inside it, and the bill at Lowcross at nineteen pounds three and fourpence that nobody is liable for and no line for a bridge in that fund in nineteen years, **and none of that can be given to four men who cannot read a paragraph, and the finding of the second week of the tenth month stands and is not said again and not improved.** And: **A thing that is written down does not need anybody to want you found. It only needs somebody to go looking.** Then the decision, read back twice before he said it: **I am going to do it again, and I am not going to write it down and I am not going to tell the foreman, and there are three things in that and I will take them one at a time.** Not writing it down, because in about four years a man with a copy of the right page can come into that building and ask which men he read to and on what days and in what words, and the man will have a day against his name on a page in a book that keeps the Company's works, **and that is how a person who cannot read a paragraph gets found and nobody has to mean it.** Not telling the foreman: **A foreman who knew would be a foreman somebody could ask** — if she knows, she is a person on that bank who knows a thing about four men in that bay, and there is no form anywhere in this empire she could be asked under, and in about four years somebody would ask her. And the third, which he is worst at: **a thing that is written down is the only thing anybody can be held to and a thing that is not written down is the only thing that costs nobody anything, and the whole of this matter from the ninth month of this year has been a thing that was written down, and the instrument that gets to a person without costing anybody is the one that leaves no mark, and there is no form anywhere in this empire for a thing that leaves no mark, and I am not going to try to invent one.** Then the man comes back into the bay and asks whether he is one of the nineteen. It takes about four minutes because the names are in a different book, about nine hundred and forty of them in nine hands over about sixty years. He is not, and he never has been, because **you have never refused anything, because nobody in about thirty-three years has asked you whether you would, and a person who has not been asked has not said no and has not said yes and is not on either list.** And: **a man who has not been asked is a third thing and it has no word and it is the only one of the three that nobody in this matter has ever been in.** And: **I have just read a name out of a book to a man in order to tell him what he was not, and that is the one thing I have done today that I would not be able to do again, and I have not got a rule for it and I am not going to make one up at the end of a morning.**

## Chapter 212 — "A Woman Stands In A Room And Says Her Own Name" (3,014)

**POV: Bess Tarrant. Auremar, a room hired by the day above a shop, and the office of a seat in a building off the old river road, the second day of the second week of the twelfth month of the year after.** Sixty-three, keeps a house about four miles off the old river road that is not shut and that she is the only person who knows is not shut, **can write and cannot read a paragraph, has been in this city since the second month of the year after, and nobody sent her, because there is no form anywhere in this empire for a person who comes on her own account.** She goes at the ninth hour, the other way. She stands in the doorway about four minutes and counts the trays: two up and one down. Then she goes in. The room is on the ground floor with a window about two feet wide and no pane in it, eleven books on a shelf, a table, and a woman of about fifty-five who did not get up. Two other people: a man of about thirty with a coat on by the door and a man of about sixty at the shelves. *Sit down if you want to sit down.* **I have come to stand.** The clerk puts her pen down, which she does about twice a year, and the two questions are ordinary and are not about a form: *Are you served.* No. *Are you in a matter.* No. **Then the third question, which is a name.** *She had heard a person say a name in that room. Not a clerk, not a party, not a return, not a book, not a hand at the foot of anything. A person, out loud, in a room, and it was not copied out of anything, and it was not written down, and it was not the second time in nineteen years because it was the first time in nineteen years.* Bess Tarrant says it in about two seconds and does not say it twice and does not spell it. The clerk says thank you and stops, because there is no form anywhere in this empire that requires a clerk to say thank you at a table. Then the old man at the shelves asks whether she is the one for the water; she says she has not come about the water; he says he has wasted her morning and goes, and does not apologise, and means it. **That is the whole of the room. Three people and a shelf of books and a tray going up a corridor.** Then *What do you want*, and Bess Tarrant tells her in nine sentences, standing: **I have come to stand in a room where boxes are filled in. That is the whole of the plan. I have read in my own coat a thing I cannot read, and I have had it read to me once in a doorway by a man who cuts kindling, and I have worked out since that asking works on a person and has never once worked on a piece of paper, and a form cannot be asked at all.** And the finding she came to deliver, to a woman and not to a room: **the machinery does not need me, it needs a person who writes, and you are that person, and you have written nineteen years of minutes and about four thousand things into them and nobody has ever once asked you what a box on a form is for, including me, until about four minutes ago, and I am sixty-three and I have come nine miles to say a thing to a person instead of to a building, and I would like it noticed that I did not write it down, and I cannot, and that is why I am standing here and not sitting down.** Then the decision, announced before it is made and unasked for: the clerk gets up off the chair, takes down one of the eleven books, does not open it, and puts it back — **that is a record of what a room decided, it is not a register of people, and this office has never kept one and never needed one, because the people are in other districts' books and we never had to look at them.** And: **A person who has been in a box is in a roll of households in a district about four hundred and thirty miles from this table, and it is in nobody's book in this building, and I could go and look at about nine hundred districts' rolls tomorrow and there is nothing whatever to stop me, and I have a book of about nine hundred and forty names on a shelf behind you that I could do it out of in about four days.** *Then do it.* **No. I am not going to, and that is the decision I made at about the third minute of this and I have not been asked for it by anybody, and I would like it entered that a person of sixty-three who cannot read a paragraph asked me for the one thing that would find her and I said no.** The reason takes about a minute and a half and is not a good reason and the woman who gives it says so: **a name in a book does not go looking, and a name in a book only goes looking when somebody goes looking, and I am the person in this building who goes looking, and if I go looking then I am doing to a woman who came on her own account the identical thing that was done to a woman of twenty in the fifth month of this year, in a box, in about nine seconds, by a person who was not a villain and who is sitting at this table — and you cannot read a paragraph, I would have to read you what I found, I would choose the words, and that is what happened to you in the ninth month and it would happen again in the first week of the twelfth, and the difference is that the second time it would be me.** Then the copy of nine lines comes out of the coat and is held out and is not taken. **That is yours. I am not giving it to you.** *I know you would have, and that is the difference between a man who cuts kindling and you, and it took me the whole of the second month to be able to say it out loud. He did not ask to keep it. You asked.* And then, last: **There is a day entered in one of the eleven books on that shelf, in the first week of the fifth month of this year, with my name at the foot of the line, and it is about four years off, and I have found out nothing whatever about it, and I am not going to find out anything about it, and I have thought about it on the walk here and I have decided that if I had found out about it I would not be able to do the thing I came here to do, and I would rather not know and stand in a room for nothing.** The clerk says she entered that day and did not know what she was entering and Bess Tarrant is the only person in this empire who could tell her and has just said she is not going to. *That is right.* **And nobody asked her one word about it, and there is no form anywhere in this empire that requires a person to be told a thing they have asked not to be told, and about four minutes later she was out in the street with her coat done up, and she stood at the end of it for about an hour and a half the way she stands at a wall most days, and the day was going, and she did not go back to the room above a shop until the light had gone off the wall.**

## Chapter 213 — "The Second Time She Said The Price" (3,148)

**POV: Ivet Sarn. The clerk's window of the Mosswake Roll Court on a flood terrace, and the embankment corridor behind it, the third day of the third week of the twelfth month of the year after.** Thirty-eight, nine years at that window, four presses in the corridor, **and a back room off that corridor she has walked past every working day for nine years and has never once been inside.** About nine people a month ask her for a book in the wrong form. **He came back.** He is about thirty-four; in the first week of the tenth month he asked what the word *resident* means on a return because he had moved in the second week of the ninth month from a street with a shop on it to rooms over a yard, four streets off, inside the same district, and he had a wife and a boy, and he wanted to know whether a word was going to be used about them. **He had said afterwards that he would rather not have asked, and she had said that that was the correct answer, and there is no form anywhere in this empire that requires anybody to be told anything after that. He did not ask her anything.** He puts down a slip with a reference on it, gives four words, pays fourpence for a copy made on a sheet of press in about a minute and a half, read out, agreed. That is the whole of the transaction: about four hundred of those a year and not one of them a question. Then he does not go. *I have got about four minutes and I would like to use them.* **What did you come back for.** *You did not answer my question. Not the word. The other thing you said first.* **I always say it first: a person who asks a question about a form in a room becomes a person somebody has answered, and there is no instrument anywhere in this empire that takes that back off him.** *I did not hear it. I heard a clerk being careful.* And then: **Nobody had told him and nobody was going to. The only reason he knew was that he had asked her to say it again in a room, and that is a thing a person can do, and it is the only thing anybody can do about it, and there is no form anywhere in this empire for asking a person to tell you what you have become.** She says it again, in about a minute, the same words, and the second time is the one that counts and no form says a thing counts twice. *It is worse than I thought.* It is exactly what he thought. Then he asks whether anybody had found him — **a plain question, in a room, out loud, and it is on the page because she has never had one of those at that window either, and the count of those is a different count and is not three and is not printed here.** And the count, stated: **You have, and there is no undoing it and no form anywhere in this empire to undo it with. And you are the second of the three. The first was a room that wanted a record, in the fifth month, in a court. The third is a woman of twenty who walked about four miles in the second week of the eleventh month and asked a clerk to explain how the box got filled, and she was the first one anybody did on purpose, and nobody sent her. Three, and none of the three of you is a plan.** Then, unasked, the thing he actually came for: **You moved in the second week of the ninth month, four streets off, inside the same district, and you did not tell anybody, and the reason is that there is nothing at this counter that asks you, and that is not a complaint, it is the shape of the building.** Your household is at a door four streets off and was at a door on a street with a shop on it, both inside this district, the roll has both, **and the roll does not say which people live at either door. It says a household is at a door.** And: **what came back to the office about your street, in the fifth month of this year, was a household. The box wanted a person, a household is what the roll had, and that is the whole of what has happened to you and your wife and your boy, and nothing has been done to you at all.** And *resident* means the roll at a door; not living in it, not paying anything, not anybody having agreed to anything; a man can be resident on four rolls in four districts and be on none of them in the sense he means; **you have been on one of them since the second week of the ninth month and you moved four streets off and the roll never noticed and the water did not care and nobody in this building ever knew there was anything to notice.** *That is what I was afraid of.* **That is the opposite of what you were afraid of, and the answer you got was an ordinary answer and it cost you the only thing you have.** Then the basket under the sill, about nine inches deep, off a form that calls its contents rubbish for about a hundred and forty years. *What is in it.* **They are returns.** Every one has a column headed for the person, institution or thing engaged in the matter, filled in at the other end, in ink, in a hand that is not hers, with a day on it, **and the day is the day the column was filled and not the day it was sent, and there is no space on the sheet for the second day.** And: **that is the only document in the world that says how a box got filled, and I have never thrown one away, and I have never shown one to anybody, and I have never told anybody what is in it, and there are about nine sheets deep and every one of them is the only one of its kind. And I have just told you.** He does not ask to see one. *You are not going to show me.* **No. You are the second person in a hundred and forty years to have asked me what a word on a form means and you came back and asked me nothing, and a man who comes back and asks nothing is the only kind of person in this empire it is safe to tell anything to at all.** And she will not take one out, because there is one in that basket about the street he used to live on, and if it goes into a man's hand then in about four years somebody can hold it up beside a sheet of hers and ask her to explain the difference, and that person would be him, about himself and his wife and his boy, and she has got no way of stopping him and would not want to. *And if I wanted one.* **You would have to come and ask me for it in a room with two people in it, and there is no form for that, and I would have to say yes in front of the other one, and you did not ask, and I noticed that you did not ask and I want it entered that I noticed.** Then the back room: *That door has been open the whole time you have been talking.* It has, a couple of inches, halfway along, every working day for nine years, and she has been past it about two thousand times. **A person who opens a room nobody has asked her about is a person who has given herself a duty, and a person who has given herself a duty cannot stop**, and one of those is the reason there is a paper about a winter in a drawer in her own room that she has never told the court about. *You have not looked at it.* No. **He nodded at it and did not ask her what was in it, and that was the second time in about ten minutes that a person had stood in front of her and failed to ask her a question, and it is the whole of the reason she has said as much as she has said.** Then the price, again, in full: **You asked me in the first week of the tenth month and I answered you, and the answer was true, and the answer was that nothing has been done to you, and you have been carrying the price of a true answer since then, and I am not going to be the reason that is a strange thing to be carrying.** And: **So there is no document in this empire that says you asked me anything, and you asked me something, and I answered you, and you are the only person who knows it, and I am the only other one, and in about four years neither of us can prove a word of it, and I would like that written down somewhere and I am not going to write it anywhere.** Then the ordinary trade, nine more copies, a man of about fifty at a minute past, and the finding: **about four hundred a year and not one of them is a question, and the reason is not that the people who come to a counter do not want to know things. It is that a person who wants to know something at a counter does not come to a counter, they come to a counter to buy fourpence worth of paper, and they would be ashamed to stand there and use up a minute of a clerk's time for nothing.** And her own register on the top shelf of the second press, **whose fourth column has had no heading over it for nine years and she has not filled it and nobody has ever asked her why, and that is a column in a book on a flood terrace and it is not a column in a book about four hundred and thirty miles up this river and she is not going to stand at a window and pretend the two of them are one thing.** Then her own book with no office on it, the day on it, read back twice, the second slower, and the reason she has written eleven times in nine years: **A hand of mine is the only hand anybody is going to be able to put side by side in about four years, and I have now done this for the twelfth time and I have not stopped and I am not going to.** And, at the foot, a second line, the only second line she has ever written in it, four words, and not a rule: **He came back and asked me nothing.**

## Chapter 214 — "The Reason She Gave To A Man With A Satchel" (2,722)

**POV: Rennick Adley. The Slade end, a bay and a shed up the road, the fourth day of the fourth week of the twelfth month of the year after.** Thirty-eight, not a clerk, the books since the second month of next year, **the Company's whole money four shillings a year and all of it the rent of the building**, and the third column of the ledger with nineteen reasons in it and a day against every one and no names in that column at all. He goes up the road because the count of the works is due and the water is due and there is nothing else in a closed season, and it takes about half an hour at the pace he walks. **The shed is about nine foot by eleven**, a bench along the north wall, a lamp not lit until about the seventh hour, and it is the third hour of the afternoon. He lets her do the ordinary things, **because a book-keeper who interrupts a foreman in the first two minutes of a visit does not get to the fourth minute, and the fourth minute is where anything happens.** The count of the works, the water, the hold, **the factor's letter, not going to be answered, and every day it is not answered is a day nobody has been entered**, the nineteen reasons read out and not the names with the second reading slower. **A person is entitled to make a refusal once and have it kept and not be troubled about it again, and there is no form anywhere in this empire that entitles anybody to be troubled twice.** Before the satchel comes in: a man of about fifty-five, one of the four, at the bench with a drum between his knees taking a third link out of a chain with a nail, because the smith is at Lowcross and Lowcross is a bridge and the bridge is shut; and a man of about forty from the third gang asks him a question about the water standing where he is, and he looks at the bench for about two seconds, and **Halla Wray answers it from behind him without turning round and in about four seconds flat, in a foreman's voice, in the plainest words there are, and the man of about forty accepts it and goes back to what he was doing, and nobody in that shed notices anything at all.** The book-keeper saw the whole of it and did not understand it for about two hours afterwards and has not entirely understood it since, and wrote nothing down then or afterwards. Then a man of about thirty from a district works with a satchel, standing in the shed in a way that says he has been in a great many of them that month. *What I have to know is who I enter.* *That depends what you want to enter him for.* *I have a column and a day, and last season the column came back with a household in it and I could not put a household on a list of works.* *I put what the man does. That is the answer and you can write it down.* **And there are four of yours that do not come to the shed and that I cannot ask, and I have been told that in about four minutes by a man in a store and not by a person, and I am asking the person.** **The shed went quiet for about a minute and a half, and Rennick Adley stood against the north wall with the ledger under his arm and did not move, and there are about nine men in that shed and not one of them has ever heard a foreman of fifty-one be asked a question about the four by anybody at all, ever, including the four.** And she answers it, in the ordinary way, standing, in about a minute and a half: **Because if I ask one of them I have asked one of them, and then there are three, and the three will be asked by whoever comes next, because a man who has been asked can be asked again, and that is the only door anybody has ever opened on a person who cannot read a paragraph. And the fourth will be found out by arithmetic.** *That is a bad reason.* **It is the reason and it is mine and I have had it since the third month, and I have not said it to a book-keeper since the second week of the eleventh month of the year after and I have just said it to a man with a satchel who had not been in the room when I decided not to say it, and I would like it noticed that the only way a sentence of mine comes out of my mouth is when somebody asks me a question about the works.** The man writes it down and then asks a second question, and the second question is not about the four: *Before I put my column in — is there anything on that bank I am going to be told about that I have not been told.* **No**, and she tells him the two things she knows of because he has a column and not because she has decided to: a guarantee standing offered and unanswered on about four hundred and forty foot of it with about sixty children under sixteen inside it, no such person has ever come forward, and she has not got the terms of it in her head and is not going to read them out in a shed at the third hour; and a bill at Lowcross at nineteen pounds three and fourpence, unpaid, nobody liable, no line for a bridge in that fund in nineteen years. *That is not my district.* **It is nobody's. That is what a bill with no line against it is.** *That is a bad reason.* And then, from the wall, Rennick Adley hears it. He has wanted that sentence since the third month of this year, and he told a foreman of fifty-one in the seventh month out loud in front of about nine men that the day he asked was the day she stopped saying the half she had got, and she heard him, and he has not asked, and he is not going to. **And it came out in a shed on the fourth day of the fourth week of the twelfth month, out loud, in a room, aimed at a man with a satchel who would not remember it in a week, and it went to a stranger.** He could not write it down: a line in the back of that book is a findable thing, and what would be in it is a foreman's own reason for a decision about four men, and a man with a copy of the right page would put it beside a note of a seat and ask why the district's man was told it in a shed and not told to the book-keeper who had been waiting nine months. He could not ask her. And he could not repeat it, which is the one he had not thought of: **The half of a sentence she has got goes to strangers, and it has always gone to strangers**, because a foreman's answer to a question about the works is said to whoever is asking about the works, and a man from a district works is a stranger, and there is no form anywhere in this empire that requires a foreman to give the same answer twice to the same person in the same room, so in a week or so she will be able to say a different thing and both of them will have been true. **So a man who is owed a sentence and is not going to be given it is a man who has it, and cannot use it, and cannot put it anywhere, and has to carry it.** She finds out afterwards, at the bench, with both hands on the ledger and doing nothing with it. *That was a whole sentence and I did not mean to say it in a room.* *I know you did not.* **I have had it since the third month, and I have given it to a district in about a minute and a half, and I have not given it to you, and you know I have not, and I would like it entered that I know you know.** *There is nothing to enter it in, and that is not a complaint.* At the gate, to his back, which she has not done in about nine years: **that was a whole sentence and a foreman who has given a reason away by accident is in a worse position than one who has not, because now there is a copy of it in a satchel going four hundred and thirty miles up this river with nobody's name on it, and I cannot get it back and I would not want to.** *I am not going to write it down.* **I know you are not going to write it down, and I know exactly why, and I have known since the seventh month, and I would have given it to you in the seventh month if you had asked and you did not ask and that was correct and it is still correct and I am not going to say anything else about it.** He walked the half hour back with the ledger and the water on his left and about four hundred yards of it in view the whole way, and wrote nothing down, told nobody, and slept little. **And on the fourth day of the last week of the twelfth month of the year after the year turned, and nobody in that bay noticed the day it turned on, and there is no form anywhere in this empire that requires a person to notice a year, and it is not a form and it is not a day and it is in nobody's book, and the season was shut and the water was down and about nineteen reasons were in a column with a day against every one of them and about four men in that bay still had never been asked anything, and a foreman of fifty-one had said a whole sentence out loud in a room to a stranger, and a book-keeper of thirty-eight had heard it and could not do one single thing with it.**

## Chapter 215 — "The Word Engaged, And The Fourth Time" (3,060)

**POV: Nell Kest. Auremar, a room over a shop, and a rented room, the second day of the first week of the first month of the year after next.** Twenty, a dye-house worker, **keeps the books of eleven houses on a lane in a furnace town about four hundred and thirty miles up this river and of four other houses in three other districts, which is what she is not paid for**, and her wage stopped in the second week of the third month of the year after and the word for it is *held*. **She walked about nine miles in one day and in about eleven hours with two stops, and she had the address in her head and not on a paper, because there is a form in this empire for the address of a place a person may be served at and there is not one for the address of a person who is not in a matter.** What she decided in the second week of the eleventh month of the year after, standing in a room about nine miles from a counter: **I cannot get out of the box, and I am going to be the person who knows how it was filled, and I am not going to be a person who knows it alone.** Four people. She has asked one. At the door: **I did not send for anybody. There is no form in this empire for a person who comes on her own account and I have looked and you are the second one I have done this to.** Marek Kest, thirty-eight, a rented room with a table in it, a book with no office on it, about four feet of a wall he does not use, no office, no fund, no register, **and a bar of his own that came off him on the twelfth of the ninth month of last year on an application of one line which he wrote himself.** Tamsin Rook, twenty-four, in the room because two instruments require it and they are not one instrument: **a paper made in a form in four days with a day on it, and a watch that does not name him and does not name her and requires only that a person who is not from the office that cannot be named be present.** He has eleven lines in the book with a day against the sheet and not against the lines, and a twelfth line with nothing on it; she looks at both and asks about neither, which he notices, and which is the reason he sits down. *What have you come for.* **What does the word *engaged* mean.** *Ask it again.* **I have just asked it. I came nine miles to ask it. I have never asked anybody anything in my life that took me nine miles and I am not going to stand on a stair and ask it twice.** *Then ask it in here, because I want it out loud in a room and not on a step.* She asks it in the room, standing, hat in hand, and it is the fourth time in about a hundred and forty years that one person in this empire has asked another person what a word on a form meant, and the first three were a court room in the fifth month of the year after that wanted a record, a clerk's window in the first week of the tenth, and a desk in the second week of the eleventh, **and two of the three were accidents and nobody chose either of them, and this one was on purpose and nobody sent her.** He says the count out loud, because a number a person says can be held to, and answers in about four minutes. **I can tell you what it has been used to do. I cannot tell you what it means**, and the difference between those two things is the whole of the question and there is nobody in this empire who can close it. A roll of households does not list rights, holdings or claims; that is on the face of the third line and is older than he is; the office asks for a person; the only question there is an answer to is who is on the roll; the answer is a household; the box takes a household because the box takes a thing; it says *the person, institution or thing engaged in the matter* and does not say which of the three is wanted, and there is no box anywhere in about nine hundred buildings that will only take one of them. **And nobody has ever needed the word defined, because a box that will take a thing can always be filled in, and a box that will only take a person cannot. Not because anybody is keeping it from you. Because a thing fits in a box and a person does not, and a form is a thing, and a form cannot be asked what any of its words mean, and a form is the only thing in this empire that has never once been asked and the only thing in this empire that has never once said no.** Then: **it means you are on a roll at a door**, and the difference between a roll at a door and her is a thing about four hundred and thirty miles away in a lane, walked once a year with a sheet on a board and a basket, and **she does not know what the fourth column of her own roll is for, and there is no fund and no form for a fund, and nobody has ever been to ask her anything, and that is the whole end of it.** And: *I have been on her list. She is the one who told me.* **Then she is the only person alive who can say how your box got filled, and she cannot be asked, and that is not anybody's plot.** Then Tamsin Rook says the price and then the other half of it: **I am going to say the price out loud and I have said it before and I am not going to be thanked for it, and there is no form anywhere in this empire that requires a person to be thanked. A person who asks a question about a form in a room becomes a person somebody has answered. Not the person the question is about. The one who asked.** And she has said the price of being a party out loud ten times and nobody has thanked her once and she did not expect to be thanked once and would like it written down that she did not. **And nobody has ever said the other half of it, and I have only just worked it out at about the fourth minute of this: Every person who has ever answered anybody about a form in this empire has been a clerk. A clerk is findable. A clerk has a window, or a counter, or a room, or eleven books on a shelf, and in about four years a man with a copy of the right page can walk in and put a line under that clerk's name and be answered. And he is not a clerk. He has no office and no register and nothing in this empire he could be looked up in. He is the first person in this matter who is answerable and cannot be found, and the reason he cannot be found is that nobody was ever going to have to look him up, and that is the same sentence as the reason the office cannot tell you how many of you there are.** *Say that again slowly.* **No. A number a person says can be held to, and if I say it again then there are two of them and they will not be identical, and I am not going to be a person who improves a thing she has already said in a room.** *Then say the part that is about him.* **There is nothing anybody can instruct him about, and nothing anybody can pay him for, and nothing anybody can thank him for, and that is the reason he is the most dangerous person in this matter and it is also the reason nobody in it can protect him**, and she said both halves in the third week of the tenth month of the year after and is not going to soften the second one now. Then his answer, standing: **I am a man with a bar that came off him on a one-line application and I have read every form in this business for about four years, and there is no definition of that word in any of them**, and there is not going to be one, because the moment there is one a keeper of a roll has to decide whether a household is engaged in a matter, and a keeper cannot be asked what a word on a form means, and a keeper has no instrument and no protection and a basket once a year. **The word is not undefined by accident. The word is undefined on purpose, and not by anybody. It is undefined the way a gap in a hedge is a shape rather than a hole.** And: **you are engaged in the matter in the only sense the form can hold, which is that you are the nearest thing to a person in it.** Then she asks whether she may write it down, he says no, she says why not, and she finishes his sentence for him: **Because a hand of mine is now the only hand anybody is going to be able to put side by side in about four years, and you have no hand to put beside mine because you have no office, and I have a book of eleven houses that nobody pays me to keep, and there is nothing anywhere in this empire that would hold this except that book.** *You have been in rooms with about four thousand entries in eleven minute books and you did not know that.* And I have known it since the second week of the ninth month, standing at a counter, where a clerk of thirty-four told me what a representative is and would not write it down, and she was right, and **this morning I have found somebody else who is carrying the same thing for the same reason.** Then she writes it at the table, on a page at the back of the book of eleven houses, in her own hand, with the day on it, **and she reads it back once and does not read it twice**, because the second reading is a rule about something a room decided and this is not a room and there are only two of us in it and one of us cannot be found. And then four lines at the foot of the page, which are the reason, and she turns the book round and pushes it across the table so that he can read them, which nobody has ever asked her to do. *A person who is paid to read is a person who can be told to stop. There is no post whose job is to ask. — N. Kest, second day of the first week of the first month of the year after next.* And the close: the year after next had been four days old, nobody had thanked her and she had not asked, **she was answerable, and he was answerable, and there were four askings in a hundred and forty years and no post and no plan, and it would not happen again by itself.**

## Chapter 216 — "The Thing He Wrote Down In Order To Be Refused" (2,908)

**POV: Marek Kest. A rented room with a table in it, a book with no office on it and about four feet of a wall he does not use, the fourth day of the second week of the first month of the year after next.** Thirty-eight, **no office and no fund and no register and nothing in this empire he could certify anything with, and a bar of his own that came off him on the twelfth of the ninth month of last year on an application of one line which he wrote himself**, and **a line about two inches long on the inside of his left wrist that reads nothing, decides nothing, and does not know where the ford is.** Tamsin Rook is in the room because two instruments require it and they are not one instrument. He could not sleep much on the night of the second day of the first week and that was nothing unusual, and on the fourth day of the second week he wrote a thing down and put a day against it in about nine seconds and had been about four days deciding to, and the whole of the four days was the question of whether doing it was fair to the woman. He asks her to answer in a room, in words, with a date, **and it is the rule of the twelfth month of last year and it is not a form and it is not on her office and it is the only instrument either of us owns, and I am going to put it in writing with a day on it and I am not going to write the day against the line.** Then the choice, in ink: *Either I write down what I said to a woman in this room on the second day of the first week of this month, and stand in front of whoever comes and be asked what I meant by it, or I do not. If I write it down then it is a document and I am a person with a document, and in about four years a man with a copy of the right page can put it beside the return that made her and ask me why a man with no office answered a question about a box. — M.K.* She reads it twice and puts her pen down beside it, which she did last time. *My answer is no, and the date is today, and I am going to give you the reason and then I am not going to discuss it.* **A document with your hand at the foot of it does not stay about you. That is the whole of what I have been trying to tell you since the second month and you have not believed a word of it.** In about four years there are two of them in the same thing: a sheet of a man's hand saying what he said to a woman about a word on a box, and a return with a column filled in at the other end with a woman's name in it that a clerk filled in in about nine seconds in the fifth month of the year after. A man with a copy of the right page does not have to know anything about either of them. **If you write that down she is findable from a page of a man with no office, and you would be doing to her the identical thing that was done to her in the fifth month, in about nine seconds, by a person who was not a villain and who is sitting at this table.** He does not argue, and she watches him not argue, **and about four hours after that she would work out for the second time in three days that it is the only evidence she has ever had of anybody's judgment and she had still not decided what to do with it.** *That is a good reason.* **It is a fact. And you have asked me this once before and I refused you in the second week of the ninth month of the year after, and you wrote that one in order to be refused as well, and you told me so afterwards, and it is the only reason I have believed a document you wrote.** *So I have written two things down in a book with no office on it in order to be refused, and I have had two real answers, and there is no office to appeal to.* **There is no post in this empire whose business it is to ask whether I was right. That is not a complaint about you.** Then the wrist, and: **Then it goes in a room and not on a page, and I am not going to thank you for telling me that you have nothing, because there is no form anywhere in this empire that requires a person to be thanked and I have asked you in advance not to and you are not going to.** Then the third thing, the one he had come to say: **I am not going to go and tell her.** A woman of twenty walked about nine miles and asked him a question and he could not answer it and has been answerable for four days for a thing he does not know, and the answer is nothing, **because there is no fund and there is no form for a fund and I have got about a fortnight's money in a drawer and a book with no office on it.** He cannot pay her, cannot buy her a copy at fourpence, cannot pay her a shilling for a question, cannot send her four hundred and thirty miles with a carriage, and **there is nothing anybody can instruct me about and nothing anybody can pay me for, and I said that out loud in this room in the third week of the tenth month of the year after and I am not going to improve it by finding a way to be generous with a person who cannot be protected.** And: **in the second week of the eleventh month she decided to be the person who knows how the box got filled and not to be a person who knows it alone, and the minute I walk about nine miles and tell her what she has become, she has a person to hand it to, and that is the end of the thing she decided and it would be me ending it for her.** *She has three other people.* **She has two other people and one of them is four hundred and thirty miles up this river with a board and a basket and no fund, and the other is four hundred and thirty miles down it at a window, and I have not met either of them and I am not going to, and about four years from now she is going to find out that she chose well or badly and I am not going to be what finds out.** Then she names the other thing, at about the seventh hour: *You could stand in the room where the boxes get filled. Nine miles.* **No.** *That was fast.* **I have been thinking about it for four days and I have got a reason and it is yours. Being served is a party. A party is the only person who can be told what a thing is going to be used for, and I do not know what that thing is going to be used for, and a man with no office and no register who walks into a building off the old river road and asks a clerk what a box is for is asking to be served, and about four years later a man with a copy of the right page will be able to say that he came asking, and there is no way in this empire to come out of a party once you are in it. And I have said the twelfth line is going to stay empty because there is no post whose job is to ask, and I am not going to be the man who walks into a building to find out whether there is one.** *That is consistent. It is also the first decision you have made in about two years that you did not make in order to be caught at it, and I have not got a rule about what to do with that, and I am not going to invent one at about the seventh hour on a day when I have been asked a question I cannot answer.* Then: she is gone six minutes, because of the paper and not the watch, and he says which one it was out loud to an empty room, **because a form gets merged by being inconvenient and he had been letting two instruments get merged in his own head for about four days.** A paper made in a form in four days with a day on it; the watch does not send anybody anywhere. Then he opens the book. Eleven lines with a day against the sheet, a twelfth with nothing on it, and he has not read the eleventh line out loud to anybody since the third week of the ninth month of the year after, and the eleventh line is the one about what a person of twenty has been put into, and she read it in that room and let him, and neither of them said anything about it for about a minute. **The eleventh line had stopped being a question. It had become a fact, and a fact on a line in a book with no office on it is the worst of the two, because a question can be answered and a fact can only be repeated.** He reads it to himself once, out loud, in about four seconds, and shuts the book with the twelfth line still empty. And when she comes back: *I did not read you the eleventh line while you were out.* **I know you did not. I heard you not read it through the door, and I am not going to ask you why and I would like it entered that I did not ask.** *Because you would be asking me to say a thing about a woman of twenty out loud in a room, and the only person in the room who could contradict me is her, and she is not in the room, and I would like it entered that I noticed that too and that I still did not read it.* Then the book with the choice in it goes into the book with no office on it at the back, after the four definitions, with the day on it: **the rule of the twelfth month used once, in writing, with a day on it, the answer no, given in about a minute by a person who had already thought about it, he did not argue, and it is the second time.** *And I have not said a word about the twelve questions on your sheet, and the twelfth line is still empty, and I would like it read back to me now, in this room, in words, whether you think that is cowardice.* **It is not, and it is the second time I have said that to you and I am not going to be thanked for saying it, and the twelfth line is still empty, and I have not ruled a third box and I am not going to.** And the last: *Four.* **Four. Four in about a hundred and forty years and no post and no plan, and three of them are a year old or more, and the fourth is a fortnight old, and it was the first one anybody did on purpose, and I am not going to be one of the three of us who is standing in a room saying it will not happen again by itself while the one person it happened to has her wage held about four hundred and thirty miles from here.**

## Chapter 217 — "Nine Years Of It And Nobody Wrote It Down" (2,795)

**POV: Halla Wray. The Slade end, a bay, the second day of the third week of the first month of the year after next.** Fifty-one, foreman of the Slade Cut, an office with no office in it, on that bank since she was nine, **can read and nobody at the district works has ever once in nine years asked her to read anything.** The coming season's list of works is made in the bay in about four minutes and the four are on it as four men whose work is on the list and who are not in the bay while it is read. She had known since the fourth day of the fourth week of the twelfth month that she had said a whole sentence out loud in a room to a man with a satchel, and had about five weeks to do something about it and had not, and worked out on the morning of the second day why: **there was nothing in the world she could have done about it.** Then a man of about forty from the third gang asks a man of about fifty-five a question about the water, standing where he is, and the man of about fifty-five looks at the bench for about two seconds, and Halla Wray answers it from behind him without turning round and in about four seconds flat, in a foreman's voice, in the plainest words there are, and the man of about forty accepts it and goes back to what he was doing, and nobody in that shed notices anything at all, and that is what a foreman is. **She has been doing that for nine years. She did it that week in the fourth week of the twelfth month, and she has done it since she was forty-two, and nobody has ever asked her to, and about nine men have seen it, and nobody has ever written it down, and she is the only person in this empire who knows it**, and she worked that out at about the ninth hour standing in a bay with a list of works in front of her. *There.* **There is the answer to the question. It has been here the whole time and it is not a form and it is not a post and it is not a person asking anybody anything, and it costs nothing and nobody can be told off for it, and it has been running for nine years without anybody deciding to.** Then the two decisions she is not going to take: **She is not going to ask the book-keeper whether he is going to keep doing it**, because asking is the only instrument there is and she has watched it cost a man of about thirty-four an afternoon and a woman of twenty about nine miles of walking, **and I am not going to spend either of those on a thing I could hear about in a bay in about four minutes.** And the bigger one: **She is not going to tell the girl of seventeen.** She is on a written engagement, there is a copy in a satchel with a date on it, nobody has ever thanked her and there is no form anywhere that requires it, she reads better than anybody in that bay, she is at the same rate as everybody else on the list, and Halla Wray has known her since she was about eleven and has never once asked her to read anything. And a book-keeper worked out in the second week of the tenth month of the year after that she was the one way of reaching the four, and said so out loud in that bay, and did not do it, and wrote down that he was not going to and read it back twice, **and the reason he gave was that a person who is paid to read is a person who can be told to stop; Halla Wray credited that argument in the second week of the eleventh month without pointing at her, and has not improved it since, and is not going to.** She could have said in about four seconds: *you are the one person here who could read that column to four men*, and it would have been true and correct and ordinary, and no foreman is stopped from saying a correct thing in the ordinary way. **And she is not going to, and the reason is that the moment I say it to her she is a person who has been asked about it, and she is paid, and that is the whole of the argument in one act. He took nine days and a written finding to get to it. I have just got it out of my mouth at about the ninth hour and it took me five weeks and a man with a satchel.** And afterwards, in about four years, a man with a copy of the right page can ask a foreman of fifty-one what she said to a girl of seventeen in a bay, and the foreman will have to say it, and the girl will have to hear that she was asked about it, and neither will be able to say nobody put it in her. **I would rather be the woman in this bay that nobody ever says one word about than the woman who said one word to the only person in it who reads for money. That is not brave and I know it is not brave. It is the same shape as the reason I gave about the four and it is the same bad reason, and I have now got two of them and they are the same one, and a woman with two bad reasons is not a woman with one good one.** Then the ordinary things, in order, because a foreman who stops doing them is a foreman who has begun to make a speech of her own job: the count of the works, the water up about a foot since the twelfth month, the hold against a company whose whole money is four shillings a year and all of it the rent of a building and which has not moved since the fourth week of the fourth month, the factor's letter **not going to be answered and every day it is not answered is a day nobody has been entered**, the nineteen reasons in a column with a day against every one and the names in a different book with about nine hundred and forty of them in nine hands over about sixty years, **a bill at Lowcross at nineteen pounds three and fourpence, unpaid, nobody liable, and no line for a bridge in that fund in nineteen years**, the guarantee standing offered and unanswered on about four hundred and forty foot of bank with about sixty children under sixteen inside it and inside a guild's blank list and inside a rotation they have not been asked about, **and the thirty-one of Mosswake, which is thirty-one, and which is another district's figure and which she said once and moved on from, and about nine men in that bay do not know whose it is and are not going to be told, because there is no form anywhere in this empire for a foreman to explain another district's number to a room full of men who have never crossed it.** Then the other thing: **There is a man in this bay who had a piece of paper read to him by a book-keeper in the first week of the twelfth month of the year after, and nobody wrote a word about it down, and the book-keeper has told me nothing about it and I have asked him nothing, and I know about it because a foreman on a bank knows everything a bay says by about the second hour, and that is the whole of how I know. He is one of the four. He is one of the four and he has had a piece of paper read to him and nothing was written down and he is not going to be asked about the hold this season and neither am I going to ask him about the paper. And I want it said in a bay that both of those are decisions and neither of them is mine.** And: **I am not going to say his name in a room and there is no form anywhere in this empire that requires a foreman to say a man's name to nine men, and the reason I have just given about the girl of seventeen is the reason I am not going to say his name about the paper, and it is the same reason three times over, and a woman who has found the same reason three times has not been thinking, she has been refusing.** Then the bay, after: a man of about fifty-five was in it for the reading, his work was in it, she read it the way she reads everything, and afterwards he asked her what the day under it meant, because there is a day against every line of a list of works and he has never once asked anybody what a day is for. *I meant whether it is the day it started or the day somebody decided.* **Then somebody decided. Then somebody decided, and you have just worked that out in about nine seconds at about the ninth hour in a bay, and there is no form anywhere in this empire that requires a man to work that out and there never has been one, and I have never once been asked to help anybody work it out before and I have been doing it since I was forty-two.** He said thank you and she has not been thanked in nine years and told him not to, and he said he had not meant it as anything. **And she had done it four times in about a quarter of an hour, on purpose, in a room, to a man who cannot read a paragraph, about a day on a list, and she has not written a word of it down, and she is not going to, and the four of them have still never been asked what the hold is.** And last, at the bench, with the lamp not lit, which is later than it ought to be, with one sheet of her own hand in a book of her own, six numbered lines and a day against it and no name on it, and the notice on the bench with a seal and nothing under the seal, **and the two of them are two sheets and only one of them is in her hand**: **Four askings in about a hundred and forty years and no post anywhere in this empire whose job is to ask**, a court room in the fifth month that wanted a record, a window in the first week of the tenth, a desk in the second week of the eleventh that a woman of twenty walked four miles to, and a rented room in the first week of the first month that the same woman walked nine miles to. **Two of the four were accidents. The third was on purpose. The fourth was on purpose and she did it on her own account and nobody sent her**, and I have not been told her name and I have not asked and I am not going to, and there is no post and there is not going to be one, and it will not happen again by itself. And a book-keeper on her own bank had read a man's own paper to him in a yard and written nothing down, **and she had been answering a man of about forty from behind a bench in about four seconds flat for nine years without being asked, and neither of those is one of the four, and neither of them is a form, and neither of them has anybody's name in it.** **Somebody asks, or nobody asks. That is still the whole of it. And the answer that has come out of this bank since the second week of the eleventh month of the year after is not a person. It is a habit that two people have and neither of them has appointed and neither of them has written down, and I have not decided whether that is better and I am not going to decide it in a bay at about the seventh hour with the lamp off.**

## Chapter 218 — "An Undertaking Agreed And No Form For A Fund" (2,864)

**POV: Tamsin Rook. Four bays, the fourth day of the fourth week of the first month of the year after next.** Twenty-four, a party to an instrument about a dead woman's name. **Two instruments require her in any room he is in and they are not one instrument and he does not merge them and she does not let him: the first is a paper made in a form in four days with a day on it, and the second is a watch that does not name him and does not name her and requires only that a person who is not from the office that cannot be named be present. About six hundred people in this city could satisfy the watch. She has satisfied it every time it has been called for and nobody has ever paid her for it.** He has a sheet of paper in his hand and wants to put it on her desk and she makes him hold it. *Read it before it goes. Read it in front of me. And if you have a reason against it, say the reason in a room and out loud and not on a page.* He has asked her to come to a counter four bays along and she has said she will not and said why, and he has come anyway. **I want to buy paper.** She puts her pen down. *You have a room with a table in it and about four feet of a wall you do not use, and I have a press in the next bay with about six hundred printed slips in it that say the fourth line is not to be completed by this office, and there are about four hundred blanks in a box under a counter four bays along. A copy is fourpence. A question is a shilling at a notary's table. I have worked out that in about nine hundred buildings in this empire there is a printed form that nobody has ever shown to a person, and that the only instrument anybody has ever found for saying no to a box is somebody asking a question out loud,** and the two have never been in the same room in about a hundred and forty years. **And the reason it has never been done is not money. It is that nobody thinks of a form as a thing you can hold.** A clerk of thirty-four stands behind a slab in this city four bays along with a fee board on it with four things written on it and none of them is time, and those four words are printed, and every person who reads them in a year reads a heading they have never been asked about, **and there is no post in this empire whose business it is to ask what a word on a board means, and the reason there is not is that a board is not a form, and a person does not think of a board as a thing that can be asked a question.** She did not say no straight away and that is on the page. *You know I am not going to be able to do it.* **I do not think you are going to be able to do it either. I have not got any money.** *I am telling you what I want and it is paper and I have not got the price of it, and a price is a small thing to say out loud in a room and it took me about a fortnight to be able to say it.* Then the reason, and she reads the four definitions twice and a third time which he had not asked for: **You are not going to buy anything with this. No. I am going to hold it. That is the entire instrument and there is nothing behind it and there is not going to be anything behind it,** and what he is proposing is that a person should be able to hold a printed form in a hand and not have to ask anybody to read it to them, **and that is a thing about paper and not about anybody's duty, and there is no post in it and there is no fund and there is no form.** *And you have brought it to a clerk of twenty-four.* **I did say that I would not go and ask anybody anything, and I said I would say no, and I am not going to unsay it, and nobody is going to ask me and I have made sure of that myself and I would like it written down that I did. And you have not asked me. You have brought me a piece of paper and a reason and you have stood in a bay and waited for me to say something about it, and that is the correct use of a room and it is the whole of what there is.** *Agreed*, written, with the day on it, in her own hand, the fourth day of the fourth week of the first month of the year after next. Then the count, itemised on a counter in about four minutes, because she is a person who counts and he is a person who counts and there is no form anywhere in this empire for counting anything: **one, a court room in the fifth month of the year after, and the room wanted a record; two, a clerk's window in the first week of the tenth month, and a man was afraid about his own household; three, a desk in the second week of the eleventh month, and a woman of twenty walked about four miles and nobody sent her; four, a rented room in the first week of the first month, and the same woman walked about nine miles and nobody sent her. Four in about a hundred and forty years. Three of them are a year old or more. One of them is a fortnight old. Two of the four were accidents and nobody chose either of them, and the other two were on purpose, and one of the two was done by the same person as the other.** And then: **in the four weeks since the fourth one, nobody has asked anybody anything. Not at this counter. Not at the one four bays along. Not in a bay, not at a window, not in a shed, not in a rented room.** And: **That is not a finding about people. That is a finding about what happens when a thing happens once. It will not happen again by itself. And the reason it did not spread is not that nobody wanted to know. It is that there is no way to want to know a thing you have not heard about, and there is no way to hear about it, and the only way anybody found out about the first three was to be in a room where somebody else was asking.** Then a man comes in for a copy at fourpence and is served in about two minutes and does not ask her anything, and the shape of it: **A room gets a day. A person can come up to a counter, be served in it, ask in it, and walk out of it, and there is nothing on the board under the rail and no fee and no form that says what may be asked at it and none that says what may not. And in the whole of the time this counter has stood nobody has asked at it, and the reason nobody has asked is not that they do not want to know. It is that a person who wants to know something at a counter does not come to a counter. They come to a counter to buy fourpence worth of paper, and they would be ashamed to stand there and use up a minute of a clerk's time for nothing, and there is no form anywhere in this empire that a person can put in front of a clerk saying I have a question and I have not got a shilling, and there is no shilling's worth of nothing in the world.** And: **the reason I have not said anything to any of them is that a clerk of this table is paid, and a person who is paid can be told to stop, and a person who is paid can be shown the day she answered and the words she used and cannot say no to any of it. And I have said that reason out loud on a bank about four hundred and thirty miles down this river and a book-keeper said it before me, and I am not going to say it as though I thought of it, and I am not going to improve it. And that is the answer to who asks, and it is the fourth time this year that the answer has come out the same way, and I am the second person in this matter to have arrived at it and neither of us appointed anybody.** Then, in the room, before the price: **And I am not going to be a room that knows a thing can be asked**, and the rest of it, and the two boxes in her book with the same name in each, **and they are the paper and the watch and they are not one instrument and they are not this piece of paper, and I have not ruled a third and I am not going to. A person who rules a box for every thing that happens to her in a year has turned a book into a form, and I would not be the first clerk in this city to do that and I would like to be the last.** Then the price, standing, because he has not asked her a question at all and that cost more: **I have said the price of being a party out loud ten times and nobody has thanked me once, and I did not expect to be thanked once and I would like it written down that I did not. And there is one thing left and I am going to say it and then I am going to serve the man at the counter who has been standing there for about four minutes, and he has a slip with a reference on the top of it and he is going to pay fourpence and he is not going to ask me anything, and about four hundred of those are bought and filled in in a year and not one of them is a question.** And the debt that is not discharged: **You have never once asked me whether I have decided whether to trust your judgment, and I have never told you that I have not, and both of those are the same silence and it has been going on for a long time, and I am not going to decide it in a bay at about the ninth hour, and the decision is not going to be made in a room and it is not going to be written down. You have now been refused by me in a room in writing twice and you have not argued once, and that is two pieces of evidence, and two is not a decision, and a woman who treats two as a decision is a woman who has been alone too long.** She serves the man, he pays fourpence, she reads his copy out, he says it is right, he goes. **A piece of paper was agreed in a bay and could not be bought, and the undertaking of the fourth of the first month had been done for the sixth time, and the reason was the best one either of them has ever brought her, and it is a reason about paper.**

## Chapter 219 — "A Question Is Not On The Board" (2,927)

**POV: Marn Ottery. The fourth counter of the Notaries' Table in Auremar, the fourth day of the first week of the second month of the year after next.** Thirty-four, eleven years at that counter, which is the one for scale instruments and has been for about a hundred and forty years, **came to it from the second counter, where estates are; not a lawyer and does not want to be one; a party to an instrument about a dead woman's name; and there is no form in this empire for a document about a person who did not ask to be in one, which she knows better than anybody in this city and has had a woman of twenty tell her so to her face in the ninth month of the year after.** About four hundred blanks in a box under the counter bought and filled in, a book of forms on the shelf under that, **and a fee board with four things on it and none of them is time.** She is on her own at the rail from the ninth hour until about the eleventh, makes nine copies and sells four blanks, and **not one of the thirteen asks her anything.** First, the part she has been thinking about since the ninth month, thought out while she wipes the slab: a woman of twenty came up to this counter three times that month, and the first two times she stood at the rail and looked at the board and went away, and a clerk notices that the way a clerk notices everything, which is to say she notices it and does nothing about it for about eleven days. **That was not the same as not asking. That was the board working exactly as it is printed, and the board is printed to be a list of what a thing costs, and a person can stand in front of a list of what a thing costs for about a minute and a half and work out in about nine seconds that nothing on it is free, and then there is no way at all to stand there, and so she goes away, and I have watched about nine people a year do it and not one of them has ever come back and told me why.** And: **And the reason I could not put a free question on that board, and the reason she had to come three times, is the same sentence, and it is the sentence about being identified,** and it took me the second week of the ninth month, the second week of the eleventh, a man of sixty and a knife in a drawer to get to it, **and nobody in this matter has said it out loud yet, and I am not going to be the one who says it in a room where it goes in a book.** Then a woman of about thirty-five asks a plain question about how long a thing stays on the counter, gets four sentences in the plainest words, and says thank you, and is thanked anyway when told there is nothing to thank her for. **Nobody has thanked her once in eleven years at that counter and a woman of thirty-five did it in about four seconds in the first week of this month, and Marn Ottery has not got a rule about that and did not have one about the other thing and is not going to get one now.** Then the man who has been coming for years: **He is not ashamed of buying fourpence worth of paper. He is ashamed of asking a question that costs him a minute of a stranger's time and nothing else.** There is a difference, and the difference is the whole of this counter and the whole of this matter, and she has never in eleven years been able to put it into a sentence a customer could read. At about the tenth hour he asks, unexpectedly, *Are you all right to be asked something*, and she puts the copy down face up. **I am going to answer that in about four minutes and out loud and for nothing, and I am going to say the price first, and I am not going to write any of it down. Here is the price: a person who asks a question about a form in a room becomes a person somebody has answered, and there is no instrument anywhere in this empire that takes that back off him** — and she has said it to two people in this city since the second day of the second week of the ninth month of the year after, and one of them said afterwards that he would rather not have asked, and that was the correct answer. *Have you had this before.* **No. Three times, in about a hundred and forty years, in this empire.** A court room in the fifth month of the year after that wanted a record, a clerk's window in the first week of the tenth, a desk in the second week of the eleventh that a woman of twenty walked about four miles to. **Two of the three were accidents and nobody chose either of them and one was on purpose and nobody sent her, and there is no post in this empire whose job is to ask, and it will not happen again by itself.** *Then I had better not.* **That is a decision and it is yours and I am not going to argue with a man of sixty about it, and there is no form anywhere in this empire that entitles anybody to be troubled a second time about it, and I am not going to trouble you about it again.** Then the thing she had worked out on the fourth day: **You may ask me anything. Not because of anything that has happened in another county, and not because a woman of twenty asked me a question in the ninth month of the year after and I answered it and could not write it down. Ask me because I have been at this counter eleven years and I have said that sentence to two people since the ninth month, and there has been a hundred and forty years of a board over my head with four things on it and none of them is a question, and I have never once had the nerve to say out loud that a person may stand here and use up a minute of my time for nothing.** *Why is it about you and not about me.* **Because a person who is paid to read is a person who can be told to stop, and a person who is paid to answer is the same thing with a different word on it.** I have been paid to answer for eleven years and have never been asked to, have said the price every time and answered anyway, **and I would like it said somewhere that a clerk of this table is the cheapest person in this city to send and nobody has ever sent me.** And: **I have said that I would not go and ask anybody anything, and I said it in a room to a woman of twenty-four in the third week of the tenth month of the year after, and I am not going to unsay it, and nobody is going to ask me, and I have made sure of that myself. So it is about me, and I am not going to be a post, and there is no post, and a person who appoints somebody to a post that does not exist is doing the thing the whole of this is about, which is filling in a box the way the box is printed.** Then he looks at the board. *Is there anything on that board about a question.* No. **Then a man of sixty has to be told he may ask, out loud, by a clerk, once, before he dares, and he has to be told it by a person and not by a slip, and there is nothing at that counter to point at. That is the whole of the finding and I have arrived at it at about the fourth minute past ten of a day in the first week of this month —** He stopped, and said he had not been here today, and put his hat on, and did not say thank you, and was not thanked, and went. **And he did not ask her a single question. She had told him in about nine sentences that he could, and he had used none of it,** and he had found the shape of the whole thing out loud in a room in about four minutes, and she has thought about that for a fortnight and is not going to improve on it. Then the decision. She takes a blank out of the box and looks at the printed strip along the top, **and it takes about four seconds to cut a line into it with a knife, and she has the knife in the drawer because it is the same knife she uses for the box. She did not cut it.** **A question is not going on the board.** Not because I have not been asked one since the ninth month, and not because it is a good idea, and not because it would cost nothing, and not because there is no post, though there is no post.
