A person who is charged for asking will not ask, and that took about a fortnight; a shilling is on that board for a question at a notary's table and there are about nine hundred of those tables in this empire, and if the asking is on the board here then it is on the boards of all of them, and then a man with a wife and a boy stands at a rail and does the sum, and the sum is that he cannot afford to be identified. **A free answer is the only thing in this empire that leaves nobody findable.** The moment there is a price on it, the person who pays has a receipt, and there is no form anywhere in this empire for a receipt about a question. The blank goes back in the box, and the box is under the counter, **and the counter is the only place in this city where a person can come up, ask a question, and walk out with nothing.** And then the second half, said to an empty counter: **A board is not a form and that is the whole reason nobody asks at it.** A form is a thing that happens to a person, printed in about nine hundred buildings, filled in by somebody else, with a box on it a person can be put in; a board is a list of what a thing costs, and a list of what a thing costs is the friendliest piece of furniture in this empire, and it is the reason a person can stand at a rail for a minute and a half and not be ashamed, and if I put a question on it I turn the friendliest thing in this empire into the thing a woman of twenty stood in front of three times in the ninth month of the year after and could not use. **And there is a line on the way to that which I have not seen anybody take, and I am not taking it now, and I want it said that I know what it is and that it is not a form and that it is not a post and that nobody sent me to think about it. A clerk of a notary's table can stand up in a public room and say, once, in front of about nine people, that a person may come and ask a question, and about nine hundred clerks can do that, and none of them has, and the reason none of them has is that saying it in a room is a thing a room writes down. So it goes on the counter and not in a room. That is the whole of where it goes.** And: **a question of mine that is free is the only thing I have that the office of a seat does not have, and I am not going to put a price on it and I am not going to write it down,** and I am not going to let a person in a room about four hundred and thirty miles from this counter decide that I should. **That is the decision, and it is mine, and it is a decision not to do a thing that would help, and I would like somebody to put that on a slate and read it back to me, and there is nobody here who is going to, and there is no form.** A man of about fifty comes in at about the eleventh hour and pays fourpence and goes. **The board over her head had four things on it and none of them was time, and none of them was a question, and she was not going to make it one, and a man of sixty had been in a room and had been told in nine sentences that he might ask and had not asked, and about four hundred blanks sat under her hand in a box, and a woman of twenty in a city about four hundred and thirty miles up this river had a book of eleven houses in it that nobody paid her to keep, and there is no post in this empire whose job is to ask, and the count is four, and it will not happen again by itself.**

## Chapter 220 — "The Woman Who Decides To Be Harder To Ask" (2,963)

**POV: Halla Wray. The Slade end, a bay and a shed, the fourth week of the second month of the year after next.** Fifty-one, foreman of the Slade Cut, an office with no office in it, on that bank since she was nine, can read and nobody has ever once in nine years asked her to read anything, **and in the third week of the first month of the year after next she worked out that she had been answering questions for four men in that bay since she was forty-two, without being asked, and that nobody had ever noticed, including her.** The water is up about two feet off the mark where it was in the twelfth month, and **there is no line for a bridge in the Lowcross fund and there has not been one in nineteen years.** The ordinary things, and then the thing she came to do, **and the two are not in that order in her own head and she has given up trying to put them in that order:** the count of the works in about four minutes with the men in it; the nineteen reasons in the third column of a book in a hired stone store off the Slade with a day against every one and no names in that column at all, and the names in a different book with about nine hundred and forty of them in nine hands over about sixty years, and a name in a room is a thing that can be carried out of a room; a factor's letter of four lines wanting a name that may be served and that name's consent, **not going to be answered, and every day it is not answered is a day nobody has been entered**, and a carter asked in the second week of the tenth month of the year after to have his own line written in the place where the no is, and went up the road for the winter, and is not coming back for the asking; a guarantee standing offered and unanswered on about four hundred and forty foot of bank with about sixty children under sixteen inside it, no such person has ever come forward, and she has not got the terms of it in her head and is not going to read them out in a bay at about the seventh hour; a bill at Lowcross at nineteen pounds three and fourpence, unpaid, nobody liable, and nobody in that bay is paying it and nobody is going to be asked for a penny; **and about four people in that bay who cannot read a paragraph, who are on the list of works, whose work is on the list, and who have still never been asked anything, and there is no column for them and there is not going to be one.** Then the day itself, with the man of about fifty-five in the bay and his work on the list read the way she reads everything, and afterwards his question about the day under it: *I meant whether it is the day it started or the day somebody decided.* **Then somebody decided. Then somebody decided,** and neither of them made anything else of it and about nine men in that bay did not hear it at all. **That is the fifth time in nine years. She has done it since she was forty-two and nobody asked her to and nobody has ever written it down, and she is the only person in this empire who knows it,** and a book-keeper of thirty-eight saw her do it in the fourth week of the twelfth month of the year after and did not understand it for about two hours, and has never been told that she knows. Then the count, said standing, with about nine men in the bay and one of the about four in it: *I told a book-keeper's face in a shed in the last week of the eleventh month of the year after that nobody had ever asked me what the words on a form mean, and it was true, and it was the only true thing I had said in a year.* **And a woman of sixty-three stood in a room in this city in the second week of the twelfth month of the year after and gave a clerk her own name out loud, and nobody sent her, and a clerk of about fifty-five said no when she was asked to go and look for her, and did not look, and was right, and has not said so to anybody.** And a man of about thirty-four stood at a window in the third week of the twelfth month and had the price said to him a second time and heard it the second time. And a woman of twenty walked about nine miles in the first week of the first month of the year after next and asked a man with no office a question out loud in a room because she had decided to and nobody sent her. **Four. A court room in the fifth month of the year after, a window in the first week of the tenth, a desk in the second week of the eleventh, and a rented room in the first week of the first month. Four in about a hundred and forty years and there is no post anywhere in this empire whose job is to ask,** and two of the four were accidents and nobody chose either of them, and the fourth was the first one anybody did on purpose, and the count has not moved since, and nothing has happened since, and it will not happen again by itself. **So the answer to who asks is that it is nobody's business, and there are four of them, and they were all found by accident or by a woman who decided on her own account, and not one of them was sent, and it will not happen again by itself.** Then it, out loud, in a room, without listing the five: **I am the person in this whole matter who has the most reason in the world to be asked about a thing. I have been in a box since the first week of the seventh month of the year after. I was not asked. And the only reason nobody has ever come and asked me is that there is no form in this empire with a space in it for a woman of fifty-one on a bank, and there is no post, and no way to serve me,** and no way for a person to stand in front of me and say the words out loud. **And I have been glad of that. I have been glad of it for about eleven weeks and I have not admitted it to anybody, and I am admitting it now because a man of about sixty in another city has just worked out that a person has to be told out loud, by a clerk, once, that they may ask, and he worked it out in about four minutes standing at a counter, and nobody told him, and he is not a lawyer and he is not a party and he is sixty.** And the decision: **And I have decided that I am not going to make myself easier to ask. That is the decision, and it is mine, and I made it in about four seconds, and I have not told anybody until now, and I am not going to be thanked for it and I am not going to be argued with, and I would like it read back to me by somebody in a room and there is nobody in this empire who is going to, and there is no form.** *Why not.* **Because of the same reason as the four, and worse, because the four cannot read a paragraph and I can, and if a person stands in front of me and asks me what the third line means then I am a woman who has been asked, and then I am a woman who has been answered, and there is no instrument anywhere in this empire that takes that back off me either. I would be found. That is the whole of it. I have spent forty-two years being unfindable and I said in this shed in the fourth week of the ninth month of the year after that I would like to be found, and I meant it,** and I am going to hold both of those at once for the rest of my life and it is not going to be comfortable and it is not going to be a rule. **And a foreman who has been found is a foreman somebody can be asked about the four, and I have already given one reason for not asking them and it was a bad one, and I gave a second one about a girl of seventeen in the third week of the first month and it was the same bad reason twice, and I am not going to hand a third one to a person in a room who writes it down.** Then she says it before anybody can: **And it is the wrong decision, and I know exactly what the right one looked like, and it was a woman of twenty walking about four miles to a desk in the second week of the eleventh month of the year after and asking how the box got filled.** Nobody sent her and nobody told her to and there is no form for it and she did it on her own account and nobody appointed her, and she is the only reason I know what I am, and I am not going to be able to say that to anybody else. **And I have not asked her. She has not come to this bay. About four hundred and thirty miles of road is what it costs anybody who wants to come and see a page in a ledger, and there is no fund and no form for a fund, and I have said out loud that I am not going to be the reason four other people are found, and that still stands and nobody has talked me out of it.** And I have now also decided not to be found myself. **A woman of fifty-one in a shed in the fourth week of the second month of the year after next has arrived at two bad reasons and one wrong decision, and she is going to have to live in the room where all three of them are.** Then the ordinary thing again: a man of about fifty-five comes in with a chain and asks about the third link, and it takes about two minutes, and every man in that shed watched a foreman do a perfectly ordinary thing to a man who cannot read a paragraph. **And she did not ask him.** Not about the hold, not about the season, not about the two sheets on the bench with a seal and nothing under the seal. And a book-keeper had read a piece of that man's own paper to him in a yard in the first week of the twelfth month of the year after and had written nothing down and had told nobody, and she knew, and she was not going to ask him about it, and the reason is the same reason she was not going to ask the book-keeper in the third week of the first month of the year after next: **asking is the only instrument there is, and I am not going to spend it on a thing I could hear about in a bay in about four minutes, and I have not spent it once in about nine years and neither has anybody else on that bank.** Then a scene at the seventh hour: a man of about fifty from the fourth gang wants to cross to Lowcross and the bridge is shut and has been shut since before the water came in and *that is not a reason the bridge knows about*, and he has a reason and it is that he has not been over it in about three weeks and there is a thing at the far end he wants, and **that is not a reason and I am not going to ask you for another one, and there is no form in this empire that requires a man to give a better reason than I want to get over there, and I have read every form in that store and there is not one page in any of them that says a person has to give you a better reason than that.** *That is the reason I am still here. You have said that in this shed as many times this year as there are weeks in the season and I have counted them and I have never been asked to count them out loud and I am not going to be.* **Nobody is going to ask you to count them out loud. If they do, there is no form for it and you do not have to help them.** And then, from a bench in a hired stone store off the Slade, **the third column of that ledger has nineteen reasons in it with a day against every one of them, and one of the nineteen is a man who wanted to get over a bridge, and the reason is in the book, and it is the same reason he gave in the seventh month, and nobody has asked him again and nobody is going to. A bill at nineteen pounds three and fourpence with no line against it in nineteen years and a foreman who will not ask a man for a better reason than he has got, and those two facts have been standing on that bank since before the woman of twenty was born and neither of them is going to be paid and neither of them is going to be forgiven,** and most of the men in that bay know both of them and about nine hundred yards away there is a woman of twenty with a wage held about four hundred and thirty miles from her own door. Then the girl of seventeen at the back of the bay on her fourth day, on a written engagement, at the same rate as everybody else on the list, not thanked, did not ask, not going to start, nobody spoke to her about the season, **and the foreman of fifty-one looked at the back of her bay twice in about four minutes and did not go over.** And the close: **And the whole of the second season and everything that came after it is on a bank about four hundred and thirty miles down this river, and about four people in a bay cannot read a paragraph,** and a reader of seventeen is the one person on that bank who is the wrong person to ask and the only one who is free to answer, and nobody sent anybody to her and nobody is going to, and there is no post in this empire whose job is to ask, and the count is four, and a foreman of fifty-one has just said out loud in a room that she is going to make herself harder to find, and the lamp is not lit yet, and that is the end of the movement and it is not the end of anything.

## The Volume 05 Batch 0002 review repair, and the nine summaries above it

**The word counts in the headings for Chapters 212 to 220 are the post-repair measurements, taken with `sed 's/[[:space:]]*$//' file | wc -w` after every chapter-level edit was finished. Nine of the ten changed, by at most forty-five words and by as little as one.** Chapter 211 is unchanged at 3,116 because the repair did not touch it. **The batch total is 29,517 and Volume 05 stands at 58,307 across twenty chapters.** No summary above this line is rewritten and no chapter's situation, decision or ending changed.

**Four of the corrections change what a summary ought to say, and are recorded here because the summaries themselves were written before the repair and are not restated:**

- **The elapsed figure for the fourth asking is now consistent across Chapters 213, 216, 218, 219 and 220** — about nine weeks, nine days, three weeks, the same morning, and about seven weeks respectively — and **Chapters 216 and 218 no longer say the first three askings are a year old or more, because no anchor supports it.** The first three are all in the year before the fourth. The summaries above still carry whatever figure they carried; **the figures on the page are the ones that govern.**
- **Chapter 219's summary reflects a count that was wrong on the page and is now four** in a clerk's mouth, matching its own closing paragraph.
- **Chapter 218's summary reflects two hand-ruled boxes that were merged with the paper and the watch and are now separate from both**, which is what Volume 04's record and the Batch 0003 lock both require.
- **Chapter 213's summary reflects a rule that had been given to the reader of seventeen and is now given to the book-keeper who wrote it down in his own hand in Chapter 0211**, which is where the rule is made on the page.
